Scripta Tychonis — The writings of Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) in the edition of 2019: a catalogue, with the texts

The 57 texts that Peter Zeeberg and Finn Gredal Jensen edited for Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab beyond the correspondence — 33 records of poems and inscriptions, the Copenhagen oration of 1574, the three royal nativities, the almanac for 1573, the recipes, the polemic against John Craig, and two of the printed books given whole, De nova stella (1573) and the Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (1598), with the prefaces, poems and descriptions that frame the third, the Epistolae astronomicae (1596), whose letters are in the Epistolarium. For each text: its form and its date with the evidence for it, its addressee and occasion, how it was transmitted and where it was first printed, its place in Dreyer’s Opera omnia and in the earlier catalogues, how securely it is attested, and what remains open. Each text is given in full on a page of its own, the edition’s Latin with every line and paragraph numbered for citation. The Danish translations and the editors' notes are the edition's and are read at the source, linked section by section.

57 texts · 33 poems and inscriptions (45 pieces) · 56 given in full, 1 in its non-letter parts · 10 with a Danish translation in the edition · 29 records researched (A 17 · B 12), 28 not yet · 15 dates corrected against the edition · 50 sources

1Introduction

This is a catalogue of the 57 texts of Tycho Brahe that the Danish critical edition of his writings prints beyond the correspondence: the web edition prepared by Peter Zeeberg and Finn Gredal Jensen for Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab in 2019. The edition's selection is the catalogue's scope. It holds the poems and inscriptions, the Copenhagen oration of 1574, the three royal nativities, the almanac for 1573, the medical compositions, the polemic against John Craig, two of the printed books entire — De nova stella (1573) and the Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (1598) — and the poems, dedication, prefaces and descriptions that frame the third, the Epistolae astronomicae (1596), whose letters are read in the Epistolarium. What the edition does not hold — the comet treatise of 1588, the Progymnasmata, the star catalogue, the verse Tycho printed inside his letters and his other books — is listed with its place in Dreyer's Opera omnia and its home in this portal in §10.

For each text the catalogue states what it is, when and on what evidence it was written, for whom and on what occasion, by which channel it reached us and where it was first printed, its place in Dreyer's Opera omnia and in the earlier bibliographies, how securely the record is attested, and what remains open. Each text is then given in full on a page of its own — the edition's Latin, section by section, with the page breaks of the Opera omnia marked, every line and paragraph numbered for citation — as the object layer of this chapter. The books as printed objects are Typographica's; the letters are the Epistolarium's; the persons are Familia's; the places are Loca's; the instruments the Mechanica describes are Instrumenta's. This catalogue bridges to each of them and duplicates none.

The record is uneven, and the catalogue says so. 29 of the 57 records carry a full apparatus — summary, occasion, addressee, printing, transmission, references and open questions, graded on their evidence; the other 28 carry their identifying fields, the edition's own data and the computed fields, and no grade. The two states are marked on every record and in the catalogue table.

How to read an entry

What a text is here. A record is one book of the edition's series that is not a Danish translation of another book in it: the edition publishes 67 web books, of which 10 are Danish translations shown here beside their Latin, and one (Occasio et argumentum) is a Danish translation whose Latin the edition does not print and which therefore stands as a text of its own. The record is the edition's unit, not a count of Tycho's works: four records are editorial groupings of several pieces (four epigrams on the death of Frederik II; nine Uraniborg inscriptions; two Kronborg inscriptions; three recipes), one is the second recension of another record's poem, two are supplements to texts held elsewhere, four are prefaces or dedications, one is Tycho's translation of a poem by James VI, and two are whole printed books whose sections include pieces by other hands — a poem by Hans Frandsen, a letter of Pratensis, a poem by Anders Sørensen Vedel, the printer's note; Holger Rosenkrantz's poem, two letters of Jacob Kurz, two of Magini, an ode by Rudolphus Caukerchius. Every such section is headed with its author on the text page and in the sections table.

Numbering and order. Records are numbered 1–57 in the order of the register: the three periods of Tycho's life in sequence, and within each the date of composition, undated last. The number is stable and is the citation key together with the record's own key, which is the edition's slug (brahe-t_…) and the address every other page of this portal uses for the text.

Sections. A text page is divided as the edition divides it, one section per page of the web edition, numbered from the title page as section 1. The edition's own chapter numbers, where it prints them, are shown beside the section number: section 12 of De nova stella is the edition's chapter 11. The section number is what the citation and the links from the other pillars carry.

Forms and channels. Each record carries one of 18 forms (defined in the table below) and, where it is established, the channel by which the text reached us: printed in one of Tycho's own books, separately printed at his order, printed by others in his lifetime, printed after his death, or in manuscript until the Opera omnia — Zeeberg's own account of the transmission, as this catalogue partitions it. A channel not yet established is left blank, never guessed.

Dates. Every date carries its basis and a certainty mark: secure where the text dates itself or two authorities agree; probable on one authority or an inference from the content; uncertain where authorities disagree or the bounds are wide; unknown where no source dates the text and the edition's year is a placement; the edition's where the edition's year has not been independently examined. Where research has corrected the edition's year, both are shown and the correction is stated in words; the 15 cases are gathered in §9.

Grades. A researched record is graded A–D on the evidence behind it, on the scale of the other pillars (A secure, B probable, C uncertain, D speculative). A record not yet researched carries no grade: its status is a state of work, not a judgement.

Text. The Latin is the edition's constituted text. Superscript figures on a text page are the edition's textual notes where this catalogue reproduces them; the page breaks of the Opera omnia and the witnesses' folios are marked inline. Prose is set in numbered paragraphs, verse in numbered lines with the pentameter indented; the four passages of De nova stella whose verses the web text runs together are set again in lines here, after the line breaks of Dreyer's edition, and each carries the note. A text of forty lines or fewer is printed entire in its register entry as well as on its own page.

What the figures are not

The count of 57 texts is the edition's row count and nothing more: it neither counts Tycho's works nor measures his output. 33 records of verse and inscriptions hold 45 separately transmitted pieces; the edition omits three pieces of Dreyer's Carmina and all the verse Dreyer prints inside the other volumes (§10), so no ratio of these figures is a completeness rate. "Given in full" means the edition's text: the figures of the 1573 almanac, the nativity charts and the woodcuts of the Mechanica are transmitted by the edition as placeholders and are not reproduced here; the Mechanica's woodcuts are seen in Instrumenta. The Epistolae astronomicae is given in its non-letter parts; its letters are the Epistolarium's. "In Tycho's own Danish" marks one text, the 1591 preface printed in Flemløs's book, which the edition prints among Tycho's writings although it speaks in Flemløs's name; the attribution is the edition's. The Danish beside the Latin is Peter Zeeberg's translation of 2019 where the edition names him, the edition's translation where it does not, and, for the Mechanica's instrument chapters, an older translation reproduced by the edition in a pre-1948 orthography whose translator the local copy does not name. Every text here but one is Latin; he also wrote Danish (the Flemløs preface, his letters home) and German (the comet tract of 1577, not in the edition of 2019).

The edition and its layers

Tycho's words are in the public domain, and so is the text of Dreyer's Opera omnia (1913–1929) on which the edition rests. The edition of 2019 adds four layers that are Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab's and the editors': the constituted Latin, which re-collates Dreyer's text against the witnesses; the editors' textual notes; Peter Zeeberg's explanatory commentary and biographical notes; and the Danish translations. This build reproduces the constituted Latin only. The layers it does not reproduce are read at the source, to which every text page links section by section; each page states, for every layer, what it carries and what it withholds. The Society's permission for the republication of its layers has been asked for and is recorded here when it is given; until then the translations and the notes stay at the source, and the commentary is never reproduced.

3Register

Every record in full, in the order of the catalogue: the edition's title and the full Latin heading where the record carries it, the English title, the form, the date with its basis and its certainty, the addressees and the occasion, the summary, the transmission and the first printing, the place in Dreyer's Opera omnia and in the bibliographies, the sections with their authors, the relations to other records, the apparatus counts, the references with what each supports, the open questions, and the links to the text, to the edition, to the printed witnesses and to the persons and places in the other pillars. Texts of forty lines or fewer are printed here entire; the text page remains the citable locus. A record not yet researched shows the fields it has and says so.

Early 1568–1576 — before the foundation of Uraniborg

Diarium anni 1573 — Diary for the year 1573

AlmanacsecureEarlyARead the text →brahe-t_diarium-anni-1573

Astrological-meteorological diary for the year 1573, casting horoscope figures for the solstices, equinoxes and lunations and judging the coming weather from them, opening with a forecast of a hard winter from the December 1572 solstice figures.

Full heading
Diarium astrologicum et metheorologicum anni a nato Christo 1573 ad loci longitudinem graduum 35, latitudinem graduum 56
Form

1572–1573 secure

Heading in the text 'DIARIUM ANNI MDLXXIII'; tekstnet publication year 1573;

Correction. Written in the autumn of 1572 for the year 1573 (this catalogue).

The almanac is for the year 1573 but was written in the autumn and early winter of 1572. Dreyer, TBOO I Prolegomena p. XII: in the autumn of 1572 Tycho 'accurato anni 1573 diario conscribendo multum temporis impenderat'. The prefatory epistle is dated 'Ex Musaeo nostro Herrizuadensi Anno 1572 Mense Decembri' (TBOO I p. 44) — i.e. Herrevad Abbey, December 1572. In his reply to Pratensis (spring 1573) Tycho calls it 'Diarium illud Astrologicum & Metheorologicum, a me circa elapsae hyemis initia elaboratum' (TBOO I p. 11). The year 1573 is the year the almanac covers, not the year of composition.

Language
Latin
Summary
A full astrological-meteorological almanac (Latin diarium) computed for the year 1573 at longitude 35 deg, latitude 56 deg — i.e. for Tycho's own place, Herrevad Abbey in Scania. It opens with a series of judicial figures: the horoscope of the winter solstice and of the new moons preceding each solstice and equinox, each followed by a prose prognostication of the coming season's weather (an 'aspera et horrida' winter, a temperate, dry and fertile spring, and so on). The bulk of it is a month-by-month day-by-day ephemeris in ruled columns: sunrise and sunset, the heliacal and acronychal risings and settings of the fixed stars, the Moon's rising, setting and zodiacal place, the risings and settings and mutual aspects of the planets, and — in the last column of each spread — the AVRAE CONSTITVTIO, the predicted state of the air for that day ('ventosum serenum', 'obscurum humidum', 'pluviae imbres'). The new star of 1572 is entered among the fixed stars of the daily tables ('Noua Stella C. M.'). Dreyer notes that Tycho corrected the tabular places of Sun and Moon against his own earlier observations — something no other maker of such almanacs was able to do (TBOO I Prolegomena p. XIII).
Occasion
Not a commission and not, in the end, a publication. Dreyer's reconstruction (TBOO I Prolegomena p. XIII) is that Tycho compiled the Diarium as an experiment in his own method: to set down predicted weather for a whole year in advance and then compare it against the weather actually observed in 1573, thereby testing the truth of the meteorological-astrological art — the procedure Johannes Werner had followed with his weather notes of 1513–1530, and the same procedure by which Tycho always computed planetary places from the tables in order to correct the tables against observation. A second, polemical motive is stated by Tycho himself in the prefatory epistle: the men who compiled the printed almanacs of the day were 'satis inculti' and had brought a serious art into ridicule, and he undertook the labour to rouse the learned to a more careful cultivation of meteorological astrology. The Diarium was written at Herrevad Abbey, where Tycho was living with his uncle Steen Bille, in the autumn and December of 1572 — the very months in which the new star appeared, which is why the star-treatise came to be prefixed to it in the same codex.
On the addressee
No individual dedicatee. The dedicatory epistle prefixed to the Diarium is addressed to the learned public at large: 'INCLYTIS VTRIVSQVE ASTROLOGIAE ALVMNIS, VBICVNQVE LOCORVM, VNIVERSIS ET SINGVLIS, DOMINIS ET AMICIS, PERPETVA LAVDE DIGNISSIMIS, TYCHO BRAHE DANVS SALVTEM' — to the students of both astrologies (the theoretical/astronomical and the judicial-meteorological), everywhere, all and each (TBOO I p. 35). The man who obtained the manuscript, pressed Tycho hard to publish it, and to whom Tycho eventually sent 'totum Diarij opusculum' so that the star-treatise could be excerpted from it, was Johannes Pratensis (d. 1576), professor of medicine at the University of Copenhagen and Tycho's closest friend of these years; their exchange of letters is printed at the head of De nova stella (TBOO I pp. 7–15). Pratensis was, however, the advocate of the book, not its dedicatee.
Transmission
A single manuscript witness and no other. Vienna, Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek, Codex Vindobonensis lat. 10932 — 'Diarium anni 1573 in uno codice Vindobonensi lat. 10932 nobis traditum est, neque umquam alii ejus codices exstitisse videntur' (Dreyer, TBOO I p. 311). The codex is the presentation booklet as Tycho assembled it, titled 'Diarium astrologicum et metheorologicum Anni a nato Christo 1573... Accessit Tractatus de nova quadam & inusitata Stella quae iuxta Finem anni praecedentis nullo aevo prius conspecta apparere caepit', and containing: foll. 2-9 the Praefatio (= TBOO I 35-44); foll. 10-22 De nova stella (= 16-34); foll. 24-51 the Diarium itself (= 75-130); foll. 52-66 De eclipsi Lunae (= 45-64); foll. 68-73 the Elegia in Uraniam (= 65-70). Dreyer records that only the tract on the lunar eclipse is in Tycho's own hand — the Diarium leaves are in a copyist's hand (TBOO I p. 311). It reached print for the first time in J. L. E. Dreyer (ed.), Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, tom. I (Hauniae, 1913), pp. 75–130, in the section 'Appendices ad librum De nova stella pertinentes', where the half-title states 'nunc primum edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 10932'. Dreyer adds that this is the only almanac of its kind by Tycho that survives: of the diaria he is known to have sent for several subsequent years to King Frederik II at the king's command, not one is preserved (TBOO I p. 312).
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (cod. Vindob. lat. 10932; first printed in TBOO I)
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia; Nielsen none — no printed Diarium 1573 exists in Nielsen's Brahe corpus (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, §§424-433); the only 1573 Tycho imprint is §429, De nova... stella (Copenhagen, Lorentz Benedicht)

The Diarium itself was never printed in Tycho's lifetime, and was first published by Dreyer in TBOO I (1913), pp. 75–130. What WAS printed in 1573, inside De nova et nullius aevi memoria prius visa stella (Copenhagen: Lorentz Benedicht; Nielsen §429), were the OTHER parts of the same manuscript booklet: the Diarium's dedicatory Praefatio (TBOO I pp. 35–44), the treatise on the new star (pp. 16–34), the commentary on the lunar eclipse of December 1573 (pp. 45–64) and the Elegia in Uraniam (pp. 65–70). Tycho gives his reasons for withholding the Diarium in his letter to Pratensis: the many astrological schemes would have had to be cut new and set with great difficulty, and the year the almanac covered was already nearly half gone (TBOO I p. 12; Prolegomena p. XII). The 1573 title-page itself advertises the dedicatory epistle and explains that the 'Exemplar' for the current year could not be included because of the difficulty of the many schemes and the shortness of time; and after the Praefatio the printed book carries the flat notice: 'Exemplar Diarij, quod hoc loco subijciendum erat, propter multiplex & operosum schematum exprimendorum artificium, desideratur' (De nova stella 1573, KB Copenhagen copy; = TBOO I p. 44 line 36). Dreyer cites exactly this line as his evidence that Tycho omitted the Diarium when publishing the book.

Open questions
  • The scribe of the Diarium leaves (foll. 24-51) of Cod. Vindob. lat. 10932 is not identified. Dreyer states only that the lunar-eclipse tract alone is in Tycho's hand; he does not say whose hand wrote the rest, nor whether the Diarium leaves are in one hand or several.
  • It is not established whether Cod. Vindob. lat. 10932 is the very 'Diarij opusculum' that Tycho sent to Pratensis in Copenhagen in 1573 (from which Lorentz Benedicht's compositor set the star-treatise), or a second copy retained by Tycho. Dreyer does not address the question, and the codex's route to Vienna is not traced in TBOO I.
  • Whether the Diarium's predictions were ever in fact checked against the observed weather of 1573 — the purpose Dreyer ascribes to it — is unknown: Tycho's observation books for 1571–1573 are missing (Dreyer, TBOO I Prolegomena p. XI; cf. TBOO X), and no comparison survives.
  • The diaria Tycho later sent annually to Frederik II at royal command are all lost (TBOO I p. 312); their relation in form and scale to this one is conjectural (Dreyer supposes they were much shorter and confined to what touched the king).

Fratri gemello — To his twin brother

ElegysecureEarlyARead the text →brahe-t_fratri-gemello

Epitaph poem spoken in the voice of Tycho's twin brother, who died in the womb; Tycho's first publication, printed as a single-leaf broadsheet by Mads Vingaard in Copenhagen in 1572.

IX 173A 1D.O.M.S

QVI prius ac vixi sum mortuus atque reuixi, Hac tumulor Terra: Conijce qualis eram? Natus adhuc nondum, matris claudebar in aluo, Cum mihi Mors vitæ ianua facta fuit. 5Tunc simul alter erat claustris sociatus eisdem, Frater adhuc viuus, namque gemellus eram. Huic Deus, vt Cœli et Terræ miranda videret, Concessit vita me seniore frui. Sum tamen haud illo peiori sorte potitus, 10Incolit hic terras, me sed Olympus habet. Incolit hic terras, expostus mille periclis, Quæ Mare, quæ Tellus, quæ simul Astra ferunt. Me sed Olympus habet, quo Dijs coniunctus in vnum Pace per æternum lætitiaque fruor. 15Ast vbi mortales tandem is quoque deserat artus Fessaque sub gelida membra reponat humo, Tunc ambo in Cœlis rursus iungem ur in vnum, Æterni compos fiet et ille boni. Corporis interea patienter pondera gestet, 20Fortunæ nec sit inuidus ille meæ. Nomen apud viuos mihi tam cita fata negabant, Ille refert nostri nomine nomen Aui. Nomen Auo fuerat Thyco, hinc illi quoque Thyco, Huic Brahe Cognomen, dictus et inde Brahe. 25Ipse est qui nostros decorauit carmine Manes, Lustra gerens vitæ quina peracta suæ.

FRATRI GEMELLO, MORTVO IN VTERO, THYCO BRAHE OTTONIS F. F.

Haffniæ apud Matthiam Vinitorem, 1572.

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
Fratri gemello, mortuo in utero
Form
Elegy (this catalogue)
Date
1572 secure

Printed colophon in the text: 'Haffniæ apud Matthiam Vinitorem, 1572'; confirmed by Nielsen §424.

The broadsheet is dated in its own imprint ('Haffniae apud Matthiam Vinitorem. 1572') and Nielsen catalogues it under 1572. The poem's own closing verse ('Lustra gerens vitae quina peracta suae') says the poet has completed five lustra = 25 years; Tycho, born 14 December 1546, turned 25 on 14 December 1571, which agrees with composition in 1571/72 and printing in 1572.

Addressee
The stillborn twin brother (subject and voice)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — the edition's translation, translator not named, complete
Summary
A Latin elegy of thirteen elegiac distichs (26 verses), headed 'D. O. M. S.' and cast in the epitaphic voice of the dead speaker: Tycho's twin brother, stillborn at their birth in December 1546, addresses the reader from the grave ('Qui prius ac vixi sum mortuus atque revixi, / Hac tumulor terra: conijce qualis eram?'). The twin explains that death was for him the door of life; that God granted the surviving twin a longer life on earth; that his own lot is not the worse one ('Incolit hic terras, me sed Olympus habet'); that the two will be rejoined in heaven when the brother in turn dies; and that, having died before he could be named, he has no name among the living, whereas his brother carries their grandfather's name, Tycho. The last distich names the living twin as the author of the poem. Below the verse the sheet is subscribed 'FRATRI GEMELLO, MORTVO IN VTERO, THYCO BRAHE OTTONIS F. F.' It is Tycho's first appearance in print — a year before De nova stella (1573) — and his debut as a poet.
Occasion
Not documented by any contemporary source; the poem itself gives no external occasion beyond the fact of the twin's death twenty-five years earlier. The standard reconstruction is Thoren's: the death of Tycho's father Otte Brahe (9 May 1571) left Tycho occupied with the family's affairs and gave him an unusual period of closeness with his mother Beate Bille at Knudstrup, which 'turned Tycho's thoughts to — or even revealed to him for the first time — the circumstances of his own birth'; he then took the finished poem to Copenhagen to be printed. Christianson (2020) states the same reconstruction more flatly ('One day, his mother told him that he had come into the world with a stillborn twin brother'). Neither cites a document for the prompt, and no letter or record of 1571-72 mentions the poem: the occasion is an inference from the biography, not an attested fact, and should be graded C on its own.
On the addressee
The dedicatee is the addressee named in the subscription: Tycho's own twin brother, stillborn at the delivery of Beate Bille at Knudstrup (Knutstorp), Scania, on 14 December 1546. He died unbaptised and unnamed — the poem makes the namelessness its point (fate 'denied me a name among the living'; the surviving twin took the grandfather's name, Tycho/Tyge). There is no second, living dedicatee: the sheet carries no patron's name, and the poem is signed simply 'Thyco Brahe Ottonis f[ilius] f[ecit]'.
Transmission
Unlike most of the minor Tycho poems, this one is not a manuscript survival: it survives as the printed broadsheet itself, in what is believed to be a unique copy at Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen (the Royal Library's 2025 exhibition text gives the shelfmark as Hielmst. 3887 2 degrees, i.e. the Hielmstierne collection). It was reprinted in Danske Magazin II (Copenhagen, 1746), pp. 170–71. Dreyer edited it in TBOO IX (1927), p. 173, among the Carmina, and his headnote states his copy-text explicitly: '[Ex exemplo a Matthia Vinitore typis descripto (Hauniae 1572)]' — i.e. from the printed exemplar, not from a codex. Dreyer's editorial note (TBOO IX p. 322) adds: 'CARMEN FRATRI GEMELLO (p. 173) per Matthiam Vinitorem (Danice Mads Vingaard) typographum in uno folio describendum curavit Tycho.' TBOO IX is therefore not the first printing but the standard critical text. An English rendering exists in J. A. Gade, The Life and Times of Tycho Brahe (Princeton, 1947), p. 12 (so Thoren's note); a Danish verse translation by Peter Zeeberg accompanies the DSL digital edition.
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the 1572 Copenhagen broadsheet (Nielsen 424))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Copenhagen, 1572 (Mads Vingaard (latinised on the sheet as Matthias Vinitor)); Nielsen Nielsen, Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, no. 424

Folio patent — a single broadsheet leaf, 33 lines, italic type, the whole text within a frame built up of printers' flowers (Roskener), with a woodcut initial; type-area including frame 238 x 123 mm (Nielsen no. 424). Nielsen records one surviving copy, at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, and Dreyer confirms it ('Reperitur exemplum in Regia bibliotheca Hauniensi', TBOO IX p. 322). Tycho paid for the printing himself (Thoren, p. 199: 'Tycho had already paid for the printing of such productions as an ode to his stillborn twin brother'). This is Tycho's first publication of any kind — the collector-bibliographies (PMM 143, Dibner 142, Horblit 15, Honeyman 486) record De nova stella (1573) as his first because they catalogue books and not occasional broadsheets.

Open questions
  • Printer discrepancy. Nielsen (no. 424), Dreyer (TBOO IX p. 322) and the sheet's own imprint ('Haffniae apud Matthiam Vinitorem') all give Mads Vingaard = Matthias Vinitor as the printer. The Royal Library's exhibition booklet of 2025 (p. 31) instead gives 'Copenhagen: Laurentius Benedictus for Jacob Vinitorem, 1572' and cites it as 'LN 19 2 degrees'. Lorentz Benedicht printed De nova stella in 1573, and the Brahe entries in Nielsen run from 424 to 433, so both the printer attribution and the 'LN 19' number in that booklet look erroneous; but the conflict is on record and has not been adjudicated against the physical sheet.
  • The occasion is an inference, not a document. Thoren (1990) and Christianson (2020) both reconstruct the prompt from Tycho's circumstances in 1571-72 (his father's death; time at Knudstrup with Beate Bille), and Christianson turns it into a scene ('One day, his mother told him...'), but neither cites a source for it. Nothing in Tycho's surviving correspondence of 1571-72 mentions the poem. Why he printed, at twenty-five, an elegy for a brother dead twenty-five years — and why he printed it rather than circulating it in manuscript — remains unexplained.
  • The KB shelfmark (Hielmst. 3887 2 degrees, i.e. the Hielmstierne collection) rests on the 2025 exhibition booklet, whose bibliographical data for this item are otherwise demonstrably unreliable. Nielsen says only 'Kbh., Kgl. Bibl.' It should be confirmed against the Royal Library's own catalogue before being cited.
  • Whether any second copy of the broadsheet survives. Nielsen recorded one; no later authority reports another, but no systematic search for a second exemplar has been made.

De nova stella — On the new star

TreatisesecureEarlyARead the text →brahe-t_de-nova-stella

Tycho's report on the new star first seen in November 1572 — his first book, printed at Copenhagen by Lorentz Benedicht in 1573 — published with a prefatory exchange of letters with his friend Johannes Pratensis, an opening poem by Hans Frandsen and a closing one by Anders Sørensen Vedel: guarantees from university and church for the noble author. The book also carries Tycho's own elegy to Urania, in which the muse appears and gives him the new star as his calling — the beginning of the allegory that runs through his poetry for the rest of his life.

Full heading
De nova et nullius aevi memoria prius visa stella, iam pridem anno a nato Christo 1572. mense Novembri primum conspecta, contemplatio mathematica
Form
Treatise (this catalogue)
Date
1573 secure

Imprint date 1573 on the title page (Nielsen §429, diplomatic transcription of the title page); the edition's year 1573

Printed 1573 (title-page and colophon: 'HAFNIAE, Impressit Laurentius Benedicti. 1573. Cum Privilegio'; Nielsen §429). The text was drafted earlier: the preface to the suppressed Diarium is subscribed 'Ex Musaeo nostro Herrizuadensi Anno 1572 Mense Decembri' (Herrevad Abbey, December 1572), and Pratensis's letter of 16 April 1573 already reports the woodblocks being cut, so composition runs from December 1572 into the spring of 1573.

Addressee
Johannes Pratensis (addressee of the dedicatory letter)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — Peter Zeeberg, complete
Summary
Tycho's first book and his report on the new star (SN 1572) that appeared in Cassiopeia on the evening of 11 November 1572, seen by him at Herrevad Abbey. The astronomical core (TBOO I pp. 16–30) records his measurements of the star's position and its distance from the stars of Cassiopeia, argues from the absence of any detectable diurnal parallax that it stands not in the elementary region but among the fixed stars of the eighth sphere, and tracks the star's fading magnitude and changing colour — a direct assault on the Aristotelian doctrine that no generation or corruption occurs in the aetherial heavens ('in aetherea coelestis mundi regione, nullam fieri alterationem generationis vel corruptionis'). The book is a composite: a commendatory poem by Johannes Franciscus Ripensis; the two prefatory letters; the treatise on the star with its astrological interpretation; the preface Tycho had written for his astrological-meteorological Diarium for 1573 (the Diarium itself being withheld, its 'Exemplar' declared 'desideratur' for the difficulty of cutting the many figures); the pragmatia of the lunar eclipse of December 1573 with a judgement on its effects; Tycho's own elegy In Uraniam; a poem by Andreas Vellejus (Anders Sorensen Vedel); and the printer's afterword. 4to, 54 leaves.
Occasion
The nova of 11 November 1572 itself. Tycho wrote the tract in the first instance not as a book but as the piece that was to be prefixed to his own astrological and meteorological Diarium for 1573; the Diarium was in the end not printed (Dreyer, TBOO I Prolegomena: only its preface and the December lunar-eclipse calculation went to the press), so the star-tract was published on its own. Tycho, a nobleman, was reluctant to print: in his letter to Pratensis he asks that his name be suppressed or inverted by anagram, on the ground that most men think it a great disgrace for one of noble birth to venture anything in the liberal and higher sciences. The published occasion is the pressure of his Copenhagen friends, staged in the two prefatory letters — Pratensis urging publication (3 May 1573), Tycho conceding it (5 May 1573). Dreyer shows that this exchange is a literary device: a transcript signed by Tycho of a letter from Pratensis dated 16 April 1573 already speaks of the figures being cut and of the difficulty of procuring paper, so the decision to publish long preceded 3 May, and the two letters 'hoc solo consilio scripta esse, ut praefationis vice fungerentur'.
On the addressee
Johannes Pratensis (Hans Philipsen Pratensis, d. 1576), to whom Tycho's letter of 5 May 1573 (dated from Knudstrup) serves as the dedicatory epistle. Dreyer identifies him as the son of an immigrant Frenchman named du Pre, professor of medicine in the University of Copenhagen from 1571, and Tycho's close friend; Tycho later wrote his Epitaphium, printed at Uraniborg in 1584 (Nielsen §431). The book's front and back matter also carry commendatory poems by two other men of the same Copenhagen circle: Johannes Franciscus Ripensis (Hans Frandsen, doctor of philosophy and medicine, leaf 1b) and Andreas Vellejus (Anders Sorensen Vedel, court preacher at Copenhagen, leaf 53b).
Transmission
Not a manuscript survival: the text reaches us through its own printed editio princeps (Copenhagen, Lorentz Benedicht, 1573), of which Dreyer in 1913 knew only ten copies — three in Copenhagen libraries and seven outside Denmark — and which he says no historian of astronomy had inspected before 1890. Nielsen (1931) was able to list some nineteen holding libraries. A photographic facsimile of the editio princeps was issued by the Royal Danish Academy of Sciences in October 1901, for the tercentenary of Tycho's death. The critical text is Dreyer's, TBOO I (1913) pp. 1–72, with editorial notes at pp. 309–11. The material Tycho left out of the 1573 book survives only in manuscript and was first printed by Dreyer in the appendices at TBOO I pp. 73–142, from three Vienna codices: the Diarium anni 1573 itself (cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10932, the only witness), the Additiones to the lunar-eclipse commentary that Tycho added after April 1588 and had set up for reprinting at his own press but never issued (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686), and Tycho's excerpts from friends' letters about the star of 1572 (cod. Vindob. lat. 13619).
Channel
In Tycho's own books (the 1573 book itself)
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Copenhagen (Hafniae), 1573 (Lorentz Benedicht (Laurentius Benedicti)); Nielsen 429

4to, 54 leaves, signatures (:)4 (::)2 A4-K4 L6, 'Cum Privilegio'. Printed in a small edition and barely distributed: Tycho himself wrote later that 'pauca enim ejus edita sunt exemplaria et multo pauciora ad exteros (quadam typographi tenacitate) allata pervenerunt' (Progymnasmata I p. 581, quoted by Dreyer, TBOO I p. 309). Because of that rarity Tycho reprinted the astronomical portion (TBOO I pp. 16–30) himself in Progymnasmata I pp. 582 ff., there correcting some of the numbers — corrections Dreyer deliberately does not carry back into TBOO, preferring to present the youthful book in its original form.

Open questions
  • The order of the prefatory letters is sometimes reversed; Nielsen's own entry §429 and the text in TBOO I p. 15 ('Datae Knusdorp die 5. Maj, Anno 1573') agree that Pratensis wrote to Tycho on 3 May and Tycho replied on 5 May. The commendatory poem by Johannes Franciscus Ripensis on leaf 1b is easily overlooked beside Vellejus's.
  • How many copies survive? Dreyer in 1913 knew ten (three in Copenhagen, seven abroad); Nielsen in 1931 lists some nineteen holding libraries; no modern census exists.
  • Nielsen's copy list for §429, as read here, gives 'Stockholm, Kgl. Bibl.; Wien, Vetenskapsakademiens Bibl.' The Vetenskapsakademien is in Stockholm, not Vienna; the location of that copy needs checking against the printed bibliography.
  • Dreyer's claim that the Pratensis/Tycho exchange of 3 and 5 May 1573 was composed as a preface rather than being real correspondence rests on a single transcript of the 16 April 1573 letter. It is a strong argument but it does not appear to have been tested against the surviving letter-copies since; whether any of the three letters survives in the original is not established here.
  • Tycho refers in the book to earlier tracts of his own on related matters; Dreyer (TBOO I p. 309) says these 'nunc omnes interciderunt' and speculates that Tycho may himself have destroyed them in later life. Their content is unrecoverable.

Astrologiæ meteorologicæ fragmentum — Fragment on meteorological astrology

FragmentunknownEarlyBRead the text →brahe-t_astrologiae-meteorologicae-fragmentum

Fragment of the opening of a treatise on weather astrology, addressed to "all students of meteorological astrology wherever they may be", arguing that prediction of celestial influence on the elementary world cannot attain the certainty of astronomy.

Full heading
Astrologiae meteorologicae fragmentum
Form
Fragment (this catalogue)
Date
undated (the edition: 1574) unknown

tekstnet edition metadata: publication year 1574 (the edition's page verified, no circa); pre-Hven per period bounds

Correction. Dreyer, who prints it after the Oration: 'Quando hoc confectum sit, non constat' (TBOO I 313). The edition's 1574 follows that placement.

Dreyer states expressly that the date of composition is not established: 'Quando hoc confectum sit, non constat' (TBOO I, p. 313). The year 1574 carried by the edition is an artefact of TBOO's placement of the piece as an appendix to the Oratio de disciplinis mathematicis, which Tycho delivered in the University of Copenhagen in the autumn of 1574 (TBOO I, p. 312); it is not an attested date for the fragment itself. The fragment carries no date, and Dreyer offers none.

Language
Latin
Summary
An unfinished Latin prose preface, breaking off in mid-sentence, to a projected work on 'meteorological astrology' (celestial prediction of weather and other general terrestrial effects). It is headed as an open address, 'ASTROLOGIAE METHEOROLOGICAE ALUMNIS VBICUNQUE LOCORUM VNIUERSIS & SINGULIS T. B. O. SALUTEM' — to the students of meteorological astrology everywhere, all and each, Tycho Brahe Otto's-son sends greeting. Its argument: astrology cannot match astronomy for certainty of prediction, because celestial motions are open to eye and instrument and can be reduced to geometrical hypotheses and arithmetical tables, whereas celestial influence is hidden from the senses and knowable only a posteriori through long and fallible experience — an experience the older astrologers pursued without the required diligence, the art having been corrupted for gain and 'negligentius per imposturas tractata'. Tycho then divides the discipline into universal and particular parts (the universal covering changes of the air, epidemic disease, harvest fertility and dearth, and the fortunes of commonwealths), quotes Cardano to the effect that many have foretold particular fates but nobody has exactly foretold universal ones, and begins to wonder why predictions should be the more certain in individuals — at which point the text stops (TBOO I, 177-178).
Occasion
Not recoverable. Dreyer, who edited the autograph, says the date of composition is not established, and the fragment gives no internal occasion; it is an opening address to readers of a book Tycho never completed. Nothing in the surviving three pages names a prompting event, and no authority known to this register supplies one. Two related Tychonic projects invite comparison but do not license an assertion: the Uraniborg 'Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum anni 1586' issued under Tycho's imprimatur by Elias Olsen Morsing, whose preface is likewise addressed 'Ad astrologiae meteorologicae studiosos', and the draft preface to a 1586 astrological-meteorological diary that Dreyer prints separately at TBOO IX, 147-150. Whether the fragment belongs to that Hven diary project of the 1580s or to the astrological interests of the 1574 Oratio beside which Dreyer placed it is an open question, not a finding.
On the addressee
No individual dedicatee. The piece is addressed collectively to 'the students of meteorological astrology everywhere, all and each' (astrologiae metheorologicae alumnis vbicunque locorum vniuersis & singulis) and signed with the initials T. B. O. = Tycho Brahe Otthonides, 'Otto's son' — the signature form Tycho uses elsewhere (cf. the 1577 Horoscopus, 'a Tychone Brahe Ottonide conscriptus'). It is a reader-preface, not a patronage dedication.
Transmission
The words survive in a single autograph witness: Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek (then Bibliotheca Caesarea), Cod. lat. 10689, whence Dreyer printed it 'nunc primum' (TBOO I, p. 176). Dreyer describes the physical state in his Annotationes: 'Scriptum est ipsius Tychonis manu, sed in media tertia pagina desinit. Charta autem lacerata et humore vitiata est' — written in Tycho's own hand, breaking off in the middle of the third page, the paper torn and damaged by damp (TBOO I, p. 313). The damage is visible in Dreyer's setting: he marks the manuscript pages in the margin (1r, 1v, 2r) and prints the losses as lacunae, the text of fol. 2r tapering to nothing as the torn corner takes the lines away. The Vienna provenance is the normal one for Tycho's unpublished papers: the Society's preface to TBOO records that the bulk of the unprinted material, apart from what is in Copenhagen, had to be sought in the Imperial Library at Vienna (TBOO I, Praefatio Societatis, p. I). Printed text: TBOO I, 175-178 (the text itself at 177-178; so also the TBOO XV index, s.v. Astrologia: 'Tychonis Astrologia meteorologica I 177-178').
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (first printed in TBOO I (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1913

Never printed in Tycho's lifetime, and never printed at all before TBOO. Dreyer's headnote is explicit: 'Astrologiae meteorologicae fragmentum nunc primum edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 10689' (TBOO I, p. 176) — 'we now publish for the first time'. Nielsen's Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600 (and Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen), the authority on Tycho's printed corpus, carries no entry for it; the only cognate Uraniborg imprint is the 1586 Diarium astrologicum et methorologicum of Elias Olsen Morsing, a different text. Since the piece is a torn autograph draft that breaks off mid-sentence, no printing was ever to be expected. First printing therefore: TBOO I (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1913), pp. 175–178.

Cited as a parallel bearing on the open dating question, not as evidence of the fragment's date.
Open questions
  • The date is genuinely unknown. Dreyer says so outright; the edition carries 1574, which follows TBOO's placement of the piece after the 1574 Oratio rather than any attested evidence. This is a live disagreement between the modern edition's implied dating and Dreyer's explicit refusal to date, and it should not be smoothed over.
  • Is the fragment a draft preface to the Hven meteorological-diary project of the 1580s (cf. Morsing's 1586 Uraniborg Diarium, and the separate 'Diarii astrologici et meteorologici anni 1586 praefationis adumbratio' at TBOO IX, 147-150), or an earlier piece belonging with the 1574 Oratio and the lost 'Contra astrologos pro astrologia' announced in De nova stella? Unresolved on present evidence; a hand-dating of Vienna Cod. lat. 10689 against the Graphonomicon's life-stage grid would be the way to test it.
  • The relation of this fragment to the 'Diarii astrologici et meteorologici anni 1586 praefationis adumbratio' (TBOO IX, 147-150) has not been collated here. The two are printed by Dreyer as separate texts, but no authority consulted states whether they are independent drafts of the same intended preface.
  • Cod. lat. 10689 has not been examined for this record beyond Dreyer's description; the extent of the loss (how much of fol. 2r-2v the tear and damp removed, and whether any further leaves of the projected work are in the same codex) is not established from the sources used here.

De disciplinis mathematicis oratio — Oration on the mathematical disciplines

OrationsecureEarlyARead the text →brahe-t_de-disciplinis-mathematicis-oratio

Oration on the mathematical disciplines delivered at the University of Copenhagen at the beginning of September 1574, at the request of King Frederik II and in the presence of the French ambassador Charles Dançay, to open Tycho's public lectures on astronomy.

Full heading
De disciplinis mathematicis oratio
Form
Oration (this catalogue)
Date
1574 secure

The oration's own heading: delivered 'anno 1574 in principio Septembris'; the edition's metadata 1574.

The year is given by the text's own manuscript heading — 'ORATIO QUAM HABUI ANNO 1574 IN PRINCIPIO SEPTEMBRIS...' (TBOO I, p. 145) — and is confirmed by every authority (Dreyer, TBOO I, p. 312: 'autumno anni 1574'; Dreyer 1890, p. 73; Thoren 1990, p. 80; Christianson 2000, p. 18). Only the DAY is contested: the Vienna manuscript heading says 'in principio Septembris' (at the beginning of September), the 1610 printed edition's heading says 'in fine anni 1574' (at the end of the year 1574), and Dreyer 1890 / Thoren / Christianson 2020 all give 23 September 1574. See open_questions.

Addressee
Frederik II (at whose request it was delivered)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — the edition's translation, translator not named, complete
Summary
The inaugural Latin oration with which Tycho, then twenty-seven and holding no academic degree, opened a course of public lectures on astronomy at the University of Copenhagen. It is a formal hour-long praelectio in praise of the mathematical disciplines: geometry (Euclid, Archimedes, Plato's alleged exclusion of the geometrically ignorant), arithmetic and the Pythagoreans, music, optics (Alhazen and Witelo), then a genealogy of astronomy running from Adam and Seth's two pillars (quoted at length out of Josephus, Antiquitates Iudaicae I) through Timocharis, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, al-Battani and Alfonso of Castile to Copernicus, 'whom you would not wrongly call a second Ptolemy' but whose theory Tycho already judges contrary to physical principles (TBOO I, pp. 145–150). More than half the surviving text is then a sustained defence of astrology — the macrocosm/microcosm doctrine, the organs answering to the seven planets, the 1563 Saturn-Jupiter conjunction and the plague that followed, the doctrine of directions — answering in turn the philosophers' and the theologians' objections (Jacob and Esau, the Mosaic prohibitions, Isaiah on the Chaldaeans, King Asa), and insisting that the stars incline but do not compel (TBOO I, pp. 156–170). Appended to the manuscript, under the rubric 'HAEC POST ORATIONEM SUBIUNGENDA' (TBOO I, pp. 170–173), is a first-person account of the delivery and its aftermath: while he was refuting the theologians' arguments the whole student body turned to stare at Niels Hemmingsen, who was sitting there as the professors' antesignanus and who — conscious that he had published exactly those arguments in his commentary on the Pauline epistles, 'mostly taken from Calvin's little book against the astrologers' — pulled his cap down over his face with a half-smile; the French ambassador and the professors then escorted Tycho to his lodging, the jurist Albert Knopper accosted him on the way, and at the dinner that followed Dançay mischievously tried to set Hemmingsen and Tycho against one another. The same appendix records that Tycho bought copies of the Prutenic Tables at his own expense and had them distributed among the poorer students, that he lectured on the theories of the Sun and Moon, and that he broke off 'circa Brumam' (around the winter solstice) because a journey to Germany fell due.
Occasion
Fully recoverable and unusually well documented. Some young noblemen studying at the University asked Tycho to lecture on a mathematical subject that was then going untaught; his friends Charles de Dançay (the French ambassador) and Johannes Pratensis (professor of medicine) pressed him to accept; he refused until King Frederick II himself added his request, and then yielded (Dreyer 1890, p. 73; Resen 1668, p. 383, following Gassendi: 'Anno 1574. jussu Friderici II. Regis Daniae, svasu Danzai Regis Galliae Legati, & Johan. Pratensis Profess. Regii'). The oration is the praefatio to that course — 'Haec oratio praefatio est praelectionum, quas autumno anni 1574 in universitate Hauniensi Tycho habuit' (Dreyer, TBOO I, p. 312) — and Tycho's own opening sentence says he was asked 'not only by certain of you, my friends, but by our Most Serene King himself'. The lectures proper, on the theory of the planets and the use of the Prutenic Tables, began the next day and ran until about Christmas (Thoren 1990, p. 85; Resen 1668, p. 374). A second, tacit occasion is legible in the text's shape: for a nobleman to lecture at all was irregular, and more than half the oration is spent squaring astrology with the Philippist theology that Niels Hemmingsen had made dominant at Copenhagen — the appendix shows Tycho was fully aware he was speaking at Hemmingsen, who was in the room.
On the addressee
No dedicatee. The oration was delivered to an assembly: 'in consessu Mag[nifici] Legati Galli, doctorum et professorum omnium atque studiosorum Academiae Hafniensis' (TBOO I, p. 145) — the whole university, in the presence of the Magnificent French ambassador. That ambassador is Charles de Dançay (Carolus Danzaeus, b. ca. 1509, d. 1589), French resident envoy in Copenhagen from 1548 until his death, Tycho's close friend, who in 1576 laid the foundation stone of Uraniborg (Dreyer, TBOO I, p. 313, ad p. 171,1). Christianson 2020, p. 62, states that Dançay lent his Copenhagen mansion as the venue and that the university gathered in his great hall — though Tycho's own appendix has Dançay escorting him from the hall back to his lodging, which sits awkwardly with that (see open_questions). The other named figures present are Niels Hemmingsen (Nicolaus Hemmingius, 1513–1600, professor of theology, the realm's foremost Philippist, dismissed 1579 for Calvinist leanings; Dreyer, TBOO I, p. 313, ad p. 170,10) and the professor of jurisprudence Albert Knopper. The 1610 PRINTED edition, by contrast, does have a dedicatee: Cort Aslakssøn dedicated it to Tycho's elder brother Steen Brahe, royal councillor and governor of Kalundborg castle (Resen 1668, p. 383; Dreyer 1890, p. 74 n.).
Transmission
Manuscript, in Vienna. Dreyer's text follows codex Vindobonensis lat. 10686-22 (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek; part of the great Tychonic composite codex 10686, other fascicles of which supplied the additions to the lunar-eclipse tract in the same TBOO volume) — 'secuti sumus codicem Vindobonensem lat. 10686-22' (TBOO I, p. 144). Tycho wrote the speech out in full and kept it, adding at the end his own record of how it had been received (Thoren 1990, p. 80). Two collateral witnesses exist, both posthumous prints made from a copy that Cort Aslakssøn obtained from Tycho himself while living in his household — Aslakssøn 'declared that he had obtained this [text] to copy from Tycho, when he was, eighteen years before, in Tycho's own household' (Resen 1668, p. 383: 'declarando se istam describendam a Tychone obtinuisse, cum foret ante annos octodecim in ipso Tychonis convictu'; 1610 minus 18 = 1592, and Aslakssøn served on Hven 26 Oct 1590 — 29 Apr 1593, Christianson 2000, p. 252). Those prints — Copenhagen 1610 (Aslakssøn) and Hamburg 1621 (Curtius) — carry a substantially shortened ending and omit the appendix entirely; Dreyer collated them against the Vienna codex but did not follow them ('Consuluimus etiam editiones ab hoc codice nonnihil discrepantes', TBOO I, p. 144). The full text, including the appendix (whose closing words are lost where the paper is torn), was first published by J. L. E. Dreyer with J. Ræder in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia I (Copenhagen, 1913), pp. 143–173, with the editor's notes at pp. 312–313. Before 1913 the oration was known only in the truncated 1610/1621 form: Dreyer's own 1890 biography summarised it from the printed edition, citing 'Oratio, p. 20'.
Channel
Printed after his death (Aslakssøn, Copenhagen 1610 (this catalogue))
Printing
printed posthumously — Copenhagen (Hauniae), 1610

not printed in Tycho's lifetime. Dreyer states this flatly in the editorial note prefixed to the text: 'In Oratione de disciplinis mathematicis edenda, QUAE VIVO TYCHONE EDITA NON EST...' (TBOO I, p. 144). It was first printed nine years after his death, in 1610 at Copenhagen, edited by his former famulus Cort Aslakssøn (Conradus Aslacus Bergensis) — 'Tychonis Brahei de disciplinis mathematicis oratio publice recitata in Academia Haffniensi anno 1574, et nunc primum edita... studio et opera Cunradi Aslaci Bergensis, Hafniae, 1610, 4to', dedicated to Tycho's brother Steen Brahe, with some of the editor's own speeches added (Dreyer 1890, p. 74 n.; Resen 1668, p. 383: 'novennio post ejus mortem edidit Conradus Aslacus'). A second edition appeared at Hamburg in 1621 with a preface (praeloquium) by Joachim Curtius and an expanded title, 'in qua simul Astrologia defenditur et ab objectionibus dissentientium vindicatur' (Dreyer 1890, p. 74 n.; Dreyer, TBOO I, p. 144: 'Joach. Curtii (Hamburgi 1621)'). Dreyer 1890 calls both editions 'very scarce'; a 1610 copy is in the Karen Brahe Library, Roskilde (shelfmark G.10 in the KBB catalogue). The item carries NO Nielsen number: Lauritz Nielsen's Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600 stops at 1600, so a 1610 Copenhagen imprint falls outside its scope, and Nielsen's enumeration of Tycho's printed corpus (§§424–433, §§975–976, plus four lost prints) accordingly contains nothing corresponding to the Oratio — consistent with, and not evidence against, the posthumous printing. The printed editions do not give the text now read. Dreyer: 'In duabus ejus editionibus, quae post mortem Tychonis prodierunt, extrema pars orationis multo brevior est quam in eo codice manu scripto, quem nos secuti sumus, et deest etiam additamentum (p. 170-173)' (TBOO I, p. 312). The whole eyewitness appendix — Hemmingsen and his cap, Dançay's dinner, the Prutenic Tables, the break-off at the winter solstice — was first printed in TBOO I (1913).

Open questions
  • The exact day. Tycho's own manuscript heading says the oration was given 'in principio Septembris' (early September 1574); the heading of the 1610 printed edition instead says 'in fine anni 1574' (at the end of the year 1574); Gassendi/Resen say Tycho began 'ruente jam hyeme' (with winter already rushing on); and Dreyer 1890 (p. 73), Thoren (p. 80), Christianson 2020 (p. 62) and Jönsson 2025 (p. 26) all assert Thursday 23 September 1574 without, in the passages consulted, citing the document that fixes it. 23 September is not 'in principio Septembris'. The source of the precise date — presumably the university's lecture-list or matriculation records — has not been traced here, and the disagreement is left standing.
  • The venue. Christianson 2020 (p. 62) says the university assembled in Ambassador Dançay's great hall. Tycho's own appendix (TBOO I, p. 171) says that when the oration was finished he withdrew 'in hospitium' (to his lodging) and that the Magnificent Lord French Legate together with the university's professors escorted him there — which reads more naturally if the oration had been delivered elsewhere and Dançay was a guest of honour. Christianson's source for the mansion-as-venue has not been checked.
  • Whether cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10686-22 is autograph. Dreyer does not say so in the passages consulted; Thoren says Tycho 'wrote out his speech in full' and preserved the manuscript, and the DSL apparatus records corrections by a first hand ('V man. pr.'), both consistent with an authorial working copy — but no authority examined here states that the Vienna leaves are in Tycho's hand. Not asserted here; a candidate question for the Graphonomicon.
  • The printer of the 1610 Copenhagen edition is not named by any source consulted (Dreyer 1890 gives only 'Hafniae, 1610, 4to'). Left blank rather than guessed.
  • The 1621 Hamburg edition: whether it is a straight reprint of Aslakssøn's text with Curtius's preface added, or an independent recension. Dreyer says only that both editions diverge somewhat from the codex and that both truncate the ending; he does not say whether 1621 depends on 1610.
  • The journey to Germany that Tycho says ('circa Brumam') interrupted the lectures. Resen (p. 374) has him leaving for Hesse only in the spring of 1575. Whether Tycho crossed in December 1574 and returned, or whether his 'circa Brumam' is loose, is not resolved by the sources consulted.

Andreæ Welleio Saxonis interpreti — To Anders Sørensen Vedel, translator of Saxo

PoemprobableEarlyBRead the text →brahe-t_andreae-welleio

Verse exhortation to Anders Sørensen Vedel, translator of Saxo Grammaticus, who was lamenting that the dearness of paper would doom his labours, urging him to persevere and pointing to the papermakers Scania offers.

IX 174M. ANDREÆ WELLEIO SAXONIS INTERPRETI EXQUISITISSIMO OB DESIDERATÆ PAPIRI DETESTANDAM CARITATEM NUNC MISERE SUOS LABORES TAM INDIGNE PERITUROS DEPLORANTI HOC CARMEN AD SPEM EXEQUENDI OPERIS ET LIBERALIS CONSTANTIÆ IMPETUM T. B. SCRIPSIT.

ERGONE Saxonis morientur scripta diserti Deficiensque tibi tot fortia facta virorum Deficere æternum cogat tam cara papirus? Ergone perpetuis finientur cuncta tenebris, 5Bellipotens multis quæ gessit Dania seclis? Tot Reges fortesque duces tantosque gigantes Holgeros Frothosque graues Risosque Rolandos Parua subire iterum permittat cartula mortem? Dij prohibete nefas, et vos prohibete puellæ, 10Lintea quin potius vestris remouete lacertis Et forte optatæ nunc conficienda papiro. Ecce suos offert expansis Scania palmis Artifices, patriæ pereat ne gloria gentis, Sed prohibet duris inclusa pecunia vinclis 15Nec sinit egregios lucem spectare labores. O semper claris inuisa pecunia factis! O semper rerum commixta pecunia satis!

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
M. Andreae Welleio Saxonis interpreti exquisitissimo ob desideratae papiri detestandam caritatem nunc misere suos labores tam indigne perituros deploranti hoc carmen ad spem exequendi operis et liberalis constantiae impetum T. B. scripsit
Form
Poem (this catalogue)
Date
1575 probable

the edition's year 1575; the poem addresses Vedel while his Saxo translation was still unfinished ('ad spem exequendi operis').

The poem carries no date. It is dated only by its occasion: Dreyer states that Vedel published his version of Saxo's Historia Danica in 1575 and that difficulties over the price of paper appear to have arisen 'ante editionem' (TBOO IX, p. 322). Late 1574 is therefore equally possible; the year 1575 is retained as the terminus the occasion points at, not as a documented date. The piece is a carmen in verse, printed by Dreyer among the Carmina, not a letter.

Addressee
Anders Sørensen Vedel (addressee)
Language
Latin
Summary
A seventeen-line Latin poem (hexameters) addressed to Anders Sørensen Vedel while he was lamenting that the scarcity and cost of paper would destroy his labours — his Danish translation of Saxo Grammaticus. Tycho asks whether the writings of eloquent Saxo, and with them the kings, captains, giants, Holgers, Frothos and Rolands of warlike Denmark, are to be doomed to a second death for want of 'a little sheet' ('parua... cartula'); he calls on the gods and on the girls of Denmark to strip the linen from their arms so that the longed-for paper may be made of it, and notes that Scania offers its craftsmen with open hands but that money 'shut in hard chains' will not let the work see the light. It closes on two exclamations against money as the enemy of famous deeds ('O semper claris inuisa pecunia factis!'). Dreyer's heading records that Tycho wrote it to give Vedel 'hope of finishing the work and an impulse to generous perseverance'.
Occasion
Recoverable, and stated in the piece's own heading: Vedel, working towards publication of his Danish Saxo, was 'misere suos labores tam indigne perituros deplorans' because of the 'detestanda caritas' of the paper he needed; Tycho wrote the poem to hearten him. Dreyer adds only that difficulties over the price of paper 'appear' (videntur) to have arisen before the 1575 edition — he cites no document for the crisis beyond the poem itself, so its precise nature (a price rise, a supply failure, a withheld subvention: the poem blames money 'inclusa vinclis') is not independently attested.
On the addressee
Anders Sørensen Vedel (Andreas Severinus Velleius), 1542–1616, Danish royal historiographer; Tycho's friend and former tutor-companion from their Leipzig student years, later the editor of Saxo and of the ballad collections. He published his Danish translation of Saxo's Historia Danica in 1575. The 'M.' of the heading is Magister.
Transmission
Manuscript. The poem survives in Tycho's own hand ('ipsius Tychonis manu scriptum') in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, among the Langebek excerpts, no. 178 (Dreyer's lemma: 'Ex excerptis Langebekianis Hauniensibus nr. 178'; the annotation's 'in eadem bibliotheca' refers back to the 'Regia bibliotheca Hauniensis' named in the immediately preceding note on the 1572 twin-brother carmen). It thus reaches us through the 18th-century antiquary Jacob Langebek's collections and was edited by J. L. E. Dreyer and J. Ræder in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (1927), Carmina, p. 174, with the editors' note at p. 322.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (Tycho's own hand in the Langebek excerpts; first printed in TBOO IX)
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1927

Not printed in Tycho's lifetime. Lauritz Nielsen's enumerative bibliography of Tycho's entire printed output (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, §§424–433, §§975–976, plus the four lost prints) contains no such item, and in 1574/75 Tycho had no press of his own — the Uraniborg press was not planned until 1583–84. Dreyer prints the poem from a manuscript, with the source lemma '[Ex excerptis Langebekianis Hauniensibus nr. 178]', and — unlike his practice elsewhere in the Carmina, where he names prior printings (Vingaard's 1572 broadsheet, Gassendi 1654, Resen 1668) — he records no earlier printing for this text. On present evidence its first printing is TBOO IX (Copenhagen 1927), p. 174; that it was never printed earlier is an argument from Dreyer's and Nielsen's silence, not a positive statement by either.

Open questions
  • Whether the poem was printed anywhere before TBOO IX (1927). Dreyer names no earlier printing, and Nielsen does not record it, but neither states that TBOO is the first printing; the possibility that Langebek — whose excerpts preserve the leaf — printed it in Danske Magazin (as the 1572 twin-brother carmen was, Danske Magazin II, 1746, p. 170) has not been checked.
  • The date. The poem is undated; 1575 is inferred solely from Dreyer's statement that Vedel's Saxo appeared that year and that the paper difficulties arose before it. Late 1574 is equally consistent with the evidence.
  • The manuscript. Dreyer's 'excerpta Langebekiana nr. 178' has not been converted to a present-day Kongelige Bibliotek shelfmark, and his attribution of the leaf to Tycho's own hand ('ipsius Tychonis manu scriptum') has not been re-verified against the Graphonomicon since 1927. An autograph leaf preserved inside an 18th-century collector's excerpt-volume is worth confirming rather than assuming.
  • The nature of the paper crisis behind the poem. The verse blames money 'shut in hard chains' and says Scania offers craftsmen; whether this points to a specific failed subvention, to a Danish papermaking venture, or is a rhetorical flourish is not established by any source consulted.
  • The piece has been typed as a letter of 1575; it is a poem (Dreyer prints it among the Carmina).

Epitaphium filiæ Kirstinæ — Epitaph for his daughter Kirstine

EpitaphprobableEarlyARead the text →brahe-t_epitaphium-kirstinae

Epitaph for Tycho's daughter Kirstine, who died of plague on 24 September 1576 aged two years and eleven months, hung in the church of Helsingborg.

IX 174A 1EPITAPHIUM QUOD IN TEMPLO HELSINGBURGENSI SUSPENSUM LEGITUR.

EXUVIAS abiens tulit huc KIRSTINA tenellas, Quæ BRAHÆI olim Nata TYCHONIS erat. Illa quidem modicum mundi fuit incola tempus: Interea modicis non tamen aucta bonis. 5Ingenio sexum superavit, moribus annos, Eloquij grata dexteritate pares. Ergo hanc quæ dederat subito Natura recepit, Consuetis maius ne quid adulta foret. IX 174Vivit at illa tamen, Naturæ obstacula vicit: 10Pro modico æternum tempore tempus habet, Æthereisque potita bonis mortalia temnit: Per CHRISTUM Civis legitimata Poli.

Obijt Peste Anno Domini MDLXXVI Septembris die XXIV. Vixit Annos II menses XI dies XI horas XI.

15MORS quo citior, dulcior, quo serior, amarior. KIRSTINÆ dulciss. filiolæ naturali præter ætatem industriæ et moratæ Pater F. et P.

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
Epitaphium quod in templo Helsingburgensi suspensum legitur (conventionally cited as Epitaphium filiae Kirstinae)
Form
Epitaph (this catalogue)
Date
1576 probable

The epitaph's own obit: 'Obijt Peste Anno Domini MDLXXVI Septembris die XXIV'; DSL edition year 1576.

The text is not itself dated as a composition; it dates the death it commemorates ('Obijt Peste Anno Domini MDLXXVI Septembris die XXIV', TBOO IX p. 175), which is a secure terminus post quem. That Tycho wrote the verses and had the tablet set up is stated by the 1746 Danske Magazin biography ('denne Grav-Skrift, som Tyge Brahe selv har giort og ladet opsette', Danske Magazin II, p. 194 n. c), but no source consulted dates the composition or the erection. 1576 is therefore the year of the occasion, and the presumptive but undocumented year of writing; a slightly later date for the tablet cannot be excluded.

Addressee
Kirstine Brahe, his daughter (subject)
Language
Latin
Summary
A funerary epitaph for Tycho's eldest daughter Kirstine Tygesdatter, in twelve Latin verses (six elegiac couplets, incipit 'EXUVIAS abiens tulit huc KIRSTINA tenellas, / Quae BRAHAEI olim Nata TYCHONIS erat'), followed by a prose subscription. The verses say that she was in the world only a short time, that she surpassed her sex in wit and her years in conduct and matched both in graceful eloquence, that Nature suddenly took back what she had given lest the child grow to be something greater than is customary, and that she nevertheless lives, made a lawful citizen of heaven through Christ. The prose subscription records that she died of plague on 24 September 1576 having lived 'two years, eleven months, eleven days, eleven hours', gives the motto 'MORS quo citior, dulcior, quo serior, amarior' ('the swifter death is, the sweeter; the later, the more bitter'), and closes with the dedication by the father to his 'sweetest little natural daughter, industrious and well-mannered beyond her years' ('KIRSTINAE dulciss. filiolae naturali praeter aetatem industriae et moratae Pater F. et P.' — fieri fecit et posuit). It is an inscription, not a book-poem: Dreyer's heading, taken from his source, describes it as hanging and legible in the church at Helsingborg (Scania, then Denmark).
Occasion
Fully recoverable. Kirstine Tygesdatter, the elder of the two daughters of Tycho Brahe and Kirsten Jørgensdatter, died of plague at Helsingborg on 24 September 1576 — three weeks short of her third birthday, and less than two months after the laying of Uraniborg's foundation stone (8 August 1576), while Tycho was on Hven and Kirsten and the children were still living in Skåne, probably in Tycho's town house at Helsingborg. Christianson: 'Little Kirstine died there of the plague on 24 September 1576... She was interred in St. Mary's Church, Helsingborg' (On Tycho's Island, p. 60); the plague had spread that summer from Copenhagen to Helsingborg, and the survivors were moved out to Tågalycka manor (Christianson 2020, p. 84). The epitaph is the tablet the father composed and set up over that grave.
On the addressee
No addressee in the epistolary sense; the commemorand is the poet's own child. Kirstine Tygesdatter (b. 12/13 October 1573; d. Helsingborg, 24 September 1576), eldest daughter of Tycho Brahe and Kirsten Jørgensdatter, named after Tycho's sister Kirstine who had died at thirteen in 1566 (Christianson, On Tycho's Island, p. 13 with n. 10, which cites this very epitaph, TBOO IX 174–5, for the birth). Because her mother was a commoner the child bore a patronymic, not the name Brahe. The epitaph calls her 'filia naturalis'.
Transmission
Inscription → printed inscription-collection → Dreyer. The words were carried in the first instance by a physical tablet hung in the church at Helsingborg (St Mary's, per Christianson), where a 17th-century antiquary could still read them: Dreyer's heading is 'EPITAPHIUM QUOD IN TEMPLO HELSINGBURGENSI SUSPENSUM LEGITUR'. His copy-text is not a manuscript but a printed antiquarian collection — the source lemma he prints above the poem reads '[E Laurentii Asseroi Inscriptionum Selandicarum Daniae Antigraphis (Hauniae 1621) fol. I]', i.e. leaf I of Laurits Nielsen Asserous's Inscriptionum Selandicarum Daniae Antigrapha (Copenhagen: Georg Hantzsch, 1621). The same leaf is cited by Langebek's Danske Magazin biography of 1746, alongside Sweertius p. 757 and Bang's Danske Samlinger II, 289. Dreyer and Ræder printed it among the Carmina in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (Copenhagen, 1927), pp. 174–175; notably they supply NO editorial note on it — the 'Ad Carmina' annotations (TBOO IX, pp. 321–323) run straight from the Vedel poem of p. 174 to the Uraniborg foundation-stone verses of p. 175, so nothing is said there about Kirstine, about the Helsingborg church, or about the fate of the tablet.
Channel
Printed after his death (Hantzsch, Copenhagen 1621 (this catalogue))
Printing
printed posthumously — Copenhagen, 1621 (Georg Hantzsch)

not printed in Tycho's lifetime, and not first printed in TBOO. (a) Not in the lifetime: the epitaph forms no part of Tycho's printed output — Nielsen's enumerative bibliography (12 publications + 4 lost prints) contains no such item, and in 1576 Tycho had no press: his only pre-Uraniborg imprints are the 1572 Carmen (Mads Vingaard) and the 1573 De nova stella (Lorentz Benedicht), and the Uraniborg press was not planned before 1583–84. (b) Printed after his death: the 1746 Danske Magazin biography states that the Latin epitaph 'can be read in print' in Franciscus Sweertius, Selectae Christiani orbis deliciae, p. 757; in Laurentius Asserøe (Laurits Nielsen Asserous), Inscriptionum Selandicarum Daniae Antigrapha, fol. I; and in 'Ol. Bangs Danske Samlinger' II, p. 289 (Danske Magazin II, p. 194 n. c). Asserøe's Antigrapha is a printed book — Copenhagen 1621, printed by Georg Hantzsch, 8vo, 71 unpaginated leaves; 'the first substantial work on the old inscriptions of Zealand' (Thesaurus Librorum Danicorum II, no. 324; Bibl. Dan. II, 605) — and it is the very copy-text Dreyer used. The place/printer/year fields above give that 1621 printing. Sweertius's Deliciae (p. 757) is undated in the Danske Magazin note and has not been verified here; it may well be the earlier printing (see open_questions), but it too is posthumous on any dating of Sweertius's collection.

ANDREAE WELLEIO (p. 174)' → 'De CARMINE FUNDAMENTALI URANIBURGI LAPIDI INSCULPTO (p. 175)': no note on the Helsingborg epitaph) — That Dreyer supplies no commentary on this piece — everything he tells us about it is in the source lemma (transmission)

SWERTII Selectis Christiani Orbis Deliciis p. 757. LAUR. ASSEROI Inscript. Dan. fol. I. OL. BANGS Danske Samlinger Tom. 2. p. 289.'; note (d) on the birth date — Printing: three attested printings, all posthumous (Sweertius p. 757; Asserøe fol. I; Bang II, 289) — hence 'printed_posthumously', not 'first_printed_in_tboo'. Also: Tycho's own authorship and his erection of the tablet; the identification of Kirstine as the elder daughter, 'filia naturalis', who died of plague 24 Sept 1576 aged 2y 11m 11d 11h; the computed birth date 12 or 13 October 1573
  • Thesaurus Librorum Danicorum, no. 324: 'INSCRIPTIONUM SELANDICARUM DANIAE ANTIGRAPHA … København 1621. Trykt af Georg Hantzsch. 8°. 71 upag. bl. … Bibl. Dan. II, 605. Første større arbejde om gamle indskrifter på Sjælland' — Printed status, place, printer and year of Dreyer's copy-text: Asserøe's Antigrapha is a printed Copenhagen book of 1621 (Georg Hantzsch), not a manuscript
  • Christianson 2000, p. 13 with n. 10 (birth of Kirstine, 12 October 1573; the note cites 'Brahe 1913–29, 9: 174–5' — this epitaph — and adds that she was named after Tycho's sister Kirstine, d. 1566 aged thirteen); p. 60 ('Little Kirstine died there of the plague on 24 September 1576 … She was interred in St. Mary's Church, Helsingborg'); notes to pp. 58–60 (Tycho and Kirsten legally married under Jutish Law by 1576; the daughters bore the patronymic Tygesdatter because their mother was a commoner) — Identification of the commemorand and the occasion: the death, the plague, the burial church, the family's status; the birth date
  • Christianson 2020, p. 84 (plague spread from Copenhagen to Helsingborg in summer 1576 and 'carried off Tycho's beloved, precocious daughter Kirstine, less than a month before her third birthday'; Kirsten Jørgensdatter and Magdalene were then lodged with the widow Margrethe Gagge at Tågalycka manor) — The occasion: the epidemic context and the immediate family circumstances of September 1576
  • Nielsen 1921, §1.1 (the only pre-press imprints: §424 Carmen ad fratrem gemellum, Copenhagen 1572, Mads Vingaard; §429 De nova stella, Copenhagen 1573, Lorentz Benedicht); §1.2 (Uraniborg press not planned before 1583–84; earliest Uraniborg imprint 1584); §3 (the four lost prints) — That the epitaph was not printed in Tycho's lifetime: it appears nowhere in his printed corpus, and in September 1576 he had no press
  • Zeeberg & Gredal Jensen 2019, https://tekstnet.dk/books/brahe-t_epitaphium-kirstinae/ — The edition of record, with a Danish translation
Open questions
  • Which posthumous printing is the earliest. The Danske Magazin note (1746) lists Sweertius, Selectae Christiani orbis deliciae, p. 757, before Asserøe 1621, but gives no date or edition for Sweertius; Franciscus Sweertius's collection has not been consulted here. If it antedates 1621 it, not Asserøe, is the editio princeps of the epitaph. Both are posthumous either way.
  • 'Ol. Bangs Danske Samlinger' II, p. 289 — the third witness named in 1746 — has not been identified or consulted; whether it is an independent transcript of the tablet or a copy of one of the printed collections is unknown.
  • Whether the tablet survives. Dreyer's heading (taken from a 1621 source) says the epitaph 'is read hanging' in the church at Helsingborg; Christianson says Kirstine was interred in St Mary's, Helsingborg. No source consulted states whether the epitaph tablet is still there, or when it perished. This should be checked against the Swedish church inventory before the register claims anything.
  • The 'filia naturalis' problem. The epitaph — Tycho's own words — calls Kirstine his natural daughter, and the 1746 biographer inferred from that word that she was born out of wedlock ('synes at have været uægte født'), adding that he could not say whether Tycho fathered her on Kirsten Jørgensdatter before taking her into his house or on another woman. Christianson holds that Tycho and Kirsten, having cohabited since c. 1571–2, were legally married under Jutish Law by 1576 and treats Kirstine as their daughter without qualification. The tension between the epitaph's own wording and the modern legal reading is real and is left standing here.
  • The birth date. The subscription's age reckoning (2 years 11 months 11 days 11 hours before 24 September 1576) yields 13 October 1573; Christianson gives 12 October 1573; Langebek in 1746 computed '12 or 13 October 1573' from the same figures. A one-day discrepancy, unresolved.
  • Authorship. That Tycho composed the verses is asserted by the 1746 Danske Magazin biography and assumed by Dreyer (who prints them among the Carmina), but no contemporary document consulted attributes them to him. The attribution rests on the dedication formula ('Pater F. et P.') and on editorial tradition.
  • Title. The edition uses the conventional modern title 'Epitaphium filiae Kirstinae'; TBOO's own heading is 'Epitaphium quod in templo Helsingburgensi suspensum legitur'. There is no authorial title.
