Additiones ad commentationem de eclipsi lunæ anni 1573 — Additions to the commentary on the lunar eclipse of the year 1573

SupplementprobableEarlyBRead the text →brahe-t_additiones-de-eclipsi-lunae-1573

Tycho's own retrospective annotation and two additions to his manuscript treatise on the lunar eclipse of 1573, recalling the observation at his manor Knudstrup with his sister Sophie Brahe, then about fourteen, and confirming that his predicted times agreed with the event.

Full heading
Additiones ad commentationem de eclipsi lunae anni 1573
Form
Supplement (this catalogue)
Date
after April 1588 probable — the edition: 1573

the edition's year 1573 — the year of the eclipse and of the parent treatise; the additions themselves are retrospective and undatable from the file

Correction. The edition files the Additiones under 1573, the year of the eclipse they annotate; the notes themselves were written after April 1588, for insertion into the book (Dreyer, TBOO I, Annotationes).

The '1573' in the title is the year of the eclipse and of the parent commentary, not of composition; the year 1573 is therefore wrong for the Additiones themselves. Dreyer fixes the terminus post quem from the text: 'Cum mortis Friderici II regis mentio fiat (p. 132), post mensem Aprilem a. 1588 has scriptas esse apparet' (TBOO I, p. 310) — the additions narrate Frederik II's death on 4 April 1588, so they were written after April 1588. The upper bound is inference, not attestation: the Vienna witness is marked up as setting copy for Tycho's own press ('in officina sua'), which operated at Uraniborg to April 1597 and at Wandsbek 1597-98; and one passage of the text (TBOO I, p. 135,4 — p. 136,4) was actually set in type in the second volume of the Epistolae astronomicae, which Tycho described as in press in February 1597 (Nielsen). Dreyer himself gives no upper bound and notes that the piece is nowhere mentioned in Tycho's surviving correspondence.

Language
Latin
Summary
Three authorial notes — one headed ANNOTATIO AVTORIS and two headed ADDITIO AVTORIS — which Tycho wrote long afterwards to be inserted into the section 'De eclipsi lunae anni 1573 mense Decembri' of his De nova stella (Copenhagen, 1573), each keyed to a precise line of the printed book (Dreyer prints the keys as 'ad p. 56,30', 'ad p. 62,11', 'ad p. 64,32' of TBOO I). The first reports the observation itself: Tycho watched the total lunar eclipse of 8 December 1573 from his manor at Knudstrup under a clear sky, measuring stellar altitudes with a gilded brass quadrant that read to five minutes of arc, and was assisted by 'dilecta mihi soror SOPHIA BRAHE, tunc temporis virgo annorum circiter 14', who held the lantern and 'willingly attended and supplied what she could'; he explains, remarkably, that he names her not because he needs a woman's testimony (which, he says, counts for little before the law) but so that readers will believe that the astronomical letters printed later in the book are genuinely her own work. The second and third additions lift the veil on the printed book's most famous evasion: the 'Phoebejus quidam Heros' whose fate Tycho had darkly forecast from the eclipse was Frederik II of Denmark, and Tycho, writing after the king's death on 4 April 1588, now identifies him, sets out his nativity (Hadersleben, 1 July 1534, 9h 30m a.m., 'prout etiam habet Calendarium Eberi'), computes the directions from the nativity and from the lunar eclipse of 2/3 March 1588 that he had observed at Uraniborg, and claims agreement with the death to the very week. Into the second addition he also folds his Rostock episode of 1566, when he anonymously posted heroic verses on a lunar eclipse foretelling the death of Sultan Suleiman, and was both praised and derided when it emerged that the sultan had died some weeks BEFORE the eclipse — an effect that could not precede its cause; his defence here is that the prediction had come from Suleiman's geniture, not from the eclipse.
Occasion
Recoverable, and unusually specific for a piece of this kind. Two things prompted it. (1) The death of Frederik II on 4 April 1588 'fulfilled' the veiled prognostication Tycho had printed in 1573 about an unnamed 'Phoebean hero', and thereby licensed him to disclose it: the whole of the second and third additions is a retrospective claim of a hit, complete with the quoted words 'multo tempore prius in nostro quodam Astrologico volumine propria manu consignata' and the marginal note he says he added on the king's death ('Obijt anno 88 die 4 Aprilis anno 53 completo'). (2) Tycho intended to reprint the eclipse commentary of De nova stella at his own press with these additions embedded in it — Dreyer infers this from the physical state of the Vienna witness, which carries quire and page numbers and instructions to the compositors written in German in the margins, among them Tycho's direction that the additions be set in small type, italic or roman, to distinguish them from the 1573 text (TBOO I, p. 310). The additions are thus a piece of authorial self-revision for a second edition that was never published. Their governing motive is apologetic: Tycho is defending judicial astrology — 'magna certe Astrologiae alias suspectae ab aspersis calumniis vindicatione' are the last words of the piece — while simultaneously retracting parts of his youthful method (he now says eclipses signify little except where they fall on the angles of a horizon, and concedes his 1573 prediction was out by about a year).
Transmission
Single manuscript witness, in Vienna: Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek (in Dreyer's day the Bibliotheca Caesarea), Cod. Vind. lat. 10686, fascicle 17 — the normal repository of Tycho's unprinted papers (TBOO I, Praefatio Societatis, p. I). Dreyer describes it: 'Insunt hae additiones in codice Vindobonensi lat. 10686[17], qui eam partem libri De nova stella continet, qua de eclipsi Lunae agitur' — the codex contains that part of De nova stella which treats the lunar eclipse, and the additions are in it; quire and page numbers stand in the margin together with instructions to the compositors written in German, Tycho directing among other things that the additions be set in small letters, italic or roman (TBOO I, p. 310). Dreyer does not state whose hand the additions are in — notably, he DOES identify autograph elsewhere in the same family of papers (the eclipse treatise in Cod. Vind. lat. 10932 is 'ipsius Tychonis manu scriptus', TBOO I, p. 309; the annotation on the eclipse calculation at Cod. Vind. 10932, ff. 57v-58r is 'manu Tychonis scripta', TBOO X, p. 39 n. 3) — so autograph must not be asserted here. The eclipse-observation portion of the text was printed by Dreyer a second time, from the same codex, among the observations of 1573 in the Thesaurus observationum: TBOO X, pp. 38–39, under 'DIE 8 DECEMBRIS, ECLIPSIS LUNAE', with the footnote 'E codice Vindobonensi latino 10686[17]. In codice observationum huius eclipsis observatio non reperitur. Cfr. vol. I p. 131 nostrae editionis' — i.e. the eclipse is not recorded in Tycho's observation books at all (they are deficient for 1571–1573, TBOO I, Prolegomena p. XI), and this text is the only witness to his having observed it. The observing sheet Tycho says was still to hand as he wrote ('adhuc charta in promtu est, in qua tunc, praesente dicta sorore, & lumen in laternula... adhibente, conscribebantur') is lost: 'Nec liber nec charta nunc superest' (TBOO X, p. 39 n. 1); 'Neque haec charta jam exstat' (TBOO I, p. 310). Editio princeps: J. L. E. Dreyer (with Ioannes Raeder), TBOO I (Copenhagen: Gyldendal / Nielsen & Lydiche, 1913), pp. 131–140. The title is Dreyer's editorial title; in the witness the pieces are simply headed ANNOTATIO AVTORIS and ADDITIO AVTORIS.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686; first printed in TBOO I)
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1913; Nielsen none

never published IN TYCHO'S LIFETIME, and never published at all before TBOO. Dreyer's headnote to the Appendices is explicit: 'Additiones ad commentationem de Eclipsi Lunae anni 1573, quas libro DE NOVA STELLA postea adjecit Tycho, nunc primum edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 10686[17]' (TBOO I, p. 74) — 'we now publish for the first time'. Nielsen (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen), the authority on what Tycho actually got printed, has no entry for it. two printing-adjacent facts must not be collapsed into A PUBLICATION. First, the Vienna witness is marked-up SETTING COPY for a projected re-setting of the eclipse commentary at Tycho's own press ('Hanc videtur Tycho in officina sua denuo typis describendam curavisse', TBOO I, p. 310); no copy of any such reprint is known, and Dreyer does not say one was executed. Second, and harder: one continuous passage of the text — TBOO I p. 135, line 4 to p. 136, line 4, the Rostock/Suleiman episode — WAS actually set in type, on fol. 51 of the SECOND volume of the Epistolae astronomicae, but, in Dreyer's words, 'hoc volumen prelum numquam reliquit' — that volume never left the press (TBOO I, p. 310; cf. TBOO X, p. 13, where the contemporary note calls the book 'excusum sed non editum', printed but not published). Nielsen independently records that Tycho described Epistolae vol. II as in press in a letter to Henrik Rantzau of 22 February 1597 and that no copy of any 1597 vol. II printing has ever been identified. So: a few lines of this text were impressed on paper at Tycho's press, and were still unpublished when he died. The parent work in which the additions were to appear — De nova stella (Copenhagen: Lorentz Benedicht, 1573) — is Nielsen 429; its 'De eclipsi lunae anni 1573 mense Decembri' section is TBOO I, 45-64. First publication of the Additiones themselves: TBOO I (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1913), pp. 131–140.

Sophie Brahe (1559–1643), Tycho's youngest sister; cf. Familia, s.v. Sophie Brahe.
  • Christianson 2020, the chapter on 1573 (page not recorded) — An English rendering of the same passage — 'Two months later at Knutstorp he observed the lunar eclipse foretold in his book, using the new quadrant and assisted by his fourteen-year-old sister, Sophie Brahe, who was "very fond of these matters by nature, took part eagerly, and helped where she could"' — confirming that the modern biographical tradition draws this episode from precisely this text.
Open questions
  • Is the Vienna witness (Cod. Vind. lat. 10686, fasc. 17) autograph? Dreyer does not say. He is scrupulous about identifying Tycho's hand elsewhere in the same body of papers, and his silence here should not be read either way. A hand-examination against the Graphonomicon (brahe-tycho) life-stage grid would settle it, and would also test the 1588-97 dating.
  • Was the projected re-setting of the eclipse commentary at Tycho's own press ever executed beyond the single leaf? Dreyer says only that Tycho 'seems to have arranged' for it ('videtur... curavisse'); no copy of such a reprint is known, and no copy of Epistolae astronomicae vol. II has ever been identified (Nielsen). Whether any further sheets of it were pulled is unresolved.
  • The direction of borrowing between this text and Epistolae astronomicae vol. II, fol. 51 is not established. Dreyer observes only that the words of TBOO I p. 135,4-136,4 stand on that leaf; he does not say whether Tycho drafted the passage for the Additiones and moved it into the Epistolae, or the reverse. Since both projects were running at Tycho's own press in the 1590s, either is possible.
  • The upper bound of the dating rests on inference from where the piece was to be printed, not on any statement. Dreyer expressly notes that the additions are nowhere mentioned in Tycho's letters of the period, so the usual correspondence controls are absent.
  • Tycho's claim (p. 134) that trustworthy friends had read his prediction of Frederik II's death in secret beforehand and marvelled at its exactness is uncorroborated by any source consulted here; the 'astrologicum volumen' in which he says he had entered the direction in his own hand has not been identified. This should be treated as an unverified authorial assertion, not a fact.

Epitaphium Johanni Pratensi — Epitaph for Johannes Pratensis

EpitaphsecureHvenARead the text →brahe-t_epitaphium-pratensis

Memorial poem for Johannes Pratensis of Aarhus, professor of medicine at Copenhagen and Tycho's friend (d. 1576), printed as a broadsheet at Uraniborg in November 1584 among the very first productions of Tycho's own press — a long-promised tribute redeemed once the press existed. It was probably printed as a pendant to a now-lost printing of Tycho's epitaph for Hans Frandsen (d. 1584), a text that survives only in seventeenth-century transmission.

Full heading
Epitaphium. Clarissimo et omnigena eruditione virtuteque ornatissimo viro D. Iohanni Pratensi Aarusiensi, medicinae Paracelsicae et Galenicae doctori excellentissimo, ob ingenitam naturae bonitatem, morumque incomparabilem suavitatem omnibus cuiuscunque status hominibus et charissimo et desideratissimo
Form
Epitaph (this catalogue)
Date
1576; printed 1584 secure

Nielsen §431: the broadsheet printing is dated 'VRANIBVRGI 7 Kal. Decemb. 1584'; DSL edition year 1584.

Correction. Composed after Pratensis's death in June 1576, on Tycho's own testimony; printed at Uraniborg in 1584. The edition dates the print.

SETTLES the 1576-vs-1584 CONFLICT: both dates are right, of different things, and the two indexes are dating different events. composition = 1576, on Tycho's own testimony. In the autobiographical narrative he wrote to frame this piece for his projected letter-collection he says that, a few days after Pratensis's death, once he had recovered from his grief, 'Epitaphium, quod illi vivo, biennio antea promiseram... confeci' — 'I composed the Epitaphium which I had promised him two years earlier while he was alive' (TBOO VII, p. 32, ll. 24-26). The poem's own subscription confirms the death year it commemorates: 'Obiit Anno 1576. Aetatis 32.' PRINTING = 1584, eight years later, on the new Uraniborg press: the same subscription ends 'Manibus Amici Optimi et desideratissimi, Vivo quod promiserat, persoluit: TYCHO BRAHE. Vraniburgi 1584' (TBOO IX, p. 177; Nielsen 431). The tekstnet/DSL index year 1584 is therefore the IMPRINT date taken from the sheet; the in-repo crosswalk's 1576 is the composition date (and the year of the death commemorated). Neither is an error; conflating them is. As a text, the piece is of 1576; as a publication, of 1584. Because the promise was made 'biennio antea', c. 1574, and the poem was written within days of a death of 1 June 1576 (Resen 1668; Danske Magazin II, p. 199), the composition date is as tight as such a date gets.

Addressee
Johannes Pratensis (subject)
Language
Latin
Summary
A Latin funerary elegy of 60 lines in elegiac couplets (30 distichs, printed in two columns), under a prose dedicatory heading and closed by a prose subscription. It opens with the topos that learning cannot buy exemption from death — 'Quid iuvat, assiduis studio impallescere chartis... Si Mors cuncta abolet?' — and then catalogues what died with Pratensis: he had mastered the ancients and 'divine Plato', had tested and understood 'your arts, Paracelsus' (while the herd of doctors gapes uncomprehending), healed the sick by Machaon's art, scanned the laws of the pole and the stars, was nursed in the arms of the Muses, and sang sweetly to the lyre. The second column turns on Death itself: Pratensis survived Germany's wars, France's slaughter, the Alps, the Apennines, Latium, Turk-threatened Hungary — only to be struck down at home, sitting and teaching ('Forte sedens, alios dum docet, ecce perit'), by an ambush rather than by open war; the poem ends with him triumphing over death through Christ. The subscription records the death ('Obiit Anno 1576. Aetatis 32'), Tycho's discharge of a promise made in the man's lifetime, and the place and year of printing, Uraniborg 1584.
Occasion
Fully recoverable, and unusually well documented by Tycho himself. Johannes Pratensis, Tycho's closest friend, died suddenly on 1 June 1576 while lecturing in the auditorium of the University of Copenhagen: he had been suffering from catarrh and a violent cough, a vessel burst, and he choked on his own blood as he was expounding Alcinous on Platonic philosophy (Tycho's own account, TBOO VII, pp. 31–32). Tycho was in Scania and did not learn of it in time to attend the funeral. Some days later he composed this poem — discharging, as both the poem's subscription and his narrative say, a promise made two years earlier, in Pratensis's lifetime, that he would write his epitaph (Pratensis himself, Tycho adds, 'had already foreboded that he would not long survive'). Tycho intended the verses for a gilded and ornamented brass tablet ('lamina orichalcica inaurata') which he had had prepared for the purpose, to be fixed publicly in the church, 'nisi alia quaedam ingrata intervenissent' — had not certain unwelcome things intervened. They did: the memorial actually recorded standing in Copenhagen a century later carries a prose epitaph by Petrus Severinus, not Tycho's verses (Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses, 1668). Tycho had in fact written to Severinus on 3 September 1576 proposing exactly that division of labour — 'huius, quantum ad sumtus attinet, ego eorum particeps ero, tu de inscriptione cogita' (I will bear a share of the cost; you think about the inscription) — and urging haste, 'lest, if long deferred, it pass into perpetual oblivion' (TBOO VII, p. 39). His own poem stayed unpublished for eight years, until the new press on Hven gave him a way to redeem the promise in print. It is a memorial poem that failed as a monument and succeeded as a broadsheet.
On the addressee
Johannes Pratensis (Danish Hans Philipsen; latinising his father's name du Pré), c. 1543-1 June 1576. Born at Aarhus ('Aarusiensis' in the heading) to a French father, Philippe du Pré of Normandy — formerly secretary in the French chancery of the captive Christian II — and a Danish mother; professor of medicine at the University of Copenhagen from 1571; died aged 32 while lecturing (TBOO VIII, p. 461, Index virorum doctorum; the fullest life is Anker Aggebo, Hans Philipsen Pratensis 1543-76, Copenhagen 1938). He was a Paracelsian in the Severinus circle, hence the heading's pointed 'medicinae Paracelsicae et Galenicae doctori'. Christianson (On Tycho's Island, 2000, p. 53) calls him simply 'Tycho's best friend': it was Pratensis who received the dedicatory letter of De nova stella (1573), who worked to keep Tycho in Denmark, who in February 1576 relayed the French envoy Dangay's counsel and first described to Tycho the 'domus plane philosophica' to be built on Hven with its gnomological inscriptions from the ancient philosophers, and who had reserved for himself the right to inscribe the cornerstone of Uraniborg with 'emblems mystical and sacred' — a right his death cancelled, so that Tycho and Dangay had to compose the cornerstone inscription instead. The poem is addressed to no living dedicatee; the subscription addresses the dead man's shade ('Manibus amici optimi').
Transmission
Print-first, unusually for the minor pieces. The words survive primarily in the 1584 Uraniborg broadsheet itself — a single transverse-folio leaf, printed recto only, of which one copy is recorded, at Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen (Nielsen 431; the census of the print documents that copy, bound in later marbled boards with a lettered label 'T. BRAHE. Epitaphium Joh. Pratensis. 1584'). A manuscript witness exists alongside it: Dreyer's source-lemma at TBOO IX, p. 176 reads '[Ex exemplo ab ipso Tychone typis descripto (Uraniburgi 1584); cf. cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10686]' — i.e. he set his text from the printed exemplar and collated it against the Vienna codex, the apograph letter-book from which the surrounding letters in TBOO VII are drawn. That Vienna copy is a consequence of Tycho's plan, recorded by Dreyer, to publish the poem among his letters: 'non solum in ipsius Tychonis typographia typis descriptum est, sed etiam inter epistulas edere propositum ei erat' (TBOO IX, p. 322), and indeed the letter-book's narrative breaks off with 'Nunc igitur Epitaphium, de quo dixi, subiiciam' — now I shall append the Epitaphium of which I have spoken (TBOO VII, p. 32). The projected second volume of the Epistolae astronomicae never appeared, so that intended printing never happened. The poem was reprinted from the broadsheet in Danske Magazin II (1746), pp. 199–201 — with the editor's gloss that Tycho 'composed for him a fine Latin epitaph, which he had promised him in his lifetime, and which he afterwards had printed at Uraniborg in 1584' — and was edited by J. L. E. Dreyer and J. Raeder in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (Copenhagen 1927), Carmina, pp. 176–177, with the editors' note at p. 322.
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the Uraniborg print of 1584 (Nielsen 431))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, Hven, 1584 (Not named on the sheet. Nielsen's entry reads 'Uvis Bogtrykker' (unknown printer). Tycho's first printer was a German called Joachim, otherwise unidentified.); Nielsen 431

Printed in Tycho's lifetime, on his own press — this is emphatically NOT a first-printed-in-TBOO piece. Nielsen, Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, no. 431: 'Tycho Brahe: Epitaphium Joh. Pratensis. Uraniborg: Uvis Bogtrykker, 1584. 1 Bl. pat. 2 Sp. 30 L. Satsflade: 276 x 258 mm. Kursiv. Initial.' — a single leaf, patent (transverse folio) broadsheet, printed recto only, two columns of 30 lines, italic type with a historiated initial Q; one recorded copy, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen. In Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen (1921), pp. 178–179, Nielsen dates it 'sikkert fremstillet i Slutningen af 1584' (certainly produced at the end of 1584) and judges it 'vistnok det aeldste af disse latinske Digte og i saa Tilfaelde altsaa det foerste Tryk, der vides at vaere udgaaet fra Trykkeriet paa Uraniborg' — PROBABLY the oldest of the Uraniborg occasional poems and in that case the first print known to have come from the Uraniborg press. Note the hedge: Nielsen writes 'vistnok'. The sheet bears no printed day-date (only 'Vraniburgi 1584'), whereas the companion Carmen ad Jac. Ulfeldium is dated 7 Kal. Decemb. 1584 (25 November), so the internal order of the late-1584 trial prints is inferred, not documented. Posthumous reprints: Danske Magazin II (Copenhagen 1746), pp. 199–201; then Dreyer, TBOO IX (1927), pp. 176–177. Nielsen records no other printing in Tycho's lifetime, and the poem does not appear in Resen's Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668), which prints Tycho's other medical epitaph (for Johannes Franciscus Ripensis) but gives Severinus's prose epitaph for Pratensis.

Open questions
  • The 1576/1584 conflict is settled (composition 1576; printing 1584), but the edition's index carries a single year; a reader must be told which date is meant.
  • Is this really the first Uraniborg imprint? Nielsen says 'vistnok' (probably) and 'sikkert fremstillet i Slutningen af 1584' (certainly produced at the end of 1584), but the sheet carries no day-date, while the companion Carmen ad Jac. Ulfeldium is dated 25 November 1584. The internal order of the late-1584 trial prints therefore rests on Nielsen's judgement, not on a document.
  • Who printed it? The sheet names no printer; Nielsen's 'Uvis Bogtrykker' means unknown. Tycho's first printer is known only as a German named Joachim. No document ties him to this sheet.
  • What were the 'alia quaedam ingrata' that prevented Tycho's gilded brass tablet from being fixed in the church? Tycho says only that they intervened. Whether they were Severinus's parallel (and successful) monument, a family or chapter objection, or Tycho's own removal to Hven is not stated by any source consulted.
  • The relation between Tycho's verse epitaph and Severinus's prose epitaph is not spelled out by any authority. Tycho's 3 September 1576 letter offers money and asks Severinus for the inscription; Resen 1668 shows Severinus's inscription standing. Whether Tycho withdrew his own verses in Severinus's favour, or was displaced by them, is an inference gap.
  • Pratensis's dates are not consistent across the authorities. The epitaph and Resen's monument give death 1 June 1576 at age 32 (Resen: 32 years, 6 months, 3 days), implying birth late 1543 — matching Aggebo 1938 and Christianson. But Christianson p. 53 says 'May of 1576', and Dreyer's own index (TBOO VIII, p. 461) gives birth 'circa annum 1538'. Dreyer's birth year is irreconcilable with the age on the monument and should not be propagated.
  • The KB shelfmark of the unique copy is still uncaptured (carried over from the census's open questions); the Vienna witness (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686) has not been examined, so whether its text differs from the broadsheet is unknown — Dreyer signals collation with a bare 'cf.'
Notes
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 15, 34-37): the Erik Lange poem, not this broadsheet, was the first item printed on the press (27 Nov 1584 in the observation protocol, TBOO X, 302), the Pratensis epitaph following within a month of it; the broadsheet's dateline 7 Kal. Decemb. (25 Nov) 1584 would then be the poem's dateline rather than the day of printing. The earlier gloss superlative 'the earliest known imprint of Tycho's own press' was dropped as contradicting the protocol-dated sequence.
  • Pendant-printing with a lost Frandsen broadsheet is a probability argument (Zeeberg 1993 with Nielsen 1921, 180) — keep hedged; the Frandsen epitaph survives in no contemporary print, only via Gassendi (1654) and Resen (1668).

Fundamentalis Uraniburgi lapis — The foundation stone of Uraniborg

InscriptionprobableHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_fundamentalis-uraniburgi-lapis

Verse inscription carved on the foundation stone of Uraniborg, recording that Charles Dançay, the French king's ambassador to Denmark, laid the stone in August 1576 for the house of Urania and Sophia that Tycho was building at King Frederick II's command.

IX 175A 1FUNDAMENTALI URANIBURGI LAPIDI HÆC FUERE INSCULPTA.

TEMPORE quo regnum qui nomine reque secundus Danorum imperio rex Fridericus habet, Carolus ad Danos Galli legatio regis Danzæus, patria cui est Aquitane solum, 5Huic domui, Uraniæ et Sophiæ quam Tycho Brahorum Clara stirpe satus, rege jubente, struit, Hunc lapidem auspicio felici, utque omne per ævum Augusti id memoret lux modo sexta, locat.

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
Fundamentali Uraniburgi lapidi haec fuere insculpta (conventionally cited as Fundamentalis Uraniburgi lapis)
Form
Inscription (this catalogue)
Date
1576 probable

The inscription dates itself to August 1576 in Frederick II's reign ('Augusti... lux... sexta'); DSL edition year 1576. Boundary case: assigned to hven by documented context — the stone was laid on Hven for Uraniborg — although the shared period bound nominally puts 1576 in 'early'.

The verses commemorate a dated act: the laying of Uraniborg's foundation stone, which Tycho himself dates to 8 August 1576 ('die octavo Augusti mane exoriente Sole', TBOO V p. 143). Every witness ties the poem to that act, and it is already in print by 1594 (Nielsen depth-layer question aside, see printed.note) and in an Uraniborg pupil's notebook of the 1580s-90s. But nothing dates the composition itself, and the verses are internally inconsistent with the event they date: they say 'Augusti... lux modo sexta' (6 August), whereas the stone as actually cut says Kal. Augusti (1 August) and the Mechanica says VI Id. Augusti (8 August). Dreyer registers the disagreement and does not resolve it (TBOO IX p. 322). If the poem is — as Dreyer's phrasing implies — a later verse paraphrase of the carved prose rather than a text composed for the ceremony, 1576 is the date of its subject, not necessarily of its writing. Hence 'probable', not 'secure'.

Addressee
Frederik II (the king named); Charles de Dançay (who laid the stone)
Place
Uraniborg
Language
Latin
Summary
Eight Latin verses (four elegiac distichs) commemorating the foundation of Uraniborg. They say: in the time when Frederick, 'second in name and in deed', holds rule over the Danes, Charles Danzaeus (Dancay), ambassador of the king of France to the Danes, whose native soil is Aquitaine, sets this stone with a happy omen for the house that Tycho Brahe, sprung of the illustrious Brahe stock, is building at the king's bidding for Urania and Sophia — and sets it so that the sixth day of August may remember it for all time. Gassendi, who first printed them, heads them 'Fundamentali Uraniburgi lapidi haec fuere insculpta' ('these things were carved on the foundation stone of Uraniborg'), i.e. presents them as the text of a physical inscription on the porphyry block that Dancay laid at the south-east corner of the house at ground level. Dreyer treats them rather as a verse rendering of the inscription — 'carmen... quo verba insculpta poetice exponuntur' (TBOO V p. 326) — and the prose inscription that Tycho himself printed in the Mechanica (TBOO V p. 143), of which a fragment survives at Lund, is a different text.
Occasion
Fully recoverable, and unusually well documented, because Tycho narrates the event himself. Frederick II granted Tycho the island of Hven for life on 23 May 1576; building began the same year, and Charles Dancay — the French king's long-resident ambassador in Denmark and one of Tycho's closest older friends — volunteered, as soon as he heard the house was to be built, to lay its first stone ('se primum lapidem angularem isthic collocaturum sponte addixit'), and had a porphyry block cut with a Latin dedication (TBOO V p. 143). On the appointed morning he came with several noblemen and learned mutual friends, and at sunrise on 8 August 1576, with Jupiter rising near the heart of Leo and the Moon on the western cardine in Aquarius (an elected horoscope), he laid the stone with libations of various wines and prayers for good fortune. Dreyer 1890 (p. 93) adds that it was placed at the south-east corner of the house at ground level. These verses commemorate exactly that act. What is not recoverable is why the verses exist alongside the prose inscription, who wrote them, and whether they were ever cut in stone at all (see open_questions).
On the addressee
There is no addressee in the epistolary sense: this is a lapidary/commemorative text with three named actors. (1) Frederick II (1534–1588), king of Denmark-Norway, 'second in name and in deed', at whose command ('rege jubente') the house is built. (2) Charles de Dancay, latinised DANZAEUS (d. 1589), the poem's grammatical subject: a Gascon/Aquitanian nobleman, resident ambassador of the king of France in Denmark for some forty years, and Tycho's friend and protector from the Copenhagen years — it was in Dancay's residence that Tycho delivered the 1574 Oratio de disciplinis mathematicis. Tycho's own obituary notice of him in the Mechanica (TBOO V p. 143) calls him 'vir integritate, virtute & rerum usu nulli secundus, & doctrinis insuper liberalibus praeclare imbutus', says he loved Tycho with a singular and constant affection as long as he lived, and dates his death 'ante octennium aetatis anno octuagesimo primo' — eight years before writing, in his 81st year, i.e. 1589. (3) Tycho Brahe himself, named in the third person as the builder.
Transmission
Not a Tycho autograph tradition, and not a first printing in TBOO. Four strands. (1) manuscript: the verses stand at p. 11 of the Uraniborg 'kollegiehaefte' — Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, MS Thott 4to 1927, lettered 'Braheana... de Tycho Brahe, Varia', a pupil's notebook from the astronomical school on Hven, written there (Norlind argues) in the 1580s-90s and containing a run of Tycho's poems; p. 7 of the same notebook gives the inscription with 'Kal. Aug.' instead (Norlind, p. 74 n., pp. 101–102). Dreyer did not use this witness. (2) lifetime print: Nathan Chytraeus, Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn 1594), p. 594 (Norlind, p. 74 n.). (3) the source DREYER actually used: Pierre Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei... Vita (Paris 1654), p. 300 — the corresponding page of the enlarged 2nd ed. (The Hague: Vlacq, 1655) is p. 460 — where the poem stands in Gassendi's closing appendix of Tycho's poems, introduced 'Superest proinde dumtaxat, ut subjiciam heic paucula... nondum edita ejus carmina... Sed Carmina ex Tychone ecce', then headed 'Fundamentali Uraniburgi lapidi haec fuere insculpta'. Dreyer's source lemma above the text reads: '[E Petri Gassendi Tychonis Brahei Vita (Parisiis 1654) p. 300; cf. P. J. Resenii Inscriptiones Haffnienses (Hauniae 1668) p. 331 sq.]'. (4) THE DANISH ANTIQUARIAN LINE: Peder Hansen Resen, Inscriptiones Haffnienses (Copenhagen 1668), pp. 331 f. — which Norlind suspects took the text from Chytraeus rather than from an independent Danish witness. Dreyer and Raeder printed it among the Carmina in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (Copenhagen, 1927), p. 175, lines 9-20, with editorial notes at TBOO IX p. 322 and, on the stone and the date, at TBOO V p. 326 (ad p. 143,2). The STONE itself partly survives: a fragment found built into the wall of a house on Hven, now in the Historical Museum of Lund University, reading '...FOELICIS AVSPICII ERGO / ANNO MDLXXVI / KAL. AVGVSTI P.' (TBOO V p. 326; Beckett & Christensen 1921, Fig. 1) — prose, not verse.
Channel
Printed by others in his lifetime (printed at Herborn in 1594 (this catalogue))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Herborn (Nassau), 1594

(a) Tycho never printed these verses. They are absent from Nielsen's enumeration of Tycho's printed output (the Brahe entries run nos. 424-433) and from the four known lost Uraniborg prints; Nielsen's bibliography, which catches the minor and occasional pieces the collector-bibliographies omit, records no printing of them. (b) What Tycho did print, in the Astronomiae instauratae Mechanica (Wandsbek 1598; TBOO V p. 143), is the prose inscription on the stone — 'REGNANTE IN DANIA FRIDERICO II. CAROLVS DANZAEVS AQVITANVS... VOTIVVM HVNC LAPIDEM MEMORIAE ET FELICIS AVSPICII ERGO P. ANNO CIƆIƆLXXVI. VI. ID. AVGVSTI.' — which is a different text from these verses. (c) The earliest printing of the verses that any authority reports is Nathan Chytraeus, Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn in Nassau, 1594), p. 594 — a humanist's printed anthology of inscriptions seen on travels, published without Tycho's involvement. This rests on Norlind (Lund 1970), p. 74 n.; the book itself has not been inspected here and Norlind names no printer, so place/year are given from him and printer is left blank. (d) Gassendi, printing the poem in 1654, believed Tycho's poems in that appendix were still unpublished ('nondum edita ejus carmina'), which suggests he did not know Chytraeus. If Norlind is mistaken, the status falls back to printed_posthumously (Gassendi 1654) — see open_questions.

This is the whole basis both for the attribution to Tycho and for the claim that the verses were carved on the stone
  • Dreyer 1890, p. 93 (citing Astron. Inst. Mechanica, fol. H.6) — occasion and date — 'on the 8th August 1576 the foundation-stone was laid. The French minister Dancey had asked to be allowed to perform this ceremony, and had provided a handsome stone of porphyry with a Latin inscription, stating that the house was to be devoted to philosophy, and especially to the contemplation of the stars'; the sunrise ceremony with Jupiter near Regulus and the Moon setting in Aquarius; and the stone's physical placement 'at the south-east corner of the house at the level of the ground'
  • Beckett and Christensen 1921, pp. 4–6 and Fig. 1; Tavle 7 (east facade, p. 53); the layer's 'Foundation-stone date' note (citing H. Mortensen, Fra Arkiv og Museum II, p. 475 f.) — occasion and transmission — foundation stone 8 Aug 1576, porphyry, with Dancay's Latin inscription; the stone shown embedded in the lower left of the east facade in the reconstruction; the surviving fragment in Lund University's Historical Museum; and the recorded discrepancy that the Mechanica gives 8 August while the surviving fragment reads 1 August
  • Nielsen 1921, Nielsen's Brahe entries nos. 424-433; the printed corpus and the four lost or disputed prints — printing (negative claim) — Tycho never printed these verses himself: they appear neither among Nielsen's enumeration of his printed output nor among the four known lost Uraniborg prints. The lifetime printing reported by Norlind is a German anthology (Chytraeus, Herborn 1594) outside Tycho's own bibliography
  • Zeeberg & Gredal Jensen 2019, https://tekstnet.dk/books/brahe-t_fundamentalis-uraniburgi-lapis/001/ — the edition of record, keyed to TBOO IX.175
Open questions
  • the date — three witnesses, three days. The stone as actually cut says KAL. AVGVSTI (1 August; Lund fragment, TBOO V p. 326). Tycho's Mechanica says VI. ID. AVGVSTI and narrates the ceremony 'die octavo Augusti mane exoriente Sole' (8 August; TBOO V p. 143). These verses say 'Augusti... lux modo sexta' (6 August). Dreyer reconciles the first two — the ceremony was planned for 1 August, the stone was cut in advance, and the laying actually happened on the 8th (the Mechanica's own astrological description requires the Moon in Aquarius, which fits the 8th and not the 1st) — and he silently notes that Tycho, printing the inscription in 1598, gave the corrected date rather than the one on the stone. Nobody explains the poem's 6 August. Metrical convenience ('sexta' scans where 'octava' will not), a copying slip, or a composer who was not present are all possible; Dreyer flags the 'dissensio' (TBOO IX p. 322) and leaves it.
  • AUTHORSHIP. That Tycho wrote these verses rests entirely on Gassendi's framing ('Carmina ex Tychone', among 'nondum edita ejus carmina') and on Dreyer's decision to print them among Tycho's Carmina. Neither adduces evidence. The verses speak of Tycho in the third person and make Dancay the subject; the inscription proper was Dancay's own commission ('verba sequentia exscindi curavit', TBOO V p. 143). Their presence in an Uraniborg pupil's notebook (Thott 4to 1927) shows they circulated in Tycho's household, which is consistent with his authorship but does not establish it. Attribution to Tycho is convention, not attested fact.
  • WERE the verses EVER CARVED? Gassendi's heading asserts 'haec fuere insculpta'. Dreyer describes the piece instead as a 'carmen... quo verba insculpta poetice exponuntur' — a poem in which the inscribed words are set out poetically — which implies the carved text was the prose one. The surviving fragment at Lund carries prose. No witness reports having seen verses on the stone. It is therefore an open question whether this is an inscription at all, or a verse epigram about an inscription.
  • CHYTRAEUS 1594 — UNVERIFIED. The claim that the verses were printed in Tycho's lifetime rests on a single footnote in Norlind (p. 74 n.) citing Nathan Chytraeus, Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn 1594), p. 594. That book has not been inspected here; Norlind names no printer. If the citation is wrong, the earliest printing is Gassendi 1654 and the status should be printed_posthumously. Two further questions follow if it is right: how did Chytraeus get the text (a visit to Hven? Tycho's circle at Rostock, where his brother David Chytraeus taught and corresponded with Tycho?), and does Resen 1668 derive from Chytraeus (as Norlind suspects) or from an independent Danish witness?
  • the HVEN NOTEBOOK. Norlind's page references within Copenhagen, KB, Thott 4to 1927 (verses at p. 11; prose with 'Kal. Aug.' at p. 7) have not been checked against the manuscript, and its dating and its character as a pupil's notebook from the Uraniborg school are Norlind's judgement. Dreyer did not know or did not use it: it would be the earliest witness to the text.

Horoscopus principis Christiani — Horoscope of Prince Christian

Nativity horoscope of the newborn Prince Christian (the later Christian IV), first-born son of Frederik II (born 12 April 1577), drawn up at the King's command and dated on Hven 1 July 1577.

Full heading
Horoscopus principis Christiani
Form
Horoscope (this catalogue)
Date
1577 secure

Dated subscription in the text: 'Datum in Insula Hvena. Cal. Iulij Anno 1577'; tekstnet 1577; written on Hven, so hven period despite the year being the boundary's first

The text dates itself twice: the title reads 'Horoscopus serenissimi regis Christiani IVti, ad mandatum serenissimi regis Friderici IIdi a Tychone Brahe Ottonide conscriptus in insula Hvena Calendis Iulij anno 1577' (TBOO I, p. 181), and the dedication is subscribed 'Datum in Insula Hvena. Cal. Iulij Anno 1577' (TBOO I, p. 184). The subject was born 12 April 1577, so the work was completed on Hven eleven weeks after the birth. Dreyer 1890 (p. 145) reports the same: Tycho was directed to prepare the horoscope and 'on the 1st July following he handed in a detailed report'.

Addressee
Christian, prince (Christian IV) (native and dedicatee); Frederik II (commissioner)
Language
Latin
Summary
A full genethliacal horoscope in Latin prose for the newborn Prince Christian, later Christian IV, cast by Tycho on Hven and dated 1 July 1577. It has three parts. First a dedicatory epistle to the infant prince, defending astrology from experience and from the microcosm-macrocosm analogy, and rebutting those who 'either from their own ignorance, or from the abuse of the art, or from practitioners' errors, take away all certainty from so divine an art' (TBOO I, 183-184). Then an astronomical section: Tycho takes the reported birth-time as 12 April 1577, 4.5 hours after noon, at Frederiksborg (lat. c. 56 deg.), computes each planet's place from the Prutenic Tables ('exactissimus prae coeteris' because founded on Copernicus's restitution of the motions), appends the Alphonsine places for comparison, and then corrects several planetary places from his own observations made on the nights before and after the birth; he divides the houses by the method of Campanus, expressly rejecting Regiomontanus's as unequal and not universal, and prints the circular figura natalis, tables of aspects, antiscia and directions (TBOO I, 185-193; figure at p. 190). Finally the 'Astrologicum judicium huius inclytae geniturae' works through the standard topical questions — nutrition, the course of life and the fatal years, the lord of the geniture, complexion, character, stature, illnesses, studies, fortune, honours and dignities, riches, journeys, marriage, children, parents and siblings, friends and enemies — closing with the caution that the whole is 'coniectura quaedam physica', not an inviolable decree, since God disposes all things freely, and with the couplet 'Ille potest Solis currus inhibere volantes, / Ille augere potest, tollere fata potest' (TBOO I, 193-208).
Occasion
A royal commission, stated in the document itself. The title says the horoscope was written 'ad mandatum serenissimi regis Friderici IIdi', and in the dedication Tycho tells the infant prince that he undertook the burden because his father King Frederik II demanded it of him and 'it would be a sin not to obey his command' (TBOO I, 181, 184). The birth of the heir on 12 April 1577 is the occasion; the horoscope belongs to Tycho's standing obligations as royal client on Hven — Oestmann 2002 (p. 87) notes that as court astronomer Tycho owed Frederik II an annual almanac and was commissioned to cast the nativities of the three newborn princes (Christian 1577, Ulrik 1579, Hans 1583). Dreyer, in his TBOO Prolegomena (p. XV), makes the same point and adds the negative control that decides it: vulgar judicial astrology did not please Tycho, and apart from these three royal horoscopes 'almost no other examples of such predictions are found among his manuscripts' — he wrote them 'regis hortatu', at the king's urging.
On the addressee
Dedicated to the infant prince: 'Inclyto & illustri infanti Christiano, opt. & potentiss. principis Friderici IIIdi Daniae & Norvegiae regis domini clementissimi filio primogenito' (TBOO I, 183) — Prince Christian (b. Frederiksborg 12 April 1577, d. 1648), firstborn son of Frederik II of Denmark-Norway (1534–1588) and Queen Sophie of Mecklenburg; king as Christian IV from his father's death in 1588 (crowned 1596). The commissioner, and the man to whom the finished report was actually handed, is Frederik II himself. Dreyer 1890 (p. 145) conjectures that the German rendering of the astrological judgement appended in the manuscripts was made 'probably for the convenience of the queen' — Sophie of Mecklenburg — but he offers this as a guess, and it is recorded here as one.
Transmission
Manuscript, in many copies, and none of them the presentation original. Dreyer's base text is Copenhagen, Kongelige Bibliotek, Gl. kgl. Samling (Ant. Coll. Reg.) 1821 in 4to; he also collated GKS 1820 in 4to, Ny kgl. Samling 620c in fol., Thott 831 in fol. and Thott 1611 in 4to, Langebek's Excerpta 179, the Ledreborg codex 108 in 4to and 8vo, and — crucially — 'primum ipsius Tychonis exemplum', Tycho's own first exemplar, in Vienna, cod. lat. 10688 (TBOO I, p. 180). In the Annotationes (TBOO I, p. 314) Dreyer adds that this Tychonic first draft was never brought to completion, and that the copy actually delivered to King Frederik II appears to have perished ('illud tamen exemplum, quod ipsi regi Friderico II traditum est, intercidisse videtur') — unlike the horoscopes of the younger princes Ulrik and Hans, whose presentation copies survive in green silk covers with gilt edges (GKS 1822 and 1823 in 4to). The surviving Copenhagen copies are demonstrably post-1588: their title calls the subject 'serenissimus rex Christianus IV', a style he did not have until his father's death (Dreyer 1890, p. 145 n.1; Oestmann 2002, p. 87). First printing: J. L. E. Dreyer (ed.), Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, tom. I (Copenhagen 1913), pp. 179–208, from GKS 1821.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (first printed in TBOO I (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1913

Never printed in Tycho's lifetime, and never printed at all before TBOO. Dreyer's headnote is explicit: 'Horoscopum principis Christiani nunc primum edimus e codice Hauniensi Ant. Coll. Reg. 1821 in 4o' — we now publish it for the first time (TBOO I, p. 180). Nielsen's Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600 and Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, the authority on Tycho's printed corpus, know twelve publications and four lost prints, and the horoscope is in neither list: it has no Nielsen number and is not among the lost Uraniborg prints. Nor would a printing be expected — this is a confidential court document delivered in manuscript to the king. First printing therefore: TBOO I (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1913), pp. 179–208, edited by J. L. E. Dreyer. Note that Dreyer prints the Latin only; the German version of the astrological judgement that accompanied the manuscript copies (TBOO I, p. 314: 'omnibus enim his horoscopis interpretationes Germanicae accesserunt') is not printed in TBOO I, 181-208.

  • TBOO I, p. XV — The occasion as a royal command and the negative control: 'Quod nihilo minus trium regis Daniae filiorum horoscopos accuratos conscripsit, regis hortatu fecit, et inter libros ejus manu scriptos alia exempla talium praedictionum fere nulla inveniuntur.'
  • Nielsen 1921, no entry; the twelve publications and four lost prints — That the horoscope has no printed edition in Tycho's lifetime, no Nielsen number, and is not among the recorded lost Uraniborg prints — i.e. the claim that TBOO I (1913) is its first printing.
  • Dreyer 1890, pp. 145–152 (esp. 145 and n.1, 146, 152) — Independent narrative account: the king directed Tycho to prepare the horoscope and he handed in the report on 1 July; the original is not preserved but two copies (of somewhat later date, since the prince was not king until 1588) are in the Royal Library; the Latin report ends with a German translation of the predictions, 'probably prepared for the convenience of the queen'; the figura natalis is circular, not the usual square; the closing couplet 'Ille potest Solis currus inhibere volantes, / Ille augere potest, tollere fata potest.'

  • Zeeberg 1994, pp. 80–81; p. 221 (commentary on v. 319); appendix by Ove von Spaeth, p. 312 — That Tycho describes his prognostic method in this horoscope as directio (one degree of equatorial arc = one year of life); that the dedication's polemic against astrology's critics is one of his sharpest statements on the subject; that he uses the medium coeli to find the dominus geniturae (citing TBOO I.197.13); and (von Spaeth) that the three princes' horoscopes, now in the Royal Library's manuscript collection, use the Campanus house system — a reconstruction that agrees with Tycho's own statement at TBOO I, 190.
Open questions
  • How many manuscript copies really survive, and where? Dreyer 1890 (p. 145) says 'two copies... in the Royal Library at Copenhagen', and Oestmann 2002 (p. 87) repeats 'two copies written after 1588'; but Dreyer's own 1913 headnote (TBOO I, 180) collates at least seven witnesses besides Tycho's Vienna draft (GKS 1821 and 1820, NKS 620c, Thott 831 and 1611, Langebek's Excerpta 179, Ledreborg 108), and calls the transmission 'satis multis libris manu scriptis'. The two statements are not strictly contradictory — 1890 may count only the two chief Copenhagen copies — but the modern literature has evidently inherited the 1890 figure without checking it against the 1913 edition, and no census of the witnesses has been made here.
  • Oestmann (2002, p. 87) says the birth-date given in the circular figure is false and 'should read April 12th'. Inspection of the plate at TBOO I, 190 confirms the discrepancy: the figure is inscribed 'ANNO 1577 Aprilis D. H. M. 11. 4. 30.' while the text at p. 185 computes for 12 April, 4.5 hours after noon. Whether this is a scribal error in the copy Dreyer reproduced, or an artefact of Tycho's astronomical day-reckoning from noon (a convention Ove von Spaeth invokes for Tycho's own nativity in Zeeberg 1994, p. 313), is not settled by any source consulted here.
  • The German version. Dreyer states in 1890 (p. 145) that the manuscript report ends with a German translation of the astrological predictions, and in 1913 (TBOO I, 314) that German interpretations accompanied all three royal horoscopes — but TBOO I, 181-208 prints the Latin only. The German text of Prince Christian's horoscope therefore appears to remain unpublished; which manuscripts carry it, and whether it is Tycho's own rendering (as he says it is for one of the other two princes), has not been established here.
  • Tycho's own first exemplar, Vienna cod. lat. 10688 — described by Dreyer as unfinished ('ad perfectionem non adductum') — has not been examined for this record. It is the only witness with a claim to autograph status, and a hand-check against the Graphonomicon's brahe-tycho grid would settle how much of it is Tycho's own writing and how far the draft got.
  • The presentation copy handed to Frederik II is presumed lost by Dreyer (TBOO I, 314). No later search for it is recorded in the sources used here; given that the presentation copies of the Ulrik and Hans horoscopes survive in the Royal Library (GKS 1822, 1823), its disappearance is worth a targeted hunt rather than an assumption.

Horoscopus principis Huldarici — Horoscope of Prince Ulrik

Nativity horoscope of Prince Ulrik, second-born son of Frederik II (born 30 December 1578), computed with planetary positions Tycho corrected from his own observations and dedicated to the infant in May 1579.

Full heading
Horoscopus Principis Huldarici
Form
Horoscope (this catalogue)
Date
1579 secure

Title-page dedication in the text: 'ANNO 1579 MENSE MAIO'; tekstnet 1579

May 1579, on the manuscript's own authority. The dedicatory heading of the presentation manuscript ends 'ANNO 1579 MENSE MAIO' (TBOO I, p. 211), and the KB catalogue title likewise reads '... dicatum 1579'. The nativity it interprets is that of a birth on 30 December 1578: 'TEMPUS huius Inclytae Geniturae mihi relatum & aestimatiue sumtum fuit Anno 1578 Decembris die 30 hora 5 m. 30' (TBOO I, p. 213). Thoren independently places the work in the spring of 1579, with the finished volume ready for the king by May. So: subject born 30 December 1578, judgement written and dedicated May 1579.

Addressee
Ulrik, prince (native and dedicatee); Frederik II (commissioner)
Language
Latin
Summary
A full genethlialogical judgement — some forty printed pages — on the nativity of Ulrik, second son of Frederick II of Denmark-Norway, born 30 December 1578 at (as reported to Tycho, and estimated by him) 5h 30m. It opens with the astronomical apparatus: the radix figure, the houses divided 'per circulum verticalem ex intersectione Horizontis & Meridiani procedentem' (the Campanus method, not the Regiomontanan one most contemporaries used), planetary places corrected in longitude and latitude 'secundum propriam in eorum motu experientiam' — that is, against Tycho's own observations — then tables of planetary latitudes, aspects and antiscia, annual profections, directions of the aphetic places, and the direction of Mars, lord of the geniture. The judgement proper runs in three parts (bodily goods: lord of the geniture, life and its course with an enumeration of the fatal years, complexion, bodily habit, diseases; goods of the soul: character, intellect, vices; external goods: fortune, journeys, work, wealth, honours, marriage, children, friends and enemies, servants, death). Tycho computes the length of life two ways — 53.5 years by the Arab alchochoden reckoning, 52 by the Latin one, 'circiter 50 vel paulo plus' — and then discards the whole procedure as insufficiently firm and neglected 'a Ptolomeo & probatioribus Astrologis', substituting a year-by-year list of the dangerous ages; he predicts death from a slow chronic disease whose origin the physicians will scarcely understand. The Conclusio is an explicit disclaimer: these are not oracles and imply no fatal necessity, only 'physicas quasdam... coniecturas', alterable by God the first cause and by man's own free will ('habet ipse Homo Mentem diuinae particulam Aurae, qua voluntatem liberam exercet').
Occasion
The birth of a second prince. Queen Sophie bore Frederick II a second son at the end of December 1578, and Tycho — who as the king's client and de facto court astronomer already owed the crown an annual astrological almanac — produced the nativity, as he had done for Crown Prince Christian in 1577 and would do again for Prince Hans in 1583. Thoren notes that the project even slowed Tycho's work on the comet of 1577 over the winter of 1578-79. The finished volume, a green-velvet presentation manuscript in his own hand, was ready to hand to the king by May 1579. The two authorities differ in emphasis on whether it was formally ordered: Oestmann says Tycho 'was commissioned to cast horoscopes for the new born princes, Christian in 1577, Ulrik in 1579 and Hans in 1583'; Christianson describes it as 'a gift and benefit to his royal patrons', 'precisely the kind of gift expected of him in the reciprocal system of scientific patronage'. No royal warrant for the Ulrik nativity has been cited by either (unlike the Christian horoscope, whose manuscript title says it was written 'ad mandatum Friderici II').
On the addressee
Dedicated to the infant himself: Prince Ulrik of Denmark (b. 30 December 1578; d. 1624), second son of King Frederick II of Denmark-Norway and Queen Sophie of Mecklenburg, and younger brother of the future Christian IV. The heading reads 'INCLYTO INFANTI HULDARICO FRIDERICI DANIAE ET NORVAGIAE REGIS POTENTISSIMI ET FOELICISSIMI FILIO SECUNDOGENITO... FECIT & HUMILITER DICAUIT TYCHO BRAHE OTTONIDES'. The actual recipient of the physical book, however, was the king: Dreyer notes that the surviving exemplars of the two younger princes' horoscopes are 'illa quidem ipsa, quae regi tradita sunt' — the very copies handed to Frederick II. Not to be confused with the later Prince Ulrik, son of Christian IV, who recovered Tycho's great globe from the Jesuit college at Neisse in 1632 (Dreyer 1890).
Transmission
A single manuscript witness, and it is the presentation copy itself. Dreyer's headnote names it: 'codex Hauniensis Ant. Coll. Reg. 1822 in 4°' = Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Gammel Kongelig Samling (GKS) 1822 kvart, catalogued there as 'Tychonis Brahei Ottonidis Genethliacon inclyto infanti Huldarico, Fred. IIdi Filio secundo genito, dicatum 1579'. In his Annotationes Editoris (TBOO I, p. 314, 'Ad horoscopos filiorum regis') Dreyer sets out the transmission of all three princely horoscopes and distinguishes them sharply: the Christian horoscope of 1577 survives in a number of manuscript copies (the copy actually given to the king being lost), whereas of the two younger princes' horoscopes only single exemplars exist — 'atque illa quidem ipsa, quae regi tradita sunt, quare viridi involucro holoserico nitide ornata et in extrema charta auro illita sunt' (the very copies handed to the king, elegantly bound in green all-silk and gilt on the edges) — and of these two the Ulrik volume is 'totum... ipsius Tychonis manu scriptum', written throughout in Tycho's own hand, whereas in the Hans volume only the German interpretation is autograph. Gigas 1900, describing the KB Tycho bindings, independently records GKS 1822 as the 1579 Ulrik horoscope in green velvet with gilt edges and lily ornaments. Dreyer further states that German interpretations accompanied all these horoscopes ('Omnibus enim his horoscopis interpretationes Germanicae accesserunt'); for Ulrik he printed only the Latin. So: the words survive in one autograph presentation manuscript, in Copenhagen, and reached print for the first time in Dreyer, TBOO I (1913), pp. 209–250.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (first printed in TBOO I (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia; Nielsen none — no horoscope appears anywhere in Nielsen's Brahe entries

never printed in Tycho's lifetime, and never printed at all before 1913. Lauritz Nielsen's enumerative bibliography of Tycho's printed output (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, §§424-433 and §§975-976; Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921) records no horoscope of any kind: the princely nativities were manuscript presentation objects, not press products, and in 1579 Tycho had in any case no press of his own (it was not planned until 1583-84 and produced its first known imprint in late 1584). Dreyer's own headnote to the text is decisive on the first printing: 'Horoscopum Principis Huldarici NUNC PRIMUM EDIMUS e codice Hauniensi Ant. Coll. Reg. 1822 in 4°' (TBOO I, p. 210). The editio princeps is therefore Dreyer's, in TBOO I (Hauniae 1913), pp. 209–250.

Reg. 1822 in 4°' (first printing, and the single MS witness); the dedication to the infant Ulrik dated 'anno 1579 mense Maio'; the birth datum 30 December 1578, 5h 30m, 'relatum & aestimatiue sumtum'; the Campanus house division and the correction of planetary places from Tycho's own observations; the computed life-span (c. 50 years) and Tycho's rejection of the method; the free-will Conclusio.
  • TBOO I, p. 314 — The transmission: single exemplars of the two younger princes' horoscopes survive, and these are the very copies handed to King Frederick II, bound in green silk with gilt edges; the Ulrik volume is written throughout in Tycho's own hand; German interpretations accompanied all three horoscopes; Dreyer's reason for printing them entire (their exceptional astronomical care, against e.g. Cardano's twelve genitures of 1554).
  • TBOO VIII, §§424-433, 975-976 (whole corpus of printed Brahe); Bogtrykkeri pp. 175–179 — The negative bibliographic finding on which the 'never printed / first printed in TBOO' claim rests: Nielsen's complete enumeration of Tycho's printed output contains no horoscope, and Tycho had no press before late 1584. This is the authority that would record a lifetime printing if one existed.
  • Thoren 1990, pp. 138 (with n. 89) and 141-142 (with n. 99) — The occasion and date: 'the birth of a second prince in December 1578 and the consequent necessity of working up a second horoscope' (n. 89: 'The horoscope is printed in I, 209-50'); 'during the spring he produced a horoscope for Frederick's second princeling. By May Tycho had a small volume "bound in pale green velvet with gilt edges, containing about three hundred pages all written in [his] own hand" ready to deliver to the king.'
  • Christianson 2000, p. 66 (with ch. 3 n. 21, p. 706); cf. pp. 62 and 107 — The occasion in patronage terms: 'At the end of the year, the queen gave birth to a second son, christened Ulrik, and Tycho Brahe duly prepared a detailed nativity as a gift and benefit to his royal patrons' (n. 21 = TBOO I, 209-50; Ulrik's life summarised in Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, Bech 1979-84, 15: 168-9); that Tycho 'drew up a horoscope for each of the sons born to King Frederick II and Queen Sophie'; and the caution that Figala 1972, p. 144, calling him 'Uldarius', reported Ulrik to have been later Tycho's assistant in chemistry, 'but I have found no evidence that this was true'.
  • Christianson 2000, p. 87 with n. 20 — The commission framing ('As a court astronomer to King Frederik II of Denmark Tycho was to deliver an annual almanac and he was commissioned to cast horoscopes for the new born princes, Christian in 1577, Ulrik in 1579 and Hans in 1583'); the shelfmark and TBOO locus (n. 20: 'Copenhagen, Det kongelige Bibliotek: Gamle kongelig Samling, 1822 4° (TBOO, vol. 1, p. 209-250)'); and the identification of Tycho's house-division system as that of Campanus rather than Regiomontanus.
  • Gigas 1900, the KB copy-list, item 10 — The physical presentation object: 'GKS 1822, 4° — horoscope for Frederik II's son Ulrik (1579); green velvet, gilt edges, lily ornaments' — corroborating Dreyer's description of the binding from an independent examination of the volume.
  • KB manuscript catalogue, GKS 1822 kvart; permalink https://soeg.kb.dk/permalink/45KBDK_KGL/16bqo9j/alma99122192378105763 — The surviving manuscript and its catalogue title: 'Tychonis Brahei Ottonidis Genethliacon inclyto infanti Huldarico, Fred. IIdi Filio secundo genito, dicatum 1579' — the sole located witness.
  • Dreyer 1890, pp. 145–152 (the Christian horoscope, treated as the type-specimen of Tycho's genethlialogy); p. 285 n. (Prince Ulrik, son of Christian IV, and the great globe at Neisse in 1632) — The technique and rhetoric of Tycho's princely horoscopes generally (Dreyer summarises the 1577 Christian horoscope, not the 1579 Ulrik one); and the disambiguation of the two Princes Ulrik.
Open questions
  • Was it formally commissioned or offered? Oestmann (2002, p. 87) says Tycho 'was commissioned to cast horoscopes for the new born princes... Ulrik in 1579'; Christianson (2000, p. 66) calls it 'a gift and benefit to his royal patrons'. Neither cites a royal warrant for the Ulrik nativity, whereas the 1577 Christian horoscope's manuscript title expressly says it was written 'ad mandatum Friderici II'. The disagreement is left standing.
  • The German interpretation. Dreyer states that German interpretations accompanied all three princely horoscopes ('Omnibus enim his horoscopis interpretationes Germanicae accesserunt', TBOO I p. 314), and for Prince Hans he printed the German text; for Ulrik he printed only the Latin. Whether the German judgement is still bound in GKS 1822, and why Dreyer did not print it, has not been established here. KB also holds NKS 296 kvart, 'Ein astrologisch Urtheil von diesem hochgeb. jungen Herrn sein Nativitet', attributed to Tycho and suspected by the KB sweep to belong with the princely horoscopes — but no link to GKS 1822 has been demonstrated.
  • The physical extent of GKS 1822. Thoren (1990, p. 142) describes the volume as 'containing about three hundred pages all written in [his] own hand', citing TBOO I, 209-50; neither Dreyer's note nor Gigas gives a leaf-count, and the manuscript has not been collated here. The figure is unverified.
  • The birth time. Tycho says the moment was 'relatum & aestimatiue sumtum' — reported to him and taken by estimate. He does not say who reported it, nor on what basis he rectified it. (For the parallel 1577 horoscope Oestmann notes that Tycho's circular scheme carries a false date of birth.)
  • Figala (1972, p. 144), calling him 'Uldarius', reported that Prince Ulrik was later said to have been Tycho's assistant in chemistry; Christianson (2000, p. 706 n. 21) states he found no evidence for this. Treat the claim as unsupported.
  • The prince's birth is sometimes given as 1579; Tycho's own text gives 30 December 1578. The TBOO title is 'Horoscopus Principis Huldarici' ('Genethliacon' is the KB catalogue's wording).

Full heading
Inscriptiones Uraniburgi (Indskrifter fra Uraniborg)
Form
Inscription (this catalogue)
Date
c. 1580–1585 uncertain — the edition: 1576

the edition's year 1576 — the founding year of Uraniborg; the inscriptions belong to the built house on Hven, so the boundary year is assigned to the Hven period by documented context

Correction. The edition's 1576 is the year of the foundation stone; no source dates the nine inscriptions, which survive only in Resen's transcription of 1668.

No source dates any of the nine inscriptions. The 1576 carried by the edition's index is Uraniborg's foundation year — the foundation stone was laid 8 August 1576 (Mechanica, TBOO V p. 143) — and is a period-assignment, not an attested date of composition. Every inscription in the set is fixed to a room or a fitting of the finished house (the Museum, the furnace, the optical mirror, the door of the hypocaust, the roof, the clock), so none can be earlier than the fabric it adorns: Tycho announced the house 'finished' to Hagecius on 4 November 1580 and the interior complete to Scultetus by 12 October 1581, the cupola clock's lantern bell was paid for by Frederik II on 4 June 1581, and the roof-turret Four Seasons statues belong to the completed roof (Beckett & Christensen, Uraniborg og Stjaerneborg, 1921). The Platonic dictum in the Museum is attested as physically present, cut in gold letters on porphyry, by Tycho himself in the Epistolae of 1596 (TBOO VI p. 269) — so that one at least stood before 1596. A range of c. 1580–1585 is an inference from the building history, not a documented date.

Place
Uraniborg
Language
Latin
Summary
Nine short Latin inscriptions — mottoes, sententiae and two pieces of verse — transmitted as a group under the rubric 'Inscriptiones Uraniburgi' and each keyed to a place in Tycho's house on Hven: 'In Museo' (NON HABERI, SED ESSE, Tycho's own motto), 'Sub Baccho' (STULTITIA IN VINIS, FERVOR IN IGNE FURIT), 'Sub Sole aureo' (CALOR ET COLOR OMNIA PANDIT), 'Dictum Platonis' (UNUM EST NATURAE VINCULUM, DOCTRINA NUMERORUM FIGURARUM ET MOTUUM COELESTIUM — from Plato's Epinomis), 'Ad fornacem', at the laboratory furnace (the paronomastic IN MVNDO CALLET CALLIDVS CALET IMMVNDO), 'Circum speculum opticum', round the optical mirror (EXTERIORA PATENT, INFERIORA LATENT), 'Supra Januam Hypocausti', over the door of the heated room (a chiasmus: DOMI LATERE / CONSPICI — CONSPICI / LATERE FORIS), 'Supra tectum in quatuor anni tempora' — four hexameters, one each for VER, AESTAS, AUTUMNUS and HYEMS, for the roof — and 'In ambitum Horologii', round the rim of the clock, an elegiac distich in which the clock speaks: 'ME TYCHO BRAHORUM SOBOLES, TESTARER UT HORAS, / IMPOSUIT CELSIS AEDIBUS URANIAE' ('Tycho, offspring of the Brahes, set me on the high house of Urania, that I might tell the hours'). The set is thus not a literary composition but the epigraphic programme of the building itself, read off its rooms and fittings: the library-museum in the south turret, the alchemical laboratory, the winter room, the roof with its four Season statues on the corner turrets, and the cupola clock. Dreyer prints them, in this order and under these rubrics, at TBOO VI pp. 368–369.
Occasion
Not an occasional piece and not recoverable as an event. The inscriptions were made for the fabric of Uraniborg as it was built and decorated, and no source records why any individual motto was chosen or when it was cut. What is documented is only the frame: Tycho furnished the Museum, in his own printed words, 'with many other elegant things suited to a Museum, and here and there with several pictures, and also with poems and shrewd sayings of the philosophers, such as that Platonic one in the Epinomis... which is inscribed in gold letters on a porphyry stone' (Epistolae astronomicae liber primus, TBOO VI p. 269). That sentence is the only contemporary statement of purpose we have for any of the nine: the mottoes are part of the decorative and didactic programme of the house, of a piece with the painted astronomer-portraits and the great globe in the same room. Beyond that, the occasion of each inscription is unknown, and no authority supplies one. Note too that not all of the nine are Tycho's composition: the Dictum Platonis is a quotation of Plato (Epinomis 976 E sq., a passage Dreyer says Tycho greatly admired and which he also set at the head of his 1589 fixed-star observations), and NON HABERI, SED ESSE is his personal motto, already in use on the de Gheyn portrait of 1586. Whether he wrote the four Season hexameters and the clock distich himself is likely but nowhere stated.
Transmission
The physical inscriptions are lost with the building. The words survive because Peder Hansen Resen (1625–1688) printed them in his Inscriptiones Haffnienses (Copenhagen, 1668), p. 334, under the head 'Inscriptiones Uraniburgi'. Dreyer reprints Resen's text in full, rubric by rubric, in the Annotationes editoris to TBOO VI, pp. 368–369, in the note on p. 269, 26 (the note that begins with Plato's Epinomis and ends 'Inscriptiones Uraniburgi sic tradit Resenius in Inscriptionibus Haffniensibus [Hauniae 1668] p. 334'). This is the whole chain: no manuscript witness is named by Dreyer, and no earlier printing is cited by him. Dreyer makes one editorial intervention, in a footnote to p. 369: against the mirror motto's 'EXTERIORA PATENT, INFERIORA LATENT' he writes 'Scriptum fuit sine dubio: INTERIORA' — i.e. he takes Resen's INFERIORA for a corruption of INTERIORA ('outward things lie open, inward things lie hidden'), which the antithesis and Tycho's portrait epigram 'Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei: / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior' (TBOO IX p. 175) both support. Note that this set sits in Dreyer's editorial apparatus, not among the Carmina: the other Uraniborg inscriptions — the foundation-stone verses (from Gassendi, Vita, Paris 1654, p. 300), the verses for the printing house, and those round Tycho's effigy and arms (from Resen, pp. 333 sqq.) — are printed as texts at TBOO IX p. 175.
Channel
Printed after his death (Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses, 1668)
Printing
printed posthumously — Copenhagen, 1668; Nielsen none

Tycho never printed this set. It appears nowhere in Nielsen's catalogue of the Tycho corpus or in his account of the Uraniborg press (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; 'Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen', 1921), whose products — the Diarium 1586, the Epitaphium Pratensis 1584, the Orthographia arcis Uranienburg 1585, the Icones, the Flemloese Astrologia 1591, and the rest — are individually enumerated and do not include the inscriptions. The only trace of any of them in a lifetime imprint is indirect: in the Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus (Uraniborg, 1596) Tycho reports that the Platonic dictum stands in his Museum in gold letters on porphyry, but he paraphrases rather than quotes it, and gives none of the other eight (TBOO VI p. 269; the German version of the same description, p. 262, expressly defers the 'Lateinische Vers und Schrifften' to the Latin explication). The group was first printed — as far as any authority in this register records — by Peder Hansen Resen, Inscriptiones Haffnienses (Copenhagen, 1668), p. 334, sixty-seven years after Tycho's death, in the same run of pages (pp. 331–335) that carries the Uraniborg foundation-stone verses, the printing-house verses, and the mottoes round Tycho's portrait and arms. Dreyer's TBOO VI (1919) is therefore not the first printing; it is a reprint of Resen. The printer of Resen's book is not named in the sources consulted here.

Open questions
  • Where did Resen get the texts? Uraniborg was derelict long before 1668 — the fabric was pulled down and quarried in the decades after Tycho left Hven in 1597, and by the nineteenth century only foundations remained to be excavated — so Resen cannot have copied the mottoes from standing walls. Neither Resen (as quoted by Dreyer) nor Dreyer names an intermediary manuscript, an earlier printed source, or an eyewitness transcript. The single most important question about this text — what stands between the walls of Uraniborg and the page of the Inscriptiones Haffnienses — is unanswered in the sources consulted here.
  • INFERIORA or INTERIORA? Resen's text of the optical-mirror motto reads 'EXTERIORA PATENT, INFERIORA LATENT'; Dreyer footnotes it 'Scriptum fuit sine dubio: INTERIORA' (TBOO VI p. 369). The DSL edition keeps INFERIORA. Dreyer's conjecture is unargued beyond the antithesis, and no independent witness adjudicates it.
  • Authorship of the individual pieces is nowhere asserted. The Dictum Platonis is a quotation from Plato (Epinomis 976 E sq.) and NON HABERI, SED ESSE is Tycho's device, in use on the de Gheyn portrait by 1586; whether Tycho himself composed the four Season hexameters (which are of a common humanist type), the furnace paronomasia, the chiastic hypocaust motto and the clock distich is likely but is not stated by Resen, by Dreyer, or by any authority in this register.
  • The boundary of the 'work' is an editorial construction, not a Tycho-authored collection. The nine mottoes are simply what Resen chose to transcribe under 'Inscriptiones Uraniburgi'. Other inscriptions from the same buildings are transmitted elsewhere and separately: the foundation-stone verses (TBOO IX p. 175, from Gassendi), the printing-house verses and the mottoes round Tycho's effigy and arms (TBOO IX p. 175, from Resen pp. 333 sqq.), the great globe's gold-letter horizon inscription of 1584 (TBOO VI p. 268, printed by Tycho himself), the verse tablet hung by Copernicus's parallactic instrument, dated 23 July 1584 (TBOO VI pp. 266–267), the Stjerneborg portal inscription of 1585 (Beckett & Christensen), and the paper-mill stone of 1590-92 (TBOO VI p. 365). Whether the Uraniborg epigraphic programme should be registered as one work or several is a decision this register makes, not one the sources make.
  • No date, and no order of composition, is recoverable for any of the nine. The c. 1580–1585 range given here is inferred from the building history alone; a narrower date would require a source none of the authorities consulted supplies.
