Horoscopus principis Johannis — Horoscope of Prince Hans

HoroscopesecureHvenARead the text →brahe-t_horoscopus-principis-johannis

Nativity horoscope of Duke Hans, third-born son of Frederik II (born 26 July 1583), prepared at the royal command in 1583, with a Latin preface defending astrological prediction as physically grounded conjecture that leaves human free will intact.

Full heading
Horoscopus Principis Johannis
Form
Horoscope (this catalogue)
Date
1583 secure

Title page in the text: 'BESTELLETT DURCH TYCHO BRAHE ANNO 1583'; natal figure dated 26 July 1583; tekstnet 1583

The German title-leaf of the manuscript is dated 'ANNO 1583' (TBOO I, p. 253), and the nativity is cast for the birth of the prince on 26 July 1583, 9h 20m (figura natalis, TBOO I, p. 255). The exact month of delivery within 1583 is not documented; for the parallel Ulrik horoscope (born 30 Dec. 1578) Dreyer records presentation in May 1579, i.e. some months after the birth (Dreyer 1890, p. 153).

Addressee
Hans, prince (native); Frederik II (commissioner and dedicatee)
Language
Latin
Summary
A full genethliacal treatise — not a chart but a book: a manuscript quarto of some 46 leaves in Latin, prefaced by a German title-leaf, casting and interpreting the nativity of Prince Hans, third and last son of King Frederik II of Denmark-Norway, born 26 July 1583 at 9h 20m. It opens with the figura natalis and two further house-schemes (by equator and by ecliptic), tables of planetary latitudes, aspects, antiscia and directions; then a Praefatio defending judicial astrology as physical conjecture (the stars incline but do not compel; 'prævisa tela minus feriunt'); then the judgement proper, section by section — De planetarum fortitudinibus, De nutritione, De vita eiusque curriculo, De huius geniturae almuten, De temperamento, De moribus, De ingenio, De conformatione et statura corporis, De morbis, De fortuna, De divitiis, De honoribus, De conjugio, De liberis, De servis, De amicis et inimicis, De itineribus, De captivitate, De morte. Its astronomical substance is the point of interest: Tycho states in the preface that he did not take the planetary places from the Alfonsine or the Prutenic tables, since 'crebris observationibus per instrumenta nequaquam fallacia' he had found all such computations to deviate from the truth — he set Sun and Moon by his own restitutions of the luminaries, corrected Saturn, Jupiter, Mars and Venus from his own observations, and kept Copernicus only for Mercury (TBOO I, p. 262). The verdict is grim and heavily hedged: a sickly life, grave danger around years 12, 15, 18, 30, 40 and 43 (both Ptolemy's apheta-to-anareta direction and the Arabs' alchocoden give the boy scarcely twelve years), no distinction of name, a middling fortune — but death natural rather than violent, possibly abroad (TBOO I, pp. 263–268, 279-280).
Occasion
A royal commission, and a contractual one. As Frederik II's court astronomer Tycho owed the crown an annual almanac and a nativity for each newborn prince; he cast three — Christian in 1577, Ulrik in 1579, and Hans in 1583 (Oestmann, in Crossroads 2002, p. 87). The preface says so in Tycho's own words: 'Cum mihi ab Illustriss. Majestate Regia injunctum sit hujus Inclytae Geniturae Astrologicam explicationem conscribere' — the king ordered it (TBOO I, p. 261). Dreyer, who read all three, judged that Tycho by now set little store by the exercise ('he did not care to waste his time on work of so very doubtful value'), and notes that in this third one he 'seems more doubtful about the results to be expected than he was in 1577' (Dreyer 1890, pp. 154, 156).
On the addressee
King Frederik II of Denmark-Norway (1534–1588), who commissioned the work and to whom the presentation volume was delivered — the surviving manuscript is that copy. The subject (the native) is his third son, Prince Hans / Johann (b. 26 July 1583 at Haderslevhus), styled on the German title-leaf 'des hochgebornen und großmechtigen Königes Fridericks des Andern zw Denemarck und Norweden etc. drittgebornenn Sons Herzuch Hans' (TBOO I, p. 253; birthplace from Danske Magazin II, 1746, p. 219). Dreyer's own note on the two younger princes' horoscopes describes them as 'de duobus regis filiis aetate inferioribus, qui amplum dignitatis statum numquam assecuti sunt' (TBOO I, p. 314).
Transmission
One manuscript, and it is the king's own copy. Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Gamle Kongelige Samling (Dreyer's 'Antiqua Collectio Regia') 1823, 4° — cited by Dreyer as the sole witness at TBOO I, p. 251, and given the modern shelfmark form 'Gamle kongelig Samling, 1823 4°' by Oestmann (Crossroads 2002, p. 87 n. 21). Dreyer's editorial note on the three princely horoscopes (TBOO I, p. 314) explains the situation: of Christian's horoscope only later copies survive and the exemplar handed to the king appears lost, but of the two younger princes' horoscopes single exemplars survive, and those are the very volumes delivered to the king — 'quare viridi involucro holoserico nitide ornata et in extrema charta auro illita sunt' (handsomely bound in green silk, the edges gilt). Of the two, the earlier (Ulrik's, GKS 1822 4°) is wholly in Tycho's hand; of this one only the German rendering is autograph — a point Dreyer repeats in English in 1890: 'the Latin part is neatly written by one of Tycho's assistants, and only the German part by himself' (Dreyer 1890, p. 154; the originals, 'and not merely copies', being 'preserved in the Royal Library at Copenhagen', p. 153). The binding is one of the twelve volumes from Tycho's own bindery catalogued by Gigas 1900: 'GKS 1823, 4° — horoscope for Frederik II's son Hans (1583); green velvet'. The volume's survival was already noted in the eighteenth century: Danske Magazin II (1746), p. 219, records that Tycho cast this prince's nativity and submitted as extensive a treatise on it as on the earlier ones, 'hvilket endnu in Originali er til' — which still exists in the original. Dreyer printed the Latin text (TBOO I, pp. 251–280); the German version that accompanied it in the manuscript is not reproduced there.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (first printed in TBOO I (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia; Nielsen none — no horoscope appears anywhere in Nielsen's enumeration of Tycho's printed corpus (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, §§ 424-433, 975-976; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921)

never printed IN TYCHO'S LIFETIME, and never printed at all before Dreyer. It was a manuscript presentation volume made for the king, and the printing-house on Hven did not yet exist in 1583 (the first Uraniborg imprints are of late 1584). Nielsen's bibliography — the authority that catches every minor Tycho printing the collector references omit — records no horoscope. Dreyer states the first printing explicitly in his headnote: 'Horoscopum Principis Johannis nunc primum edimus [e] codice Hauniensi Ant. Coll. Reg. 1823 in 4°' (TBOO I, p. 251). The editio princeps is therefore TBOO I (Hauniae 1913), pp. 251–280, 330 years after composition.

References

  • TBOO I, p. 253 (German title-leaf, transcribed) — The date (ANNO 1583), the title, and the identification of the native as Frederik II's third-born son, Duke Hans: 'DES HOCHGEBORNEN VND GROSZMECHTIGEN KONIGES FRIDERICHS DES ANDERN ZW DENEMARCK VND NORWEDEN etc. DRITTGEBORNENN SONS HERZVCH HANS NATIVITET BESTELLETT DURCH TYCHO BRAHE ANNO 1583.'
  • TBOO I, p. 255 (figura natalis); pp. 255–260 (tables of latitudes, aspects, antiscia, directiones) — The moment of birth for which the chart is cast — 'Anno 1583 Julii D. 26 H. 9 M. 20' — and the technical apparatus of the horoscope.
  • TBOO I, pp. 261–263 (Praefatio) — The occasion (royal command: 'Cum mihi ab Illustriss. Majestate Regia injunctum sit hujus Inclytae Geniturae Astrologicam explicationem conscribere'); the doctrine that the stars incline but do not compel; and the astronomical method — planetary places not from the Alfonsine or Prutenic tables but from Tycho's own restitutions and observations, Copernicus retained only for Mercury; Campanus-type house division by the prime vertical, with two comparison schemes; directions per Regiomontanus's canons with the time-measure conformed to the true diurnal solar motion.
  • TBOO I, pp. 263–268 (De vita eiusque curriculo); pp. 279–280 (De captivitate, De morte) — The substance of the judgement: danger to life at years 12, 15, 18, 30, 40, 43; Ptolemy's direction of the apheta to the occasus and the Arabs' alchocoden both allowing only about twelve years; the terminal limit at year 66; a natural rather than violent death, and the hint of death away from the fatherland.
  • TBOO I, p. 314 — Transmission and physical form: single exemplars of the two younger princes' horoscopes survive, and they are the copies delivered to the king, bound in green silk with gilt edges; the former (Ulrik's) entirely autograph, of the latter (this one) only the German interpretation in Tycho's hand; all three horoscopes were accompanied by German versions. Also Dreyer's judgement that these treatises surpass all others of their kind in diligence and astronomical subtlety (he compares Cardano's twelve genitures of 1554).
  • Dreyer 1890, pp. 153–154 (also p. 156) — Independent English account: the king's 'third and last son, Hans, was born on the 26th July' 1583; Tycho 'sent in a volume like the last one, bound in the same manner... but the Latin part is neatly written by one of Tycho's assistants, and only the German part by himself'; the two extra square house-figures (by equator and ecliptic); 'He has again corrected the places of the planets by his own observations'; Mercury the strongest planet; only 'mediocre' fortune foretold; the originals — not copies — preserved in the Royal Library, Copenhagen; and Tycho's growing scepticism about the whole exercise.
  • Christianson 2000, p. 87 with n. 21 — The commission as a duty of the court-astronomer's office ('he was commissioned to cast horoscopes for the new born princes, Christian in 1577, Ulrik in 1579 and Hans in 1583'); the shelfmark and TBOO concordance: 'Copenhagen, Det kongelige Bibliotek: Gamle kongelig Samling, 1823 4° (TBOO, vol. 1, p. 251-280)'; and Tycho's use of the Campanus house-division rather than the Regiomontanus 'rational method'.
  • Gigas 1900, §2, no. 11 in the list of Royal Library volumes — The binding of the surviving exemplar: 'GKS 1823, 4° — horoscope for Frederik II's son Hans (1583); green velvet' — one of the twelve volumes attributable to Tycho's own bindery (cf. no. 10, GKS 1822 4°, Ulrik's horoscope of 1579, green velvet with gilt edges).
  • Danske Magazin 1746, p. 219 — Birth data and the survival of the manuscript in the eighteenth century: '1583. den 26. Julii blev Hertug Hans, Kong Friderik den Andens tredie Søn, født paa Haderslevhus. Denne Prindses Nativitet har Tyge Brahe ogsaa stillet, og indgivet lige saa vidtløftigt et Skrift derom, som om de forriges, hvilket endnu in Originali er til.'
  • Nielsen 1921, the complete enumeration of Tycho's printed corpus (12 publications + 4 lost prints) — Negative evidence for printed.status: no horoscope of any of the princes appears among Tycho's printed works, and the Uraniborg press did not begin production until late 1584 — i.e. the piece was never printed in his lifetime.
Open questions
  • Has the German version — which is the part in Tycho's own hand — ever been printed? Dreyer edits the Latin only (TBOO I, pp. 251–280, with the German title-leaf transcribed at p. 253) and does not say whether he omitted the German rendering deliberately; the autograph portion of the volume is therefore the portion that has never appeared in print.
  • The physical extent of GKS 1823, 4° is not consistent across the sources. Dreyer 1890 (p. 153) puts Ulrik's volume at 'about 300 pages' and says the Hans volume contains 'about the same number of pages', whereas the foliation of the Latin part runs only to fol. 46r (about 92 pp.). The likeliest reconciliation is that Dreyer counted the Latin and German parts together (or estimated loosely) — but the leaf-count of the volume has not been verified here against the manuscript.
  • The place-name in the natal figure (TBOO I, p. 255) reads 'Harsleffij'. Danske Magazin II (1746), p. 219 gives the birthplace as Haderslevhus, and the two are presumably the same place, but the reading of the figure has not been checked against the manuscript (the TBOO figure pages are plates).
  • The month of presentation in 1583 is undocumented. Dreyer records that the Ulrik horoscope (birth 30 Dec. 1578) was presented in May 1579; no equivalent date is recorded for this one.
  • Whether Tycho's grim prognosis was ever read against the event is not addressed by any source consulted here: the horoscope's most conspicuous warnings cluster on the prince's youth (years 12, 15, 18) and it hints at death outside the fatherland — but no authority was found comparing the prediction with Prince Hans's actual death, so no such comparison is asserted.
Notes
  • The title page is German ('… NATIVITET BESTELLETT DURCH TYCHO BRAHE …'); the preface and the judgement are Latin.
  • Natal figure place 'Harsleffij' — presumably Haderslev, but the identification is not made in the file itself, so it is kept out of the gloss

Erico Lange — To Erik Lange

ElegysecureHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_erico-lange

Verse epistle to the young nobleman Erik Lange of Engelsholm, advising him to cure lovesickness by taking up instead the loves of astronomy, alchemy and poetry that Uraniborg offers — the first item printed on Tycho's own press, its printing entered in his observation protocol under 27 November 1584; no copy of the printing survives, and the text is transmitted in a later transcript (Copenhagen, Royal Library, Thott 1044 4º).

Full heading
Et generis et ingenij nobilitate juveni claro Erico Lange, dn. de Erigstholm, praesidi arcis Bygholmensis, amico suo integerrimo. S. D.
Form
Elegy (this catalogue)
Date
1584 secure

DSL edition year 1584; Nielsen records the (lost) Uraniborg printing as late 1584, one of the companion poems named in the Ulfeldt broadsheet; Zeeberg 1993 dates the printing 27 November 1584 from the observation protocol (TBOO X, 302) and identifies it as the first item printed on the press.

Subscribed in the text itself: 'Datum Vraniburgi | Anno 1584, 9 Calend. Decembr.' (TBOO XV, p. 5), i.e. Uraniborg, 23 November 1584 — two days before the companion Carmen ad Jacobum Ulfeldium, which is dated VRANIBVRGI 7 Kal. Decemb. (25 November) 1584. The year 1584 is confirmed.

Addressee
Erik Lange (addressee)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — Peter Zeeberg, complete
Summary
A verse letter in elegiac couplets — 84 lines plus a two-line EPILOGUS — addressed by Tycho from Uraniborg to his friend Erik Lange, and built as a rhetorical tour de force in which every pentameter closes on the word amor. Tycho first anatomises the sickness of love (the lover is never at home in himself, 'nunqvam secum habitans, alieno in corpore vivit'; sleepless, blind alike to the Muses, to the fire-secrets of the Vestals and to 'lucidaqve astra poli'), then diagnoses Lange, who is secretly consuming himself in a hidden flame, and prescribes the cure: one love must be the medicine of another ('Fac novus alterius sit medicamen amor') — for Venus and Cupid substitute the love of Pallas, of star-bearing Urania by night, of Vesta's bright fire; come to Uraniborg, where 'in amore potes discere qvid sit amor', and take up either the aethereal art (astronomy) or the fire-bearing art (alchemy). The last third turns the whole thing into a conceit on Tycho's brand-new press: writing was not enough unless the letter came *pressed*, so that the old love should go *sup-pressed* and a new one be *im-pressed* on the mind ('Id si noster amor, si typi et littera pressa / Expedient, aderit mox tibi qvantus amor?'; 'Verior et major typis tua pectora nostris / Musa omnes superos orat ut intret amor').
Occasion
Recoverable from the poem itself and from its companion piece, on two levels. (1) The personal occasion: Erik Lange was in the grip of an unhappy or secret passion — Tycho asks 'Cur flagrante volens furtim te conficis igne?' — and Tycho wrote to cure him of it by redirecting his ardour to learning, astronomy and alchemy, and to draw him to Hven. Tycho names this occasion himself in the Ulfeldt poem, where he says one of his letters seeks Falk Gjøe and 'another wills that Erik Lange should not love' ('Altera vis, LANGVS non vt ERICVS amet', TBOO IX p. 179, l. 10). (2) The occasion for printing it: it belongs to the burst of occasional poems Tycho ran off in late 1584 partly to give his new Uraniborg press something to do — in the Ulfeldt poem of 25 November he tells Ulfeldt to read 'what we sent to Falk, and what to Erik' as written equally for him (TBOO IX p. 179, ll. 23–24). The woman is never named, and Dreyer expressly leaves open whether she was Sophie Brahe (see open_questions).
On the addressee
Erik Lange (1553–1613), Danish nobleman and alchemist; in the heading 'lord of Erigstholm [recte Engelsholm], governor of Bygholm castle' — i.e. Erik Lange til Engelsholm, then lensmand of Bygholm len. A close friend and distant kinsman of Tycho, he pursued the Great Work to his own ruin, was betrothed to Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe (usually dated 1590) and married her only in 1602; he died at Prague in 1613. He is the 'Titan' of Tycho's later elegy Urania Titani (TBOO IX, pp. 193–207), written in Sophie's name to him. It was Lange who brought Nicolaus Reimers Ursus to Uraniborg in 1584, the visit behind the later plagiarism quarrel.
Transmission
Manuscript. The 1584 Uraniborg printing is wholly lost; the words survive because the poem was copied into a Copenhagen codex, Kongelige Bibliotek, coll. Thott. 1044 4to, a miscellany of notes and commentaries written from 1640 onwards and entitled 'Gemmulae selectiores per Achillem Andream Toxotium' (i.e. Achilles Andersen Skytte). The poem was found there by C. Behrend, librarian of the Royal Library, a few years before 1929, and was first printed — 'nunc primum editur' — by J. L. E. Dreyer and J. Ræder in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia XV (Hauniae, 1929), Carminum Appendix, pp. 3–5, with the editors' annotations at p. 6, where the source lemma reads '[E codice Hauniensi coll. Thott. 1044 in 4°]'. It is therefore absent from the Carmina of TBOO IX (1927), which is why accounts built on Nielsen describe the piece as known only from Tycho's own allusion to it.
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the Uraniborg print of 1584, no copy known; the text from the Thott transcript)
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, Hven, 1584 (Tycho Brahe's own press at Uraniborg (pressman not named in the sources))

No exemplar survives. Dreyer: 'Sicut alia carmina Tychonis, quae edidimus in tom. IX pp. 176–177 et 179–190, hoc quoque in ipsius typographia descriptum esse videtur, sed omnia exempla typis descripta perierunt' (TBOO XV, p. 6) — note the hedge 'videtur'. The inference is nevertheless strong: the poem's closing thirty lines are themselves a sustained conceit on being set in type ('nisi pressa veniret / Littera'; 'typi et littera pressa'; 'typis … nostris'), and Tycho's printed Ulfeldt broadside of 25 November 1584 refers to what he had 'sent' to Falk Gjøe and to Erik. Nielsen accordingly enters it among the four lost/disputed Uraniborg prints (Carmen ad Erik Lange, Uraniborg, late 1584); it carries no Nielsen catalogue number, unlike the surviving Uraniborg poems (§§426, 427, 431). The text, by contrast, was first printed only in 1929, in TBOO XV — see transmission.

Open questions
  • Who is the woman? The poem never names her. Dreyer raises the question and leaves it open — 'Ceterum dubitari potest, hujusne amore jam a. 1584 captus fuerit' (TBOO XV, p. 6): whether the passion Tycho is trying to cure in November 1584 was already the attachment to Sophie Brahe. Sophie was then still married to Otte Thott (d. 1588) and the Lange betrothal is usually dated 1590. Nothing consulted here settles it; a reading of Zeeberg's commentary (Urania Titani, 1994, and the DSL edition) would be the next step.
  • 'DN. DE ERIGSTHOLM' in the heading. Dreyer prints the reading of the 1640s Thott codex without comment, although Erik Lange was lord of Engelsholm — as Dreyer himself says elsewhere (TBOO IX p. 323, 'Ericum Lange, domino praedii Engelsholm'; TBOO VII p. 366, 'Erico Langio de Engelstholm'). 'Erigstholm' looks like a copyist's corruption, and possibly a contamination with ERIKSHOLM, Sophie Brahe's estate by her first marriage. Dreyer emended GENIJ to GENERIS two words earlier but left this. Unresolved; the codex should be inspected.
  • The printing is inferred, not proved. Dreyer says only 'videtur'; no exemplar and no external contemporary description of the printed leaf is known — unlike the companion Carmen ad Falk Gjøe, whose printed form is attested by Rothmann's letter of 21 September 1587. The evidence here is the poem's own typographic conceit plus Tycho's allusion in the printed Ulfeldt poem.
  • Accounts built on Nielsen describe this piece as known only from Tycho's mention in the Ulfeldt poem. That is true of the printed edition but not of the text, which Behrend recovered from Thott 1044 4to and Dreyer printed in TBOO XV (1929), pp. 3–5.
  • Whether Nielsen assigned this lost print a catalogue number has not been checked against the printed Dansk Bibliografi.
  • Whether the 17th-century compiler of Thott 1044 (Achilles Andersen Skytte) copied from a surviving printed leaf or from an intermediate manuscript is not stated by Dreyer and is unknown.
Notes
  • Nielsen records the 1584 Uraniborg printing as lost (no copy survives); the text is transmitted in manuscript (siglum A) / TBOO XV.
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 15–17): the very first item printed on the Uraniborg press, the printing dated 27 Nov 1584 in the observation protocol with solar/lunar positions confirming the timestamp (TBOO X, 302; n. 12 defends the date); the poem's own dating 23 Nov 1584 is a composition date, not the printing date (p. 16); the surviving text is the transcript Copenhagen, KB, Thott 1044 4º (n. 10); as of 1993 none of the four surviving 1584-85 carmina was known in more than one exemplar (p. 15).

Jacobo Ulfeldio — To Jacob Ulfeldt

ElegysecureHvenARead the text →brahe-t_jacobo-ulfeldio

Printed verse epistle of 44 elegiac verses to the Danish nobleman Jacob Ulfeldt of Ulfeldsholm, dated Uraniborg 25 November 1584 — a composition date, not the printing date — and sent as an early specimen of the new Uraniborg press together with companion poems for Falk Gjøe and Erik Lange, both printings now lost (the Lange poem survives in transcript and is readable here; the Gjøe poem is entirely lost). Its verses on the exiled Urania who has found rest on Hven (verses 21-28) carry the theme that runs through the whole 1584-85 group.

Full heading
Nobilitate ingenii generisque viro inprimis conspicuo, D. Iacobo Vlfeldio, domino de Vlfelsholm, amico suo plurimum colendo. S. D.
Form
Elegy (this catalogue)
Date
1584 secure

The poem's own dateline, 7 Kal. Decemb. 1584 (= 25 November 1584); Nielsen §426 and the DSL's own descriptive label '(1584)' agree

Correction. The edition's 1585 corrected to 1584: the print carries the date 25 November 1584 (Nielsen 426).

The printed sheet subscribes itself 'Datum VRANIBVRGI ANNO 1584. 7 Kal. Decemb.' (TBOO IX, p. 180). The year is beyond doubt; the day is not agreed. Strict Roman inclusive reckoning makes 'a. d. VII Kal. Dec.' = 25 November, which is how Nielsen reads it; Peter Zeeberg (Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006, p. 90) and Håkansson (2006, p. 234 n.) both date the poem 26 November 1584. The year 1585 sometimes given is wrong: 1585 belongs to the next poem in the series, the New Year carmen to Niels Kaas (Kal. Ian. 1585, Nielsen §427), which stands immediately after the Ulfeldt poem in TBOO IX.

Addressee
Jacob Ulfeldt (addressee)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — Peter Zeeberg, complete
Summary
A verse epistle in elegiac couplets — forty-four lines (twenty-two distichs), filling the first two pages (fol. 1r–1v) of a folio sheet printed on Tycho's own new press at Uraniborg. Tycho addresses not the man but his own letter: while one of his letters is on its way to Falk Gøye and another is telling Erik Lange not to be in love, is no letter to go to learned Jacob Ulfeldt? He then sends his Muse off as the letter itself, tells her to read Ulfeldt the two poems sent to Falk and Erik ('change the names and the same thing is written to all of you'), and — the substance of the piece — supplies the answer she is to give if Ulfeldt asks why she comes to him PRINTED and not written by hand ('venias cur pressa labore, / Curque sies nulla Littera scripta manu'): Urania, driven out of the whole world, has come north, pitched her tent on tiny Hven, and had these types made so that her work might be known over the whole earth; but now that the types are ready the paper does not suffice and winter forces submission to the price ('quia non satis ampla Papyrus / Suppetit, et pretio cedere cogit Hyems'), so rather than let the press stand idle she sends these letters out to learned friends. It closes on a conceit on 'typus': if friendship can be figured in printed type, love may use the types too — and this love is pressed deeper into the heart than the letter is pressed on the page.
Occasion
Recoverable, and unusually well documented — the poem states its own occasion. Tycho's press at Uraniborg had just been set up (types procured in 1584 through his old Rostock teacher Heinrich Brucæus); the types were ready but the paper was not, and Tycho, rather than leave his new printer idle, ran off a short series of printed verse epistles to friends. Nielsen states this flatly: 'Tycho Brahe fortæller heri om sit nye Bogtrykkeris Oprettelse og omtaler, at han har ladet Digtet trykke bl. a. for at give sin Bogtrykker noget at bestille' (Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921, p. 179). The poem is thus part of a deliberate 1584–85 series of printed poems to the learned nobility and to patrons — Erik Lange, Falk Gøye, Jacob Ulfeldt, then Niels Kaas (Jan. 1585) and Heinrich Rantzau (Mar. 1585) — which Zeeberg reads as a printed self-presentation of Tycho's social and learned network on the model of Ovid's letters from exile (Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006, p. 88). Zeeberg further suggests that Ulfeldt was ADDED to the series after Lange and Gøye because he happened to be visiting Hven in those days; that is an inference from the poem's opening (Ulfeldt is 'nearest', met across the water, 'primus adest'), not a documented fact.
On the addressee
Jacob (Jakob) Ulfeldt, lord of Ulfeldtsholm (Kogsbølle, Funen), d. 1593. Danish nobleman and member of the Rigsråd — Dreyer: 'Fuerat Ulfeldius senator regni usque ad annum 1579 … mortuus est a. 1593' (TBOO IX, p. 322); Nielsen calls him 'Rigsraad Jacob Ulfeldt' (1921, p. 179). He is the ambassador who fell into disgrace after the failed mission to Moscow of 1578–79, about which he later wrote a famous Latin book, and who then devoted the rest of his life to learned pursuits; he was the grandfather of the notorious Corfitz Ulfeldt (Zeeberg in Grinder-Hansen, ed., Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006, p. 89). At the date of the poem he was, on Zeeberg's account, at work on a Latin historical work surviving in a manuscript dated 1585, in whose preface he singles out Tycho Brahe, Heinrich Rantzau and Niels Kaas as his like-minded contemporaries. He is NOT in Christianson's Biographical Directory of the familia — he was a learned friend and correspondent, not a member of Tycho's household. Falk Gøye and Erik Lange, the recipients of the two companion poems, are named in the text itself.
Transmission
Print, not manuscript — an important distinction for this register. The words reach us from the Uraniborg-printed folio sheet itself, of which the single known copy is at the Royal Library, Copenhagen; Dreyer took his text directly from that printed exemplar and cites no manuscript for it (lemma at TBOO IX, p. 179: 'Ex exemplo ab ipso Tychone typis descripto (Uraniburgi 1584)' — contrast the neighbouring Pratensis epitaph, for which he adds 'cf. cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10686'). TBOO is therefore not the first printing, nor even the first modern reprinting: Nielsen records the poem as reprinted in Danske Magazin II, pp. 223–24 (1921, p. 179 n. 1) — the same 18th-century Danish antiquarian series that reprinted Tycho's 1572 carmen on his twin brother. Dreyer & Ræder then edited it in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (Copenhagen 1927), Carmina, pp. 179–180, with the editors' note at p. 322.
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the Uraniborg print of 1584 (Nielsen 426))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, island of Hven, 1584 (Tycho Brahe's own press at Uraniborg (no printer named on the sheet; Tycho's first Uraniborg printer was a German named Joachim)); Nielsen §426 (Lauritz Nielsen, Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600); described at length in Nielsen, 'Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen' (1921), p. 179

This is one of the very first products of the Uraniborg press. Physical form: folio, 2 leaves; the poem occupies the first two pages (TBOO's marginal leaf-signatures '1r' and '1v' at IX pp. 179–180 confirm Nielsen's 'fylder de to første Sider af et Folioark'). one copy is known, at Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen (Nielsen 1921, p. 179; the census brahe-carmen-ulfeldt-1584, which records the KB shelfmark as unverified — the tycho-thesaurus carries it as 'LN 426 2°'). Dreyer independently confirms the printing: 'CARMEN IACOBO ULFELDIO missum (p. 179 sq.) sicut duo sequentia in ipsius Tychonis typographia typis descriptum est' (TBOO IX, p. 322), and his source-lemma for the text reads '[Ex exemplo ab ipso Tychone typis descripto (Uraniburgi 1584)]'. Nielsen judges Epitaphium Joh. Pratensis (§431, Uraniborg 1584, undated within the year) the earliest known Uraniborg imprint; the Ulfeldt carmen is the earliest surviving Uraniborg imprint that carries a precise date. The two companion sheets to Falk Gøye and Erik Lange, printed in the same season and named in this poem, do not survive in any copy (Nielsen 1921, p. 179) — this poem is the primary evidence that they existed.

Open questions
  • The day of the month. TBOO prints 'ANNO 1584. 7 Kal. Decemb.' Strict Roman inclusive reckoning gives 25 November (so Nielsen); Zeeberg (2006, p. 90) and Håkansson (2006, p. 234 n.) both print 26 November. Neither side argues the point. The year is not in doubt.
  • Whether the companion poem to Erik Lange really is lost. Nielsen (1921, p. 179; DB §, lost-prints list) states that neither the Gjøe nor the Lange sheet survives, and Dreyer prints no 1584 Lange poem in the TBOO IX Carmina. But Zeeberg (2006, p. 88) writes that the press was inaugurated with the Latin poem to Erik Lange, printed November 1584, and (p. 89) that 'the poem to Erik we do have' — apparently editing it himself (Zeeberg 1995/1996, cited at Håkansson 2006, p. 234 n.). The likeliest reconciliation is that the Hven-printed sheet is lost but the text survives in another witness that Dreyer did not use; this has not been checked, and it bears directly on which piece was the Uraniborg press's first product.
  • Dreyer states that Ulfeldt 'edidit a. 1585 Historiam Daniæ ab anno 1333 ad annum 1559' (TBOO IX, p. 322), i.e. that he published a history of Denmark in 1585; Zeeberg (2006, p. 89) says the Latin historical work Ulfeldt was writing at just this time survives in a manuscript dated 1585. The two statements may not be compatible, and Dreyer's 'edidit' has not been verified against any bibliography.
  • The KB shelfmark of the unique copy is not verified. The census carries it as an open question; the tycho-thesaurus records it as 'LN 426 2°'.
  • What is on the second leaf. The poem occupies fol. 1r–1v of a 2-leaf folio; nothing is recorded of the remaining pages. Rothmann's letter of 21 Sept. 1587 reports that the (lost) Falk Gøye sheet from the same season carried two emblem woodcuts printed on its back; whether the Ulfeldt sheet does the same has not been established from the KB copy.
  • Zeeberg's explanation of why Ulfeldt joined the series — that he happened to be on Hven in those days — is an inference from the poem's opening lines, not an attested fact, and no independent evidence of such a visit has been produced.
Notes
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 15–17): 44 elegiac verses; the dateline 25 Nov 1584 is a composition date, not the printing date (p. 16); the Urania-exile passage (vv. 21-28) is analysed as the kernel of the 1584-85 group; as of 1993 the original print was known in a single exemplar (p. 15).

Typographiæ — On printing

InscriptionuncertainHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_typographiae

Four-line epigram on printing, in which a work brought forth by Urania's lofty enterprise is committed to the press and bidden to travel the realms of the vast world with the blessing of the Creator of the heavens.

IX 175TYPOGRAPHIÆ

URANIÆ ingenuo et celso molimine parte Imprimeris manuum sic ne labore labos? I mundique diu vasti pete Regna, superstes Successus tribuat conditor Uraniων.

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
Typographiae
Form
Inscription (this catalogue)
Date
1584 or later uncertain

The DSL's own descriptive label uses circa — '(c. 1580)'; the edition's year 1580

Correction. The edition's 'c. 1580' predates the press it celebrates: Tycho's printing house was set up in 1584. Transmitted only by Resen (1668), the epigram is undated.

No source dates the piece. The 1580 comes from the edition, whose metadata heads the text 'Typographiae / Om bogtrykning (c. 1580)'. That date cannot be right if the verses belong, as the heading and their transmission indicate, to Tycho's printing house on Hven: Tycho did not begin planning a press until 1583-84, sent his printer Joachim to Wittenberg to procure presses and type in 1584, and the press — housed in a small dedicated building south of the castle — was only producing in late 1584/early 1585 (Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen). The Hveen press ran to 1597. Hence the floor of 1584 and the working range 1584–1597; anything narrower would be invention. Dreyer prints the verses with no date and no annotation.

Place
Printing House
Language
Latin
Summary
Four Latin verses — two elegiac couplets — printed by Dreyer among the Carmina under the bare heading TYPOGRAPHIAE: 'Uraniae ingenuo et celso molimine parte / Imprimeris manuum sic ne labore labos? / I mundique diu vasti pete Regna, superstes / Successus tribuat conditor Uraniomega-nu.' They are not addressed to a person but to the work itself ('labos', the archaic nominative of labor): begotten by Urania's noble and lofty endeavour, is the work now being pressed out by the labour of hands? — go, then, and make for the realms of the vast world; may the Founder of the heavenly things grant it lasting success. The heading 'Typographiae' is most naturally read as a locative ('in the printing house'), and it stands in Resen's 1668 collection inside an unbroken topographical run of Uraniborg's placed inscriptions — the King James verses, then TYPOGRAPHIAE, then 'In Museo. NON HABERI, SED ESSE', 'Sub Baccho', 'Sub Sole aureo', 'Ad fornacem', 'Circum speculum opticum', 'Supra Januam Hypocausti', 'Supra tectum in quatuor anni tempora', 'In ambitu Horologii'. The Latin is transmitted corruptly ('parte' will not construe; the last word is printed in Greek letters) and no editor has emended it.
Occasion
Not recoverable from any contemporary document. Nothing in Tycho's correspondence, in Dreyer's Annotationes, or in the modern literature consulted discusses these verses at all — Dreyer annotates the pieces on either side of them (the Uraniborg foundation-stone poem; the CIRCA EFFIGIEM / CIRCA ARMA epigrams, which he locates on the bindings of Tycho's books) and passes over this one in silence. What the text and its transmission jointly support, and no more, is that the verses belong to the equipping and running of Tycho's own printing house at Uraniborg: they are an envoi wishing the press's product a long life in the world, set up (on the natural reading of the locative heading) in the room where the press stood. Why they were composed at that moment, and on whose prompting, is not attested. Graded C.
Transmission
No manuscript witness is known, and Dreyer names none. The words survive because Peder Hansen Resen copied them into his Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen, 1668), pp. 333–334, among the inscriptions of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg; Resen prints them without comment and without naming his source (for neighbouring items on the same pages he cites Gassendi's Vita and Tycho's Progymnasmata, but for these verses he cites nothing). Dreyer took the text from Resen and nowhere else: his headnote at TBOO IX p. 175 reads '[E P. J. Resenii Inscriptionibus Haffniensibus (Hauniae 1668) p. 333 sqq.]'. Dreyer's text differs from Resen's only in normalisation ('Uraniae' for Resen's 'Urania'; 'mundique' for 'mundisq;'); he neither emends nor annotates it, and TBOO XV p. 52 (Addenda et corrigenda) carries no correction to IX 175. The editors themselves classify the page as inscriptional: TBOO XV, Index hominum et rerum, p. 51, s.v. Uraniburgum, lists 'inscriptiones V 143, 148, VI 266-276, 365, 368 sq., IX 175'. Resen's page and the TBOO page were read on the page images.
Channel
Printed after his death (Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses, 1668)
Printing
printed posthumously — Copenhagen, 1668 (not established (publisher: Peder Hansen Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses)); Nielsen none — no Nielsen number

There is no evidence that these verses were ever printed in Tycho's lifetime, and none that they were printed on his own press. Nielsen's Brahe entries (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, nos. 424-433, with 975-976) contain nothing corresponding to them, and they are not among the four lost/disputed Hveen prints (Carmen ad Falk Gjoee; Carmen ad Erik Lange; the Hans Frandsen elegy; the 1591 Craig Apologia). Their first appearance in print is posthumous, sixty-seven years after Tycho's death: P. J. Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Hauniae, 1668), pp. 333–334, in the section whose running head is 'Inscriptiones Uraniburgicae et Stellaeburgicae'. TBOO IX (1927) p. 175 is therefore NOT the first printing — Dreyer's own headnote says so, naming Resen as his copy-text.

Open questions
  • The date is in open conflict. The DSL/tekstnet edition dates the verses c. 1580; the Uraniborg printing house did not exist before 1584 (Nielsen). Either the DSL date is a loose or inherited guess, or the verses are not a printing-house inscription at all but a poem 'on printing' that Resen filed among the Uraniborg inscriptions. Nothing in TBOO decides it, because Dreyer prints the piece undated and unannotated. Until the edition's grounds for c. 1580 are examined, the conflict stands.
  • Is TYPOGRAPHIAE a locative ('in the printing house') or a dative/genitive ('for/of the printing house')? The surrounding headings in Resen are locative or prepositional ('In Museo', 'Sub Baccho', 'Ad fornacem', 'Circum speculum opticum', 'Supra Januam Hypocausti'), which favours the locative and hence a physically placed inscription; but no source states where in the building the verses stood, or in what medium.
  • Resen's source is unknown. He prints the verses without a citation, whereas for the items immediately before and after them he cites Gassendi's Vita and Tycho's own Progymnasmata. Whether he transcribed from the building, from a lost written record of the Uraniborg inscriptions, or from Tycho's papers, is not established — and it matters, because Resen is the single witness.
  • The text is corrupt and has never been edited. 'Uraniae ingenuo et celso molimine parte' will not construe as it stands (one expects 'parta' or 'partus' agreeing with 'labos'), and the final word is printed in Greek characters (Resen and Dreyer both print it in Greek). Dreyer neither emends nor discusses. Any translation, including the paraphrase given in the summary, is therefore provisional.
  • No scholarly discussion of these four verses has been found — not in Dreyer 1890, Nielsen, Thoren, Christianson, Norlind, or Beckett & Christensen. They may be the least-examined text in the Tycho corpus; a search of the Danish inscription-literature (Resen's manuscript Atlas Danicus; F. R. Friis) is the obvious next step.

Henrico Ranzovio — To Heinrich Rantzau

ElegysecureHvenARead the text →brahe-t_henrico-ranzovio

Verse epistle of 114 verses to Heinrich Rantzau, the Danish king's governor in Holstein, praising his book on the kings and princes who cultivated astrology and describing Uraniborg and its instruments, with letter-like greetings to Rantzau's wife and children; printed at Uraniborg on 1 March 1585 — months after the other Uraniborg press poems — and sent to Rantzau with a printed view of the building. The original print survives, and from it Zeeberg's edition corrects three misprints in the Opera omnia text.

Full heading
Nobilissimo et amplissimo viro, sapientia et eruditione inprimis excellenti, D. Henrico Ranzovio, potentiss. Regis Daniae in Holsatia vicario et consiliario, praefecto arcis Segebergae et domino in Bredenberga etc., astrologiae omniumque liberalium disciplinarum excultori et promotori laudatissimo, amico suo plurimum colendo
Form
Elegy (this catalogue)
Date
1585 secure

Nielsen §425: the printing is dated 'VRANIBVRGI Kal. Martii' (1 March) 1585; DSL edition year 1585.

The poem is dated in its own subscription: 'Datum VRANIBVRGI Kal. Martii Anno 1585' (TBOO IX, p. 190) — Uraniborg, 1 March 1585. Nielsen §425 gives the same date from the surviving printed leaves. It is the third of the three printed verse-letters of the winter 1584/85 series (Ulfeldt, 25 Nov. 1584; Kaas, 1 Jan. 1585; Rantzau, 1 Mar. 1585).

Addressee
Henrik Rantzau (addressee)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — Peter Zeeberg, complete
Summary
A verse letter of about 114 lines in elegiac couplets (incipit 'Salve praelustris Majorum Henrice propago, / Ranzovidumque ingens Fama, Columna, Decus'), addressed to Heinrich Rantzau, royal Statthalter of Holstein and Schleswig, and printed as a small folio on Tycho's own Uraniborg press. It praises Rantzau's lineage and his standing as a poet and patron of learning, and then his astrological book — the catalogue in which he 'teaches that the stars bring praise to kings' and traces star-lore from Adam through Seth, Enoch, Terah and Abraham to Atlas, Hercules, Hermes, Orion and Prometheus — extending that roll of royal patrons of astronomy to Frederik II, under whose auspices Uraniborg was built. Its practical core is a correction and an invitation: Rantzau had called Tycho's house a mere 'specula' (watch-tower), 'from which it is clear that the form of the house has escaped you' ('Quippe vocas speculam, quas Divae struximus Aedes, / Unde liquet, formam te latuisse Domus'), so Tycho sends him a picture of it — 'Artifici pictam calamo tibi mitto Figuram, / Qua domus Uraniae conspicienda patet' — noting that only the exterior can be shown, and begs him to cross to Hven when he is next in Zealand. It closes by recalling that their friendship began years before at Rostock ('Urbs velut est testis Stipite dicta Rosae'), when Rantzau passed through with a Danish royal embassy, and with wishes for his long life, his wife and his sons and grandsons.
Occasion
Recoverable and unusually well documented. (a) Institutionally, the poem belongs to the run of printed occasional verse with which Tycho exercised and displayed his new Uraniborg press in its first winter: Dreyer notes that the Ulfeldt poem 'like the two following' — Niels Kaas and Rantzau — 'was printed in Tycho's own printing house' (TBOO IX, p. 322), and Tycho had announced these very sheets to Rantzau in advance, writing on 8 January 1585, 'Mittam vero brevi literas impressas tibi aliisque Nobilibus et eruditis Amicis inscriptas, quamprimum omnes absolutae fuerint, ut Typos nostros videas' — I shall shortly send printed letters inscribed to you and to other noble and learned friends, as soon as they are all finished, so that you may see our types (TBOO VII, p. 90). (b) Personally, Tycho was courting his most important Holstein patron: the same January letter asks Rantzau for 20-25 reams of paper from his paper mill for the calendar then on the press, and offers to print Rantzau's own astrological writings. (c) Within the poem, the immediate prompt is Rantzau's having called Uraniborg a 'specula': Tycho corrects him, sends a picture of the building, and presses the invitation to Hven that Rantzau had long promised to accept.
On the addressee
Heinrich Rantzau (Henrik Rantzau, Henricus Ranzovius), 1526–1598, royal Statthalter (vicarius) of Holstein and Schleswig for the King of Denmark, governor of Segeberg castle, lord of Breitenburg; the richest and most bookish nobleman of the duchies, a prolific Latin author, print-patron and astrologer, and — in Dreyer's words — 'multos per annos fautor Tychonis', Tycho's patron for many years (TBOO IX, p. 322-323). He was to be Tycho's host at Wandsbek in 1597-98, where the Mechanica was printed. The book praised in the poem is his Catalogus imperatorum, regum ac principum qui astrologicam artem amarunt, ornarunt et exercuerunt (Antwerp: Plantin, 1580; reprinted Leipzig 1581, enlarged Leipzig 1584 and Cologne 1585) — Dreyer's note at p. 323 refers the passage to 'catalogum a Ranzovio confectum', and Tycho himself later cites 'liber Domini HENRICI RANZOVIJ de Regibus et Principibus, qui Astronomiam foverunt' (TBOO VIII, p. 412).
Transmission
The text reaches us through the printed sheet itself, not through a manuscript. Dreyer edited it 'Ex exemplo ab ipso Tychone typis descripto (Uraniburgi 1585)' — from a surviving copy of the 1585 Uraniborg folio (Nielsen §425 locates a copy in the Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen) — and printed it among the Carmina in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, tom. IX (Hauniae, 1927), pp. 187–190, with the editors' notes at pp. 322–323. It is therefore not a 'first printed in TBOO' piece: TBOO is its modern critical edition, and the 1585 Uraniborg print is the first and only early edition. No manuscript witness is cited by Dreyer.
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the Uraniborg print of 1585 (Nielsen 425))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, island of Hven, 1585 (Tycho Brahe's own press (printer not named; his first Uraniborg printer was a German known only as Joachim)); Nielsen 425

Folio, 2 leaves; the only recorded copy is in the Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen (Nielsen §425). Dreyer's source-lemma is explicit: '[Ex exemplo ab ipso Tychone typis descripto (Uraniburgi 1585)]' — from a copy printed in type by Tycho himself, Uraniborg 1585 (TBOO IX, p. 187) — and his annotation states that the Ulfeldt carmen 'sicut duo sequentia' (i.e. the Kaas and Rantzau poems) was printed 'in ipsius Tychonis typographia' (TBOO IX, p. 322). This is one of the Uraniborg occasional prints that the standard collector bibliographies (PMM, Dibner, Horblit, Honeyman, Norman) omit entirely and that only Nielsen records. Nielsen further states that the poem was sent together with a printed picture of Uraniborg, which he identifies with the Orthographia arcis Uranienburg broadsheet (Uraniborg 1585; sole surviving copy at the Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg) — see open_questions.

Martii (= 1 March) 1585 … Sent together with a printed picture of Uraniborg'); §1.2 (the Hveen press, its establishment 1584-85, the printer 'Joachim'); §426-427 (the Ulfeldt and Kaas companion prints); §4 (the standard collector references omit the Uraniborg occasional poems) — That the poem was printed in Tycho's lifetime, at Uraniborg in 1585, in folio, 2 leaves, with a surviving copy in the Kongelige Bibliotek; the Nielsen number; the claim that a picture of Uraniborg accompanied it
  • TBOO VII, pp. 89–90 (lemma '[E codice Vindobonensi lat. 9737f]'); at p. 90: 'Mittam vero brevi literas impressas tibi aliisque Nobilibus et eruditis Amicis inscriptas, quamprimum omnes absolutae fuerint, ut Typos nostros videas … Si catalogum Astrologicorum tuorum librorum ex amplissima tua Bibliotheca descriptum mihi transmittere non displicuerit, rem feceris longe gratissimam' — The occasion: Tycho announced the printed verse-letters to Rantzau two months before this one was dated, as showpieces of his new types; the same letter documents the paper request to Rantzau's mill, Gerhard Rantzau's visit to Uraniborg, and Tycho's offer to print Rantzau's astrological work
  • TBOO VIII, p. 412 ('liber Domini HENRICI RANZOVIJ de Regibus et Principibus, qui Astronomiam foverunt') — That the book of Rantzau's alluded to in the elegy is his catalogue of kings and princes who fostered astronomy/astrology
  • Lohmeier 2000, pp. 95–97 (the 1580 Plantin/Antwerp astrology book with its 'Catalogus imperatorum, regum ac principum qui astrologicam artem amarunt, ornarunt & exercuerunt'; reprints Leipzig 1581, enlarged Leipzig 1584 and Cologne 1585) — Identification and printing history of Rantzau's astrological Catalogus, and Rantzau's lifelong practice of astrology
  • Familia, s.v. Heinrich Rantzau, the record (1526–1598; Statthalter of Schleswig-Holstein; Breitenburg; Wandsbek host 1597–98; presentation recipient of De mundi, the Epistolae and the Mechanica) — Identification of the addressee and his later role in Tycho's career
  • Zeeberg & Gredal Jensen 2019, https://tekstnet.dk/books/brahe-t_henrico-ranzovio/001/ — The edition of record, with a Danish translation
Open questions
  • The enclosed picture. The poem says Tycho sends 'artifici pictam calamo … Figuram' — a figure drawn with a craftsman's pen — showing only the exterior of the house. Nielsen equates this with the printed Orthographia arcis Uranienburg broadsheet of 1585 (sole surviving copy, Marburg). The equation is an identification, not a statement in the poem: the Latin would equally describe a pen drawing, and the only recorded copy of the Orthographia has no Rantzau provenance. Whether the sheet Rantzau received in March 1585 was the Orthographia has not been independently verified here.
  • The Rostock meeting. Dreyer glosses 'Urbs Stipite dicta Rosae' as Rostock and says Tycho met Rantzau there as a youth ('adulescentulus'), which points to Tycho's Rostock years 1566-68; the poem adds that Rantzau was passing through with a Danish royal embassy ('Dani Legatio Regis'). Neither Dreyer nor the poem gives a year, and the embassy has not been identified from an independent source.
  • The printer. Nielsen assigns the sheet to Tycho's Uraniborg press but records no printer's name; the only name attached to the press's first year is 'Joachim', the German Tycho sent to Wittenberg for presses and type. Who actually set this sheet is unknown.
  • Survival. Nielsen records a copy at the Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen, and no other; no census of surviving copies of the 1584-85 Uraniborg verse-letters has been made here, and the present shelfmark has not been confirmed.
  • Length. The poem runs to roughly 114 lines (57 elegiac couplets) across TBOO IX pp. 187–190; the count is taken from the TBOO text layer and has not been checked line by line against the printed page images.
Notes
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 27–29, n. 29) edits from the original print ('Uraniborg 1585'), correcting three misprints in TBOO IX 187-190: ob for ab (v. 19), Vestrarum for Vestarum (v. 75), Supera for Superos (v. 104); as of 1993 the print was known in a single exemplar (p. 15).

Nicolao Kaasio — To Niels Kaas

ElegysecureHvenARead the text →brahe-t_nicolao-kaasio

Printed New Year verse epistle of 288 verses, dated Uraniborg 1 January 1585, to Niels Kaas, chancellor of Denmark, in which the muse Urania sings Kaas's praises. Her epiphany reprises the 1573 elegy of De nova stella; her tale of exile through the lands that failed astronomy, ended at last on Hven, is Tycho's private version of the translatio Musarum; an episode modelled on Ovid's Invidia makes Kaas the saviour of Uraniborg's establishment; and Tycho closes by inviting him to visit Uraniborg and its instruments when spring comes.

Full heading
Magnifico, amplissimo nobilissimoque viro, sapientia, doctrina omnimodaque virtute praeeminenti, D. Nicolao Kaasio, domino de Taarup, Regiae Maiestatis Daniae cancellario et consiliario prudentissimo, utilitatis et tranquillitatis publicae suasori conservatorique fidelissimo, amico suo inprimis observando (short title: Nicolao Kaasio; Nielsen's supplied title: Carmen ad Nic. Kaasium)
Form
Elegy (this catalogue)
Date
1585 secure

The poem's printed dateline, Kal. Ianuarij 1585 (= 1 January 1585); Nielsen §427 and the edition's year 1585 agree

The poem carries its own date: it is subscribed 'Datum VRANIBVRGI Kalend: Ianuarij Anno 1585. Tui obseruantiss. TYCHO BRAHE' (Nielsen 427, collating leaf 4a; TBOO IX, p. 187) — 1 January 1585, i.e. a New Year's-day piece, written in the winter of 1584-85 and printed early in 1585. Nielsen (Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921, pp. 178, 180) places it in the group of Latin poems Tycho 'forfattede i Vinteren 1584-85' and prints it as the earliest of the 1585 Uraniborg sheets. There is no rival date in any authority consulted; The year 1585 is correct.

Addressee
Niels Kaas (addressee)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — Peter Zeeberg, complete
Summary
A Latin poem of 288 lines (144 elegiac couplets) under a prose dedicatory heading to the Danish chancellor Niels Kaas, printed as a four-leaf folio pamphlet on Tycho's own press. Tycho opens in his own voice — he had set pen to paper to write to Kaas and did not know where to begin ('Iam Veneranda tibi fuerat Mens scribere KAASE') — when Urania descends from Olympus and takes over the poem: the greater part of the piece (roughly lines 33-268) is her speech. She tells how she is a fugitive driven through Ethiopia, India, Arabia, Chaldaea, Egypt, Greece, Italy, Spain, Gaul and Germany, finding no rest because greed, frivolity, ignorance, luxury, war and barbarism rule the world; how she complained to her father Jupiter, who consoled her with the promise of honour in the north, where he had marked out a young man devoted to the stars and had put it into the northern king's heart not to let him leave his country; how a house was then built for her on Hven and instruments forged such as antiquity never had — not Egypt, not Timocharis, Hipparchus or Ptolemy, not al-Battani in Syria, not Archimedes at Syracuse, not Rome with Menelaus, not King Alfonso, not even Copernicus, 'who is believed lately to have put the finishing hand to our art'; how Envy (Invidia, daughter of Pluto), egged on by Ambition and the mad lust for gain, then attacked the work, persuading others that Tycho's labour was useless and impossible, so that Urania nearly quit Denmark ('Vndique Terra infra est, Coelum patet undique supra, / Omne solum Patria est, cui mea Sacra placent'); and how Jupiter roused one man — Kaas — who alone, by his counsel, saved the enterprise ('Vnus enim nobis suadendo restituit Rem'), drove Envy back shamefaced into her cave, and secured Urania's camp under the north. She therefore charges Tycho to carry her thanks to Kaas and to ask him to persevere. Tycho then resumes in his own person, thanks Kaas for his merits, and asks him to come to Hven as his most welcome guest as soon as spring drives out the winter — a visit Kaas had long since promised ('Id quia pollicitus dudum es').
Occasion
Fully recoverable, and double: a New Year's greeting and an act of political thanks. Tycho's press had been set up in the summer/autumn of 1584 and stood idle over the winter; the Uraniborg occasional poems (Pratensis, Ulfeldt, Falk Gøe, Erik Lange, and this one) were written and printed in the winter of 1584-85 partly to give the new printer work — Tycho says so himself in the companion poem to Jacob Ulfeldt (TBOO IX, p. 179; Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri, p. 179). This piece was dated to 1 January 1585 and is, in Nielsen's words, 'det første trykte Nytaarsdigt fra Tycho Brahe' (Bogtrykkeri, p. 180). Its substance, however, is a thank-offering: the whole central section of Urania's speech says that the Hven enterprise had been attacked by detractors — moved by ambition and greed — who argued that the work was useless and impossible, that Tycho came near to abandoning it and leaving the country, and that Kaas alone, by his counsel at court, saved it and shamed Envy into silence. The poem ends by pressing an invitation Kaas had already promised to honour: to come to Hven in the spring and see for himself what the great expenditure had produced. The 1746 Danske Magazin editors, who reprint the sheet, summarise exactly this ('han var og den eneste, som i det Fald holdt Hæderen ved lige for Danmark, og drev Sagen igiennem, at Astronomien blev fastsat her i Landet, og at al Misundelse maatte saaledes staae beskæmmet... beder, at han dog, efter forhen giorte Løfte, vil selv til Foraaret komme over til Hveen', II, pp. 225–226). What is not recoverable is the concrete episode behind the allegory: no letter, council record or other document identifying the detractors or the crisis of 1584 has been found in the sources consulted here, and the poem itself is the only witness to it. See open_questions.
On the addressee
Niels Kaas (Nicolaus Kaasius, Latinised; 1535–1594), lord of Taarupgaard, Chancellor of the Realm of Denmark from 1573 until his death, and from 1588 head of the four-man regency (guardian government) that ruled for the boy-king Christian IV — 'homo nobilis Danus, nat. 1535, cancellarius 1573, princeps quattuor procuratorum regni a senatu institutus 1588, mortuus 1594' (Dreyer & Raeder, TBOO VIII, Index virorum doctorum, pp. 457–458). As royal chancellor he was ex officio head of the University of Copenhagen. A former pupil of Niels Hemmingsen who had studied abroad under Melanchthon, he had been the rising man of the Danish central administration since 1560 and, in Thoren's words, 'later became an important patron of Tycho's interests' (Lord of Uraniborg, p. 43). The poem's heading styles him 'Regiae Maiestatis Daniae cancellario et consiliario prudentissimo' and the verse calls him the man 'cui datur a Dano Rege secundus Honor' — second in honour only to the king of Denmark. He is not a member of Tycho's familia and so has no entry in Christianson's Biographical Directory; the identification here rests on Dreyer's indexes and Thoren.
Transmission
Print-first, and — unlike the Pratensis epitaph — with no manuscript witness signalled by its editor. The words survive primarily in the 1585 Uraniborg folio pamphlet itself, of which Nielsen records exactly one copy, at Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen (Nielsen 427; the KB copy, read on a surrogate, is bound in marbled boards with a pasted label 'T. BRAHE Nic. Kaasio. 1585.'). Dreyer's source-lemma at TBOO IX, p. 180 reads simply '[Ex exemplo ab ipso Tychone typis descripto (Uraniburgi 1585)]' — he set his text from the printed exemplar, and cites no codex (contrast his Pratensis lemma, which adds 'cf. cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10686'). Before Dreyer, the poem had been reprinted once, in Danske Magazin II (Copenhagen 1746), pp. 226–234, from a copy the editors owed to Provost [Peder] Terpager ('for hvilket vi ogsaa have Hr. Provst Terpager at takke', II, p. 225). The sheet also circulated in Tycho's own lifetime as a gift-object: on 25 August 1585 he sent the group of Uraniborg poems, together with pictures of Uraniborg, to Thaddaeus Hagecius in Prague (Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri, p. 182, citing the letter, TBOO VII, pp. 93–97), and in 1587 M. Hans Aalborg carried Tycho's printed verses to the Frankfurt fair, where Christoph Rothmann obtained them (Danske Magazin II, p. 226 n. (a); Rothmann's letter names the Falk Gøe poem specifically, not this one). Finally, Tycho himself quarried the poem: the distich at TBOO IX, p. 184, ll. 15-16 ('Vndique Terra infra est, Coelum patet undique supra, / Omne solum Patria est, cui mea Sacra placent') reappears, with an adapted pentameter, in the Astronomiae instauratae Mechanica of 1598 — 'Undique terra infra, Coelum patet undique supra, / Et patria est forti quaelibet ora viro' (TBOO V, p. 63, ll. 13-14) — in the passage complaining that politicians deem astronomy useless and that the astronomer must be ready to take himself and his work elsewhere. Dreyer cross-references the two places at TBOO IX, p. 321.
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the Uraniborg print of 1585 (Nielsen 427))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, Hven, 1585 (Not named. Nielsen's entry reads 'Uvis Bogtrykker' (unknown printer); the press was manned at this date by a German printer called Joachim, otherwise unidentified, whom Tycho had sent to Wittenberg in 1584 to buy presses and type (Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri, p. 178) — but no document ties Joachim to this particular sheet.); Nielsen 427

Printed in Tycho's lifetime, on his own press, within days or weeks of the date it bears — emphatically NOT a first-printed-in-TBOO piece. Nielsen, Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, no. 427: 'Tycho Brahe: [Carmen ad Nic. Kaasium.] [Uraniborg: Uvis Bogtrykker, 1585.] 2°. 4 Bl. [Laeg 1⁴] 44 L. Kolumnestørrelse: 246 × 120 mm. Antikva. Initial.' — a folio pamphlet of four leaves in a single gathering (two sheets), 44 lines to the page, roman type, with a floriated woodcut initial I; leaf 4b blank; one recorded copy, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen. NOTE THE BRACKETS: title, place, printer and year are all editorially SUPPLIED. The sheet carries no title-page and no imprint; 'VRANIBVRGI' appears only in the subscribed dating clause of the poem ('Datum VRANIBVRGI Kalend: Ianuarij Anno 1585'). Nielsen assigns it to the Uraniborg press because the type and ornament stock are those of the later, signed Uraniborg imprints (Bogtrykkeri, p. 178: 'Ingen af dem er forsynet med Angivelse af Trykkested, men det anvendte Materiel er det samme, som er brugt i de senere Uraniborg-Tryk'). Dreyer states the printing flatly: the Ulfeldt poem 'sicut duo sequentia' — like the two that follow it, i.e. the Kaas and Rantzau poems — 'in ipsius Tychonis typographia typis descriptum est' (TBOO IX, p. 322). Thoren independently lists 'poems to ex-rigsraad Jacob Ulfeld, Chancellor Niels Kaas, and Governor (of Holstein) Heinrich Rantzov' among the first productions of the Hven press (Lord of Uraniborg, p. 186). Reprinted posthumously in Danske Magazin II (1746), pp. 226–234, and then in TBOO IX (1927), pp. 180–187.

Open questions
  • The concrete occasion behind the allegory is not recoverable from the sources consulted. The poem says that Ambition and greed set Envy on the Hven enterprise, that others were persuaded the work was 'useless' and 'impossible', that Tycho came close to abandoning it and leaving Denmark, and that Kaas alone reversed this by his counsel. No letter, council minute or Kancelliets Brevbøger entry identifying the detractors, the moment or the decision has been located here. The poem is its own only witness, and the 1746 Danske Magazin editors merely paraphrase it. Anyone citing 'the 1584 crisis' should be told that its documentation is the poem.
  • Dreyer's own two indexes disagree on Kaas's birth year: TBOO IX, p. 322 gives 'natus 1534', TBOO VIII, pp. 457–458 gives 'nat. 1535'. Not resolved here; 1535 is the more commonly cited year and is preferred in the addressee field, with the conflict recorded rather than smoothed.
  • Did Kaas ever accept the invitation? The poem asks him to come 'as soon as spring drives out winter' and says he had long promised to. No visit in 1585 is recorded in any source consulted. The Uraniborg weather-diary's index registers him exactly once, at TBOO IX p. 64, where the margin under 8 July 1588 reads 'Cancelarius Georg. Ros.' — apparently a visit three and a half years later, in the company of Jørgen Rosenkrantz. That entry has not been collated against Dreyer's editorial notes, and the identification of the 'Cancelarius' is Dreyer's index, not the diary's words.
  • Who printed it? The sheet names no printer and carries no imprint at all; Nielsen's 'Uvis Bogtrykker' means unknown, and the attribution to the Uraniborg press rests on the type and ornament stock matching the later signed Uraniborg imprints. Tycho's first printer is known only as a German named Joachim; no document ties him to this sheet.
  • Whether the Kaas poem in particular was among the printed verses M. Hans Aalborg carried to the Frankfurt fair in 1587 is not established: Rothmann's letter, quoted in Danske Magazin II, p. 226 n. (a), names only the poem to Falk Gøe. The Kaas sheet's circulation beyond Denmark is therefore inferred from the group, not documented for this piece.
  • Copy census: Nielsen records a single copy, at Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen, and gives no shelfmark; no the census exists for LN 427, and no systematic search for further copies (e.g. among the Uraniborg presentation sheets in German and Swedish libraries, cf. the Marburg finds) has been made.
Notes
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 18–26): 288 verses; Urania's epiphany reprises the 1573 Urania elegy; her exile narrative is Tycho's private version of the translatio Musarum; the Invidia episode (modelled on Ovid, Met. II.775-82) makes Kaas the saviour of Uraniborg's establishment — Zeeberg explicitly finds no concrete funding episode behind it (guard: do not tie it to the 1579/1580 crises); as of 1993 the original print was known in a single exemplar (p. 15).

Si quid agat — If you ask what she is doing

EpigramunknownHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_si-quid-agat

Fragment preserved on a water-damaged leaf (Vienna, ÖNB Cod. Lat. 10689, fol. 40), printed by Dreyer as an epigram but read by Zeeberg as part of a longer poem belonging with the 1584-85 Uraniborg press poems: Urania, long an exile driven through the whole world, has at last set her weary feet on little Hven — the island an image of the wide world in miniature — and the reader is bidden to spread sail for its shores.

Date

The DSL's own descriptive label uses circa — '(c. 1585)'; the edition's year 1585

Correction. Dreyer prints the fragment undated ('non apparet, quo pertineat', TBOO IX 328); the Hven years are the only bound.

Dreyer prints the piece without a date and offers none; his editorial note says only that it is not apparent what it belongs to ('sed non apparet, quo pertineat', TBOO IX, p. 328). The '1585' comes from the edition, whose title-line reads 'Tycho Brahes digt Si quid agat (c. 1585)' — a circa date whose evidential basis is not stated there and is not supported by anything in TBOO. The only firm dating evidence is internal: the poem tells its reader to make for the shores of Hven, where the goddess 'has been glad to plant her weary feet', which presupposes that Urania is already installed on the island. That places composition inside Tycho's Hven years — he took possession of the island in February 1576 and left it in 1597 — and no closer. The range given here is that inference, not an attested date.

Language
Latin
Summary
A short Latin epigram in elegiac couplets, surviving as an unfinished draft: three complete distichs and the opening words of a fourth line, which breaks off in mid-verse ('Chaldeos Arabes Graeco...'). It answers an implied question about Urania, the muse of astronomy, known throughout the whole heaven yet present on the globe of the earth: if you ask what she is doing, spread sail and oars and make for the shores of little Hven ('Vela pande et remos Huaenae pete littora paruae'), for the little island is perhaps the image of the great world ('Parua orbis magni forsitan instar [erit]'); here the goddess, long driven out and an exile in all the world, has been glad to set down her weary feet. The truncated seventh line — 'Chaldeans, Arabs, Greeks' — was evidently beginning the roll-call of the peoples among whom astronomy had previously sojourned. Four words at line-ends are supplied by Dreyer in square brackets (c[oelo], [fui]t, [erit]), the manuscript being defective there. It is thus a Hven advertisement in miniature, and belongs with Tycho's recurrent conceit of Uraniborg as the refuge of a homeless Urania, but it was never finished.
Occasion
Not recoverable. Dreyer, the only editor of the text, states this in as many words: the epigram 'is found in the same codex from which we took the Astrologiae meteorologicae fragment; but it does not appear what it relates to' (TBOO IX, p. 328: 'sed non apparet, quo pertineat'). No prompting event, dedicatee or intended setting is named in the draft, and no authority consulted for this record supplies one. The invitation-to-Hven motif is the same one Tycho used in the occasional poems his own Uraniborg press printed in 1584-85 — to Jacob Ulfeldt (Nielsen 426), to chancellor Niels Kaas (Nielsen 427), to Heinrich Rantzau (Nielsen 425), all of which summon a great man to visit the island — so a discarded draft towards such a piece, or towards a prefatory epigram, is the obvious guess; but it is a guess, no source states it, and it is recorded here as a question, not a finding.
On the addressee
None named. The verse addresses an unidentified second person — the reader who is imagined asking after Urania ('si quid agat quaeris') and who is told to take ship for Hven. There is no dedicatee, no heading and no subscription in the manuscript as Dreyer prints it, and no addressee can be recovered.
Transmission
Manuscript only. The words survive in a single witness among Tycho's unprinted papers in Vienna: Dreyer's source lemma at TBOO IX, p. 215 reads '[E codice Vindobonensi lat. 10689]' (the printed lemma carries a superscript, set as '10689 40'), and the margin of the same page marks the manuscript leaf as fol. 5r. His note at TBOO IX, p. 328 identifies the codex as the one that yielded the Astrologiae meteorologicae fragmentum printed at TBOO I, pp. 177–178 — which Dreyer's headnote there (TBOO I, p. 176) cites as 'codex Vindobonensis lat. 10689', a Tycho autograph whose paper he describes as torn and damaged by damp (TBOO I, p. 313). The bracketed supplements at the line-ends of the epigram (c[oelo], [fui]t, [erit]) are consistent with the same physical damage. The Vienna location is the ordinary one for Tycho's unprinted papers, which passed to the Imperial Library after his death (TBOO I, Praefatio Societatis, p. I). The text was edited and first published by J. L. E. Dreyer and J. Raeder, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (1927), Carmina, p. 215, with the editors' note at p. 328; nothing further is added in the Carminum Appendix of TBOO XV (1929), pp. 1–6.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (cod. Vindob. lat. 10689; first printed in TBOO IX (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1927

Not printed in Tycho's lifetime. Lauritz Nielsen's bibliography of Tycho's complete printed output (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen), the authority on any printing claim for Tycho, has no entry for it; the carmina that Tycho did put through his own Uraniborg press in 1584-85 are the Epitaphium Johanni Pratensi (Nielsen 431), the Carmen ad Jac. Ulfeldium (426), the Carmen ad Nic. Kaasium (427) and the Carmen ad Henr. Ranzovium (425), and this is not among them, nor among Nielsen's four lost prints. Nor could it have been printed: it is an unfinished draft that breaks off in mid-line. Dreyer names no prior printing for it (contrast his practice elsewhere in the Carmina, where he cites Vingaard's 1572 broadsheet, Gassendi 1654, Resen 1668 and Studnicka 1901 as earlier witnesses). Its first printing is therefore TBOO IX (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1927), p. 215. That TBOO is the first printing rests on the combined silence of Nielsen and Dreyer, not on a positive statement by either.

Open questions
  • The date is not established. Dreyer gives none; the edition carries 'c. 1585' with no stated evidence. Nothing but the Hven setting of the verse constrains the date, and that only to 1576–1597. The disagreement between Dreyer's silence and the DSL's confident circa-date should not be smoothed over; whether Zeeberg has argued the 1585 dating in print elsewhere (e.g. in his editions of Tycho's Latin poetry) has not been checked.
  • The occasion is unknown, and Dreyer says so ('non apparet, quo pertineat'). The suggestion that it is a discarded draft towards one of the printed Uraniborg invitation-poems of 1584-85 (Ulfeldt, Kaas, Rantzau) — or towards a prefatory epigram for a book — is an untested inference from the shared motif, not a finding.
  • Whether the poem breaks off because the manuscript is damaged or because Tycho abandoned the draft is not stated. Dreyer marks four line-end lacunae with brackets (which implies physical loss) but prints the final line 'Chaldeos Arabes Graeco' without brackets or an editorial mark, as if the writing simply stops. The leaf itself (Vienna, Cod. lat. 10689, fol. 5r) has not been examined for this record.
  • The codex signature needs verification against the Osterreichische Nationalbibliothek's present-day cataloguing. Dreyer's lemma at TBOO IX p. 215 prints '10689' with a superscript that the type renders as '40' (probably a part- or format-designation, cf. his '10686(5)', '10686(6)', '10686(7)' for the neighbouring Carmina, and 'Thott. 1044 in 4to' at TBOO XV p. 6); TBOO I p. 176 cites the same codex simply as 'Vindobonensis lat. 10689'. The relation of fol. 5r to the leaves of the Astrologiae meteorologicae fragmentum in the same codex is not established.
  • No authority outside TBOO is known to discuss this epigram. It is absent from Dreyer 1890, Thoren, Christianson, Norlind and Nielsen, and a search on its incipit and on 'Chaldeos Arabes' finds only TBOO itself and the edition. Whether the Tycho-Latin-poetry scholarship (Zeeberg in particular) has treated it has not been established.
Notes
  • Text is fragmentary — lacunae in most lines and it breaks off mid-verse ('Chaldeos Arabes Græco...')
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 30–31, n. 31) re-edits the water-damaged leaf (Vienna, ÖNB Cod. Lat. 10689, f. 40) with new readings, against Dreyer's classification of it as an epigram (TBOO IX 215 + 328): clearly a fragment of a longer poem of the 1584-85 group, on Hven as an image of the whole world.
