De cometa anni 1585 — On the comet of the year 1585

TreatisesecureHvenARead the text →brahe-t_de-cometa-1585

Account of the round, tailless comet first seen at Uraniborg on 18 October 1585, printed in Elias Olsen Morsing's Diarium for 1586 — the first book from the Uraniborg press — together with Tycho's positional observations of it.

Full heading
De cometa anni 1585
Form
Treatise (this catalogue)
Date
1586 secure

the edition's year 1586 = printing year of Morsing's Diarium (Nielsen: calendar section printed late 1585, front matter early 1586); the comet itself was observed October-November 1585

The comet was observed at Uraniborg from 18 October to 15 November 1585 (TBOO IV, 399, 407-408); the text was therefore written after mid-November 1585. It speaks of 'this present year' 1586 throughout its predictive sections ('post medietatem Martij huius instantis anni', TBOO IV, 414; 'in vere huius anni 1586', TBOO IV, 407), and the booklet in which the first version was printed carries a dedication dated 1 January 1586 and was 'Excusum in Officina Vraniburgica' in 1586 (Nielsen, Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, no. 1170). Dreyer's own running head is 'De cometa anni 1585 (1586)' (TBOO IV, 397). Composition therefore falls in the winter of 1585/86; the printing is 1586. The year 1586 is the printing year, not the year of the phenomenon.

Addressee
Elias Olsen Morsing (under whose name the first treatise was printed)
Language
Latin
Summary
Two related Latin treatises on the faint tailless comet of October-November 1585, printed together by Dreyer under one head. Each falls into the same two halves: first an observational report (the comet first seen at Uraniborg on 18 October 1585 near the southern cord of Pisces, round, nebulous, without a tail, its light dull and lead-coloured like the Praesepe cluster; a night-by-night table of longitudes, latitudes, right ascensions and declinations to 12 November; a demonstration that it moved on a great circle with a steadily decreasing daily motion and vanished after 15 November); then a much longer 'Coniecturae astrologicae' on its effects, argued under three heads — what kinds of events it portends, for which regions and peoples, and when the effects begin and how long they last. The astrological verdict is Saturnine: plague and creeping epidemic disease, chronic melancholic illness, dearth and famine, floods, earthquakes, storms at sea, sedition and war conducted by fraud rather than open battle, worst in Italy, Germany and England, beginning in the spring of 1586 and lasting about a year. On the physical question Tycho states his key result without proof: the parallaxes were so small that the comet must have run its course high in the aether, not far below the solar sphere, and by no means in the upper air below the Moon 'as the Peripatetics have hitherto tried to persuade us' — the full demonstration being reserved for the comet book he was preparing (TBOO IV, 401).
Occasion
The apparition itself. A comet appeared in the autumn of 1585 and Tycho observed it at Uraniborg on every clear night from 18 October to 12 November, losing it after 15 November; he had learned from a copy of Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse's letter to Heinrich Rantzau that Christoph Rothmann had already seen it at Kassel on 8 October, and his own student Elias Olsen had noticed something unfamiliar around 10-13 October (TBOO IV, 403 and 513; the Landgrave's letter at TBOO VI, 31). The occasion of the writing, as distinct from the observing, is the Uraniborg press: Tycho wanted a public statement on the new comet in the almanac his assistant Elias Olsen Morsing was issuing for 1586 — the first proper book from his own press — while the geometrical demonstration waited for the large comet volume. The text says so in its own voice: the sufficient proof will come 'when what my master has clearly written on the whole business of comets shall come out in public' (TBOO IV, 401). The second, unprinted commentatio has no separately recoverable occasion; it is Tycho's own fuller working-out of the same material, left unfinished with blanks for figures and numbers (TBOO IV, 409-410, 514-515).
On the addressee
None. Neither treatise carries a dedicatee; both are addressed to the reader at large. The booklet that carried the printed version was dedicated by Elias Olsen Morsing (Elias Olai Cimber, from the isle of Mors in the Limfjord; Tycho's assistant at Hven from c.1583 to 1589) to the eight-year-old crown prince Christian, later Christian IV, in a dedication dated 1 January 1586 — and Dreyer found that preface partly drafted in Tycho's own hand in Vienna Cod. lat. 10689-6 (TBOO IV, 513; the draft preface printed separately at TBOO IX, 147-150). The one person named in the treatise itself is 'Herus meus', 'my master' — Tycho, referred to in the third person because the piece went out under Elias's name (TBOO IV, 401).
Transmission
Three channels, all converging on Dreyer. (1) print: the first treatise reaches us in the Uraniborg 1586 Diarium, 4to, of which Nielsen lists copies in some twenty libraries (Copenhagen KB 2, Univ. Bibl.; London BM; Oxford Bodleian; Cambridge; Vienna; Wolfenbuttel; Munich; Berlin; Bern; Uppsala; Lund; Oslo; and others: Dansk Bibliografi no. 1170). (2) manuscript: Vienna, Osterreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. lat. 10689, the great bundle of Tycho's loose papers. For the first treatise Dreyer found fragments covering most of the text in fascicles 10689-23, -27, -30 and -44/45 — some in Tycho's own hand, others neatly written by two other hands, one of them that of Peter Jacobsen Flemlose, Tycho's pupil, evidently fair copies made for the printer. The second treatise Dreyer restored from three fascicles, 10689-18, -11 and -26, its leaves torn apart and scattered, 'tota ipsius Tychonis manu scripta' — entirely in Tycho's own hand; the rough drafts, calculations and excerpts from the astrologers that lie behind it are in 10689-30 and -31 (TBOO IV, 512-515). (3) edition: J. L. E. Dreyer printed both treatises together as 'De cometa anni 1585 (1586)' in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, tom. IV (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1922), pp. 397–414, with his account of the manuscripts and of the Elias attribution in the Annotationes Editoris, pp. 512–515. For the printed piece he set 'talia plerumque verba... qualia Uraniburgi typis descripta erant' — substantially the Uraniborg text — while adding from the codex passages that had not been taken into the printed booklet (TBOO IV, 513, and annot. ad p. 407,20). The second treatise appears in print for the first time in TBOO IV. Tycho's raw observations of the same comet are printed separately at TBOO XIII, 336-371 ('Observationes cometae anni 1585'). That so much of Elias's booklet was Tycho's had not been known before Dreyer ('Ex Eliae libello tam multa Tychoni deberi, antea notum non fuit', TBOO IV, 513) — though Thaddaeus Hagecius, sent a copy, had already suspected in a letter of 9 May 1586 that it was Tycho's 'genuinus partus', while Heinrich Brucaeus, writing from Rostock on 15 March 1586, took it for the pupil's own work.
Channel
Printed by others in his lifetime (printed in Morsing's Diarium of 1586 (Nielsen 1170))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, island of Hven, 1586 (Unnamed ('Excusum in Officina VRANIBVRGICA'; Nielsen records the printer as 'Uvis Bogtrykker', printer unknown)); Nielsen 1170

PARTLY printed, and not under Tycho's name. The first of the two treatises ('De cometa seu stella crinita rotunda, quae anno antecedente in Octobri et Novembri apparuit') was printed at Uraniborg in 1586 as the opening section (foll. Bb2v-Dd2v) of Elias Olsen Morsing's 'Diarium astrologicum et metheorologicum anni a nato Christo 1586. Et de Cometa quodam rotundo omnique cauda destituto... per Eliam Olai Cimbrum' — 4to, 30 leaves, the first proper book to issue from Tycho's own press (Nielsen, Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, no. 1170, which cites 'T. Brahe: Opera omnia IV, S. 397-414'; Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, p. 186). The comet treatise was thus published in Tycho's lifetime, from his own press, but under his assistant's name; Dreyer established from the Vienna autographs that Tycho is its true author and that this was the intention from the start ('jam ab initio consilium ejus fuisse videtur, ut Eliae nomine libellus emitteretur', TBOO IV, 513). The SECOND treatise ('De crinita stella non caudata quae anno 1585 antecedente mense Octobri et Novembri apparuit') was NEVER printed in Tycho's lifetime or afterwards until Dreyer reconstructed it from the Vienna codices and first printed it in TBOO IV (1922), pp. 408–414. Nielsen has no entry for it — it is not in the printed corpus at all. Note also that the printed booklet's title-page, colophon and January diary-opening were reproduced photographically in G. Hellmann (ed.), Neudrucke von Schriften und Karten uber Meteorologie und Erdmagnetismus, No. 12 (Berlin, 1899) (TBOO IV, 513).

Open questions
  • The order of the two treatises is not established. Dreyer prints the published one first and the autograph 'De crinita stella non caudata' second, and says only that Tycho wrote it 'besides' (praeter) the one issued in Elias's name (TBOO IV, 514). Whether it is an earlier, fuller draft that was cut down for the almanac, or a later expansion begun after the booklet went to press, is not stated by any authority consulted here. Its unfilled blanks — 'inclinasse vero portionem sui circuli ad Eclipticam p... M...', 'pone hic figuram transitus per Eclipticam' (TBOO IV, 409-410) — show only that it was left unfinished, not when.
  • How much of the rest of Elias Olsen Morsing's 1586 Diarium is Tycho's remains open. Dreyer admitted only the comet section into the Opera Omnia, 'utpote quae tota huic deberi videretur' (TBOO IV, 513), and found Tycho's hand in the draft preface and in corrections to two diary pages; but the contemporary witnesses disagree — Hagecius (9 May 1586) thought the booklet Tycho's 'genuinum partum', Brucaeus (15 March 1586) thought it the pupil's work — and the calendar and general prognostic sections have not been assessed here.
  • The printed extent given by Dreyer (foll. Bb2v-Dd2v, TBOO IV, 513) and the collation given by Nielsen (leaves 6b-16b, the section ending '... subsequens Diarium discriminatim exhibebit') do not describe the same span: Nielsen's runs on past Dreyer's, because Dreyer excluded the closing non-cometary prognostic matter. Exactly where he stopped, and what the excluded leaves contain, has not been verified against a copy of the booklet for this record.
  • Whether the unprinted second treatise was ever intended for the Uraniborg press, or was from the outset a working draft toward the large comet volume promised in the printed text (which became De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis, 1588, and its planned companion on the later comets), is not determinable from the sources used here.
  • The fascicle sigla of the Vienna manuscripts are given here as Dreyer prints them (Cod. lat. 10689 with superscript numbers 11, 18, 23, 26, 27, 30, 31, 44-45). They have not been checked against the modern Osterreichische Nationalbibliothek shelfmark structure, and the physical state of the torn and scattered leaves of the second treatise is known only from Dreyer's description.

tekstnet edition metadata: publication year 1586 (the edition's page verified); the diary it prefaces is for the year 1586 (Nielsen: calendar section printed late 1585, front matter early 1586)

Not dated in the manuscript. The date is fixed by the printing it precedes. Tycho commissioned the almanac from Morsing in 1585 (Christianson, On Tycho's Island, p. 324); Nielsen shows from the signatures (Aa1-Dd4 A4-C4 D3) that the last 14 leaves, the calendar proper, were printed first, i.e. probably in late 1585, and that the front matter followed: the dedication is dated 1 January 1586 and the book went out early in 1586 (Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, pp. 186–187). Brucaeus had already read the book by 15 March 1586 (Dreyer, TBOO IV p. 513, citing TBOO VII p. 100). A draft of the front matter therefore belongs to late 1585 / the first days of 1586. The year 1586 is the year the almanac covers and the year of the printed dedication, not a documented date of composition for the draft.

Addressee
Christian, prince (Christian IV) (dedicatee)
Language
Latin
Summary
A working draft — Dreyer's title uses Tycho's own register, adumbratio, a sketch or outline — of the astrological preface to the Diarium astrologicum et metheorologicum anni 1586, the almanac that came off the Uraniborg press under the name of Tycho's assistant Elias Olsen Morsing. It begins as finished encomiastic prose: sideral science, which contemplates the revolutions and harmonies of the aetherial world and its influx into the elemental one, is the oldest of the liberal sciences, coeval with the heaven it is founded on, and was anciently disclosed only to kings, men of royal blood and priests — a claim carried by a long quotation from Manilius (Astronomica I.35-42, 46-47, 51-54), then by the names of ancient kings set among the constellations (Orion, Hercules, Arctophylax, Perseus, Erichthonius, Chiron), then by Julius Caesar, whose reform of the civil year through Sosigenes Tycho rates above all the wars he waged (with Lucan, Pharsalia X.184 sqq., on Caesar conferring with the astronomers of Egypt). At that point it stops being prose and becomes a memorandum to whoever will finish it: 'Hic oportet numerare alios imperatores post Iulium huic arti addictos et... ad Alphonsum, Carolum quintum, Philippum landgravium Hassiae, et postea ad avum et parentem ducatur oratio, et postea ipsum excitare, ut similia faciat' — followed by a bare list of names still to be worked up (Alphonso X, who is said to have refused the Roman empire for love of this art; Augustus, Tiberius, Vespasian, Titus, Hadrian 'qui sibi ipsi annua prognostica e sideribus composuit', Antoninus, Severus, Censorinus, Theodosius, Charlemagne, Frederick II, Maximilian, Charles V, Philip Landgrave of Hesse). It is thus not a text Tycho published but the scaffolding he handed to his pupil.
Occasion
In 1585 Tycho set Morsing to compile an astrological-meteorological calendar for the coming year, to be printed in some 2,000 copies as the first real book of his new Uraniborg press; the book was to go out over Morsing's name, not Tycho's. Tycho nevertheless directed it throughout — the comet section is his own work, two of the diary pages carry his corrections, and he drafted the preface for his assistant. Dreyer states the point of publishing the draft exactly: 'Hanc adumbrationem nunc publici juris facimus, ut intellegi possit, quomodo discipulo suo in publicum prodeunti viam monstraverit Tycho' — to show how Tycho showed his pupil the way when the pupil made his public debut (TBOO IX p. 320). The occasion is therefore documented and specific: it is a master's draft for an assistant's first book, and the earliest surviving evidence of Tycho ghost-writing for a member of his familia.
On the addressee
Prince Christian of Denmark (b. 12 April 1577; from 1588 King Christian IV), then not yet nine years old. The draft addresses him directly ('Princeps illustriss[ime]'), and Dreyer identifies the addressee: the preface of the booklet, 'in qua Christianum principem scriptor alloquitur', was found partly sketched in Tycho's hand (TBOO IV p. 513). The draft's own plan confirms it — after the Roman and modern emperors the oration is to turn 'ad avum et parentem', to the prince's grandfather (Christian III) and father (Frederik II), and then to rouse the boy himself to do likewise. Nielsen independently records that the printed book opens with a dedication by its author to 'den da knap niaarige Kronprins Christian', dated 1 January 1586. The nominal author of the finished preface is Elias Olsen Morsing (Elias Olai Cimber; c. 1550, Mors — 11 March 1590, Hven), Tycho's leading assistant on Hven 1583-90, who was sent to Frombork in 1584 to redetermine the latitude of Copernicus's observatory and who returned with Copernicus's own triquetrum (Christianson, On Tycho's Island, pp. 323–325).
Transmission
One manuscript witness. Vienna, Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek, Codex Vindobonensis lat. 10689(6) — part of the great Vienna group of Tycho's working papers that reached the Hofbibliothek from his heirs. The headnote to the piece in TBOO IX p. 148 reads: 'Adumbrationem praefationis Diarii astrologici et meteorologici anni 1586 nomine Eliae Olai Cimbri Uraniburgi in lucem emissi nunc primum edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 10689(6)' (verified on the page image). The same codex-number is given, independently, in the earlier volume, where Dreyer announced the find: 'praefationem quoque libelli, in qua Christianum principem scriptor alloquitur, in codice 10689(6) aliqua ex parte Tychonis manu adumbratam invenimus' (TBOO IV p. 513) — i.e. the sketch is, at least in part, an autograph. TBOO's printed margins carry the manuscript foliation (7v, 8r), so the piece occupies roughly ff. 7-8 of that codex. The text was thus unknown to the whole earlier biographical tradition (Gassendi, Friis, Dreyer 1890 all lacked it); Dreyer flagged its existence in TBOO IV (1922) and printed it in TBOO IX (1927), pp. 147–150, where it stands between the Uraniborg meteorological diary and the Craig additamenta. There is no evidence of any other copy.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (the sketch itself was first printed in TBOO IX; the finished preface went out under Morsing's name in 1586)
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia; Nielsen No Nielsen entry, and none is possible: Nielsen catalogues printed books, and this draft was never printed. The book it was drafted for is in Nielsen's Uraniborg bibliography under Morsing's name — 'Diarium astrologicum et metheorologicum anni a nato Christo 1586... per Eliam Olai Cimbrum... Excusum in Officina VRANIBVRGICA', 4to, 30 leaves, colophon 'IMPRESSVM VRANIBVRGI IN INSVLA CELEBRIS PORTHMI DANICI HVAENA', no printing year on the title (Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921, pp. 186–187; three copies at KB Copenhagen, one with an autograph dedication from Tycho to the Schleswig pastor Albert Meier). Nielsen enters the book under Morsing rather than under Brahe.

The adumbratio AS SUCH was never printed in Tycho's lifetime or at any time before Dreyer. What was printed, at Uraniborg early in 1586, is the finished preface that Morsing wrote up from it — and Dreyer is explicit that the working-up was largely left to Morsing: 'ita tamen, ut Eliae arbitrio plerumque permissum sit, quomodo Tychonis praecepta sequens singula absolveret' (TBOO IV p. 513). The two texts are therefore not the same text. Nor does TBOO print the finished preface: of the Diarium, TBOO IV prints only the comet section (De cometa anni 1585, IV pp. 397–414), which Dreyer demonstrated to be Tycho's own work. The draft was first published by Dreyer in TBOO IX (Hauniae, 1927), pp. 147–150, with the half-title's flat statement 'nunc primum edimus'.

References
  • TBOO IX, pp. 147–148 (headnote on p. 148; read from the page image) — First printing and transmission: 'nunc primum edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 10689(6)'. Establishes that TBOO IX is the editio princeps of this text and names the sole manuscript witness. Also gives the work's formal title and its attachment to the Diarium issued under Morsing's name at Uraniborg.
  • TBOO IX, pp. 149-150 — Content and form: the opening praise of sideral science as the oldest of the liberal sciences, anciently reserved to kings and priests; the address 'Princeps illustriss.'; the Manilius quotation; the kings among the constellations; Julius Caesar and the calendar reform through Sosigenes; and the abrupt collapse into a working memorandum ('Hic oportet numerare alios imperatores post Iulium huic arti addictos... et postea ad avum et parentem ducatur oratio, et postea ipsum excitare, ut similia faciat') with the bare list of emperors, Alphonso X, Charlemagne, Frederick II, Maximilian, Charles V and Philip of Hesse still to be worked up. This is the evidence that the piece is a draft, not a finished preface.
  • TBOO IX, p. 320 — Occasion, and the editors' rationale: 'Hanc adumbrationem nunc publici juris facimus, ut intellegi possit, quomodo discipulo suo in publicum prodeunti viam monstraverit Tycho.' Also the source-identifications: the verses are Manilius, Astronomica I.35-42, 46-47, 51-54; cf. Lucan, Pharsalia X.184 sqq.; cf. Ovid, Ars amatoria I.184; and the reference back to TBOO IV p. 513.
  • TBOO IV, pp. 512–513 (read from the page image) — Addressee and manuscript status: the preface of the booklet 'in qua Christianum principem scriptor alloquitur' was found 'in codice 10689(6) aliqua ex parte Tychonis manu adumbratam', with the working-up left largely to Morsing's discretion. Also the full transcribed title-page of the printed Diarium (30 foll. in 4to, 'Excusum in Officina Vraniburgica'); Dreyer's demonstration that the comet section is Tycho's, not Morsing's; and the contemporary suspicions of the two correspondents — Hagecius, writing 9 May 1586, called the book Tycho's 'genuinum partum', while Brucaeus on 15 March 1586 took it for the pupil's work.
  • Nielsen 1921, pp. 186-187 — The printing question. The Diarium is the first true book from the Uraniborg press: 4to, 30 leaves, signed Aa1-Dd4 A4-C4 D3 — a signing pattern proving the last 14 leaves (the calendar) were printed first, hence probably in late 1585; 2,000 copies were planned, on paper Tycho had to beg from Henrik Rantzau (letter of 8 Jan. 1585); the book opens with the author's dedication to the not-quite-nine-year-old Crown Prince Christian dated 1 January 1586, followed by an astrological preface, then the comet sections; colophon 'IMPRESSVM VRANIBVRGI IN INSVLA CELEBRIS PORTHMI DANICI HVAENA'; no year on the title-page; three copies at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, one containing a leaf with Tycho's autograph dedication to Albert Meier. Nielsen does not mention the draft — it was not printed.
  • Nielsen 1921, s.a. 1586, 'Diarium astrologicum et methorologicum anni 1586' — Negative evidence for the printing status of the draft: Nielsen's complete enumeration of the Uraniborg press's output contains the Diarium (under Morsing) but no separate printing of any prefatory draft by Tycho. Corroborates the 2,000-copy print run, the imported paper, the SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO emblem, and the dedication to Prince Christian.
  • Christianson 2000, pp. 323-325 — Identification of the nominal author: Elias Olsen Morsing (Helias, Elias Olai Cymber, Morsianus), b. c. 1550 on the island of Mors, leading assistant to Tycho on Hven 1583-90, sent to Frombork in 1584 to redetermine the latitude of Copernicus's observatory and given Copernicus's triquetrum, died on Hven 11 March 1590. Also: 'In 1585, Morsing was assigned by Tycho Brahe to prepare an astrological calendar for 1586, which Tycho wanted to print in some two thousand copies on his new press... The printing was dated 1 January 1586, and the work came out under the name of Morsing. It was the first bound product of the Uraniborg press' — and the comet appendix was 'written in part by Tycho'. Christianson elsewhere calls it plainly 'the 1586 almanac by Tycho and Morsing' (p. 300).
  • TBOO IV, entry on the 1586 Diarium apparatus — Corroboration of the manuscript identification: in Cod. Vindob. lat. 10689(6) the preface addressing Prince Christian is 'aliqua ex parte Tychonis manu adumbratam' (partly drafted in Tycho's hand), and two diary pages ('De Aestate', 'De Autumno') carry corrections manu Tychonis.
Open questions
  • Exactly which piece of the printed front matter the sketch underlies is not settled. Nielsen distinguishes two things in the printed book — a DEDICATION by the author to Prince Christian dated 1 January 1586, and then 'en astrologisk Fortale' — whereas Dreyer speaks of a single 'praefatio libelli' addressing the prince. The draft's content (an astrological encomium building to an exhortation of the prince) fits the Fortale, but Dreyer nowhere collates the two and the point is left open here rather than resolved by inference.
  • How much of Morsing's finished preface actually follows Tycho's sketch is unknown and cannot be checked in TBOO: Dreyer says the execution was mostly left to Morsing ('Eliae arbitrio plerumque permissum'), and TBOO prints only the draft (IX 147-150) and the comet section (IV 397-414), never the printed preface itself. A collation would require the Uraniborg imprint (KB Copenhagen holds three copies).
  • The extent of the autograph is stated only loosely. TBOO IV p. 513 says the preface was found 'aliqua ex parte' sketched in Tycho's hand; neither TBOO IV nor TBOO IX says whether the whole of the four printed pages is autograph or only part, nor identifies the hand of any non-autograph portion.
  • The draft contains an internal dating hint that is not followed up by Dreyer: 'Quod felici et firmo sidere ante annum electus sit' — the prince is said to have been elected about a year before writing. Which act of election or homage is meant (and therefore what precise year the sketch belongs to) is not established by any authority consulted here, and no guess is recorded.
  • The DSL Tekstnet edition (Zeeberg / Gredal Jensen), which carries 21 editorial notes on this text, was not consulted — the edition was not consulted directly — so it is unknown whether its editors depart from Dreyer on the codex, the date, or the relation of draft to printed preface.
Notes
  • Addressee not named in the draft itself; identified as Crown Prince Christian via the printed 1586 Diarium's dedication (Nielsen) and internal evidence (addressee 'elected a year before' = the 1584 hyldning; oration to proceed to his grandfather and father)

Inscriptiones Croneburgensis — Inscriptions from Kronborg

InscriptionuncertainHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_inscriptiones-croneburgenses

Latin verse inscriptions composed for Kronborg castle, praising its builder King Frederick II and Queen Sophie and adding a distich on fleeting time for the clock tablet.

IX 190INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES.

INCLYTUS hanc celsam FRIDERICUS condidit Arcem, Nomine qui simul et sorte SECUNDUS erat, Rex pius et justus, mitis, robustus in armis, Qui tamen invitus prætulit arma togæ, 5Cui Regina toro vixit sociata Regali, Mechelburgiaca nata SOPHIA domo. Quæ pariter virtutis amans, studiosa mariti, Pignora conjugii plena decore dedit. IX 191Ergo ubi placatos ageret Rex impiger annos, 10Structuræ tanta mole peregit opus, Munivitque arcem, velut adspicis, haud quod in ista Spem sibi tutelæ præsidiique locet, Nec velut antiquo structo Babylonis ovando Jactet, ut humana robora facta manu. 15Iste dedit pœnas fastus, dum septimus annus Cerneret amentem persimilemque feris. Rex nihil ostentat Danus. Se credit et optat Præsidio tutum solius eße Dei. Scit bene, ni faveat Numen, quod robora nulla 20Vel chalybe et duro facta adamante juvent. Ergo det astrorum terræque marisque Creator, In quo spem solo Rex FRIDERICUS habet, Prosper ut ille diu et soboles serique nepotes Has habitent, firma pace vigente, domos.

IN TABULA HOROLOGII.

25Transvolat hora levis neque scit fugitiva reverti, Nostra simul properans vita caduca fugit.

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Form

Date

tekstnet's own subtitle dates the work '(c. 1586)'; the edition's year 1586

No source dates either piece. Dreyer prints them undated and unannotated as to date (TBOO IX pp. 190–191; the Annotationes editorum at p. 323 discuss only where the first one stood). The 1586 comes from the edition, whose metadata heads the text 'Inscriptiones Croneburgensis / Indskrifter fra Kronborg (c. 1586)'; the grounds for that year are not stated in its metadata. The range given here is the interval the text itself supports. Floor: the poem speaks of a completed and fortified castle ('Structurae tanta mole peregit opus, / Munivitque arcem, velut adspicis') — Frederik II's modernisation of the fortifications round the medieval Krogen ran through the 1570s (the works were renamed Kronborg in 1577) and the rebuilding of the castle proper was carried to 1585 (Vellev, Renaessanceforum 12 [2017], pp. 108–109). Ceiling: the poem prays for the living king's long life and for his descendants' long possession of the house, so it is earlier than Frederik II's death on 4 April 1588, which Tycho marked in separate epigrams (TBOO IX p. 192; Dreyer's note, p. 323). Anything narrower than c. 1585–1588 would be invention.

Addressee
Frederik II (subject)
Language
Latin
Summary
Two Latin inscriptions from Kronborg castle at Elsinore, printed together by Dreyer under the rubric INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES. The first is twenty-four lines (twelve elegiac distichs) spoken from the building to the beholder ('velut adspicis'): the renowned FRIDERICUS, 'second both in name and in fortune', founded this lofty castle — a king pious, just, mild, strong in arms yet one who unwillingly preferred arms to the toga — whose queen SOPHIA, born of the house of Mecklenburg, bore him children full of grace; in peaceful years he finished the great mass of the structure and fortified the castle, yet not so as to lodge his hope of protection in it, nor to boast, as the builder of Babylon exulted, that human hands made these strongholds — that arrogance paid its penalty when the seventh year saw the man mad and like the beasts (Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 4) — for the Danish king makes no display, trusting to be safe under God's protection alone, well knowing that without the favour of the Deity no bulwarks avail, not though made of steel and hard adamant; so may the Creator of stars, earth and sea, in whom alone King Frederik places his hope, grant that he, his offspring and his late descendants may long inhabit these houses in firm and flourishing peace. The second is a single distich headed IN TABULA HOROLOGII, for the face of a clock: 'Transvolat hora levis neque scit fugitiva reverti, / Nostra simul properans vita caduca fugit' — the light hour flies past and, a fugitive, does not know how to return; our frail life, hurrying, flees along with it. The first was a placed, carved inscription: Dreyer records that in his own day a tablet was still shown on the outer face of Kronborg's north-facing bastion, on which the poem had been cut, but that the lettering had by then worn away.
Occasion
The subject is the building of Kronborg — Frederik II's transformation of the medieval Krogen into a fortified renaissance residence, the fortification works of the 1570s and the castle carried to completion by 1585 — and the poem's whole argument is a courtier's theological compliment: the king builds and fortifies, but places his trust in God, not in his walls. That is the *matter*. The *occasion* in the strict sense — who asked Tycho for the verses, when, for what ceremony or dedication, and by whose warrant they were cut into the bastion tablet — is not recoverable from any source consulted here. Dreyer prints the pieces with no occasion, no date and no comment beyond their (lost) physical location; nothing in TBOO XIV's document series, in Nielsen, in Friis 1871, or in the modern literature consulted discusses them. One piece of contemporary context should be recorded and then explicitly not over-read: on 28 September 1585 Frederik II wrote to Gert Rantzau, lensmand of Kronborg, ordering the castle painter to copy for Tycho the portraits of the kings from the great Kronborg tapestries and to have the Danish and German rhymes belonging to them transcribed for him (Friis 1871, p. 151). That shows Tycho in working traffic with Kronborg's decorative and epigraphic programme in precisely the years in question — but no source connects that traffic to these verses, and the inference must not be made. The occasion is unknown.
On the addressee
None in the epistolary sense: this is monumental verse, addressed grammatically to the passer-by who looks at the fortified castle ('velut adspicis'), and, in its closing prayer, to God ('det astrorum terraeque marisque Creator'). Its honorands are King Frederik II of Denmark (1534–1588, r. 1559-88), Tycho's patron — the donor of Hven and of Uraniborg's building costs — who is named in the first line and again in line 22, and, jointly with him, his queen, Sophie of Mecklenburg (1557–1631), named in line 6 as 'Mechelburgiaca nata SOPHIA domo'.
Transmission
No manuscript witness is known and Dreyer names none — unlike the neighbouring Carmina in the same volume, for which he cites the Vienna codex (Vindobonensis lat. 10686) or the Langebek excerpts, these two pieces come to Dreyer from a printed antiquarian source only. His headnote at TBOO IX p. 190 reads '[Ex Erici Pontoppidani Marmoribus Danicis I p. 136 (Hauniae 1739)]': the text descends from the carved tablet at Kronborg through Pontoppidan's collection of Danish inscriptions, printed in Copenhagen in 1739, and from Pontoppidan to Dreyer, who prints the two inscriptions at TBOO IX pp. 190–191 among the Carmina. Dreyer makes exactly one editorial intervention, recorded in the Variae scripturae at TBOO IX p. 314: 'AD INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES. p. 191 v. 2 Structurae e Structura correximus' — i.e. he corrects the source's 'Structura' to 'Structurae' in the line 'Structurae tanta mole peregit opus'. In the Annotationes editorum (TBOO IX p. 323) he adds the only note that exists on the pieces: 'INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES (p. 190 sq.) non jam exstant, sed monstratur etiamnum tabula in exteriore parte propugnaculi adversus septentriones spectantis, cui prior inscriptio insculpta fuit; nunc vero evanuit' — the Kronborg inscriptions no longer exist, but the tablet on the outer face of the north-facing bastion, into which the first of them had been cut, was still shown in his day, its lettering by then effaced. The editors themselves index the group as inscriptions: TBOO XV, Index hominum et rerum, p. 19, 'Croneburgenses inscriptiones IX 190-191'; and s.v. Fridericus II (pp. 22–23), 'Croneburgum condidit IX 190'. That is the entire chain of transmission as the sources give it: stone (lost/effaced) -> Pontoppidan 1739 -> Dreyer 1927.
Channel
Printed after his death (Pontoppidan, Marmora Danica, 1739)
Printing
printed posthumously — Copenhagen, 1739; Nielsen none — no Nielsen number

There is no evidence that these verses were ever set in type in Tycho's lifetime. They carry no Nielsen number: they are absent both from Nielsen's enumerated Brahe corpus (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, nos. 424-433 with 975-976) and from his list of the lost/disputed Hveen prints (Carmen ad Falk Gjoee; Carmen ad Erik Lange; the Hans Frandsen elegy; the 1591 Craig Apologia). Their lifetime 'publication' was the stone itself — the tablet cut on the outer face of Kronborg's north bastion (Dreyer, TBOO IX p. 323). The earliest printing traced here is posthumous and late: Erik Pontoppidan, Marmora Danica, tomus I (Hauniae, 1739), p. 136, which is the copy-text named in Dreyer's own headnote, '[Ex Erici Pontoppidani Marmoribus Danicis I p. 136 (Hauniae 1739)]' — 138 years after Tycho's death. TBOO IX (1927) is therefore NOT the first printing. Two negatives are worth recording: the poem is not in Resen's Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668) — a page-by-page search of Resen finds no 'Inclytus hanc celsam' and no trace of the text, which is consistent with Resen's Copenhagen/Hven scope — and Dreyer cites no other witness. The printer of Pontoppidan's volume is not named in the sources consulted here. See open_questions for the one live possibility of a lifetime printing (Nathan Chytraeus, Herborn 1594).

  • TBOO IX, p. 192 (the four epigrams on the death of Frederik II, the first two chronograms on 'FrIDrICVs qVarto... aprILIs'); p. 323 (Annotationes: 'DISTICHA DE OBITU FRIDERICI II REGIS (p. 192)... annum mortis 1588') — date: the terminus ante quem — Frederik II died on 4 April 1588, and the Kronborg poem prays for the living king's long life and his descendants' long possession of the castle
  • Friis 1871, p. 151 (the royal letter to Gert Rantzau, lensmand of Kronborg, Antvorskov, 28 September 1585: the castle painter is to copy for Tycho the kings' portraits from the Kronborg tapestries and to have the Danish and German rhymes belonging to them transcribed for him) — context only, expressly not the occasion: Tycho was in working contact with Kronborg's decorative and epigraphic programme in the mid-1580s; no source links this to the inscriptions
  • Resen 1668, checked negatively, page by page: no occurrence of 'Inclytus hanc celsam' or of any part of these two texts — printing/transmission: Resen — the collection that transmits several other Tychonic inscriptions (Uraniborg, Stjerneborg, Urania Titani) — does not carry the Kronborg inscriptions, which is why Dreyer had to go to Pontoppidan
  • Zeeberg & Gredal Jensen 2019, https://tekstnet.dk/books/brahe-t_inscriptiones-croneburgenses/001/ ; publication_year 1586; copy-text anchored to TBOO IX.190-191; one text-critical note, 'Structurae] TBOO, Structura A' — the edition of record, its title-form 'Inscriptiones Croneburgensis', the c. 1586 date this record contests, and its adoption of Dreyer's emendation
Open questions
  • The date is unsupported. The edition gives c. 1586; no authority consulted here states a year, and Dreyer prints both pieces undated. The c. 1585–1588 range recorded above is inferred from the building history and from Frederik II's death, not documented. If the edition has grounds for 1586 (perhaps from Pontoppidan, or from a year on the stone), they are not stated.
  • On what basis are the verses Tycho's? This is the record's weakest joint. Dreyer prints them among Tycho's Carmina, but his only citation is Pontoppidan's Marmora Danica (1739) — a collection of Danish carved inscriptions compiled 138 years after Tycho's death — and he nowhere states, in the headnote, the Variae scripturae or the Annotationes, what evidence assigns the poem to Tycho. Whether Pontoppidan himself names Tycho as author, and on what authority, has NOT been verified: Marmora Danica has not been seen for this record. Until it is checked, the ascription rests on Dreyer's editorial decision alone, and is a weaker claim than the text or the transmission.
  • Was there a lifetime printing after all? Tycho supplied Nathan Chytraeus with the Danish inscriptions for his Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn: Christoph Rab, 1594), which acknowledges the debt in the preface and prints a selection of the Hven inscriptions at pp. 593–601 (Vellev 2017). Whether the Kronborg tablet — a royal inscription that Tycho, if he wrote it, would have been well placed to supply — is among Chytraeus's Danica has not been checked; the book has not been seen for this record, and Dreyer does not cite it. If it is there, the printing status of this record changes from posthumous (1739) to printed in Tycho's lifetime (1594). This is the single most valuable next check.
  • Where was the clock inscription? The rubric IN TABULA HOROLOGII gives the fitting but not the building; Dreyer's note specifies the placement only of the 'prior inscriptio' (the bastion tablet) and says merely that the Kronborg inscriptions 'non jam exstant'. That the clock in question was Kronborg's is the natural reading of the shared rubric and of Pontoppidan's context, but no source says so. Note that Tycho used the same conceit at Uraniborg, where a distich ran round the rim of the cupola clock (TBOO VI p. 369).
  • Does the bastion tablet still exist? Dreyer reported in 1927 that it was 'still shown' on the outer face of the north-facing bastion with its letters effaced. No modern report — archaeological, conservation, or Kronborg-museum — has been checked; whether the stone survives, and whether raking-light or photogrammetric re-reading could recover any of the lettering (as Vellev and Zeeberg did in 2001 for Tycho's Hven paper-mill votive stone), is unknown.
  • Title form: TBOO's rubric and the TBOO XV index give the plural 'Inscriptiones Croneburgenses'; the edition heads the piece 'Inscriptiones Croneburgensis'. The plural is Dreyer's and is adopted here; nothing of substance hangs on it, but the variant should be kept searchable.
  • The 'work' is an editorial grouping, not a Tycho-authored collection: two separate inscriptions, of very different scale and character (a 24-line dynastic-theological poem for a bastion; a two-line memento-fugit for a clock-face), printed under one rubric because Pontoppidan found them together at Kronborg.
Notes
  • The edition's display title has the form 'Croneburgensis'; the text's own heading reads INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES.

Apologetica responsio ad Craigum Scotum de cometis — Apologetic reply to the Scot Craig concerning comets

TreatisesecureHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_apologetica-responsio

Tycho's reply to the Scottish mathematician John Craig, defending against Craig's objections the argument of his De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588) that comets are celestial bodies above the moon.

Full heading
Apologetica responsio ad Craigum Scotum de cometis (heading in the Copenhagen codex, printed by Dreyer at the head of the text: 'Apologia illustriss. viri domini Tychonis Brahe ad Craigum Scotum de cometis'; fuller heading in the Berlin codex: 'Apologia Dn. Tychonis Brahe ad D. Johannem Craigum, qva ipsius placita disqviruntur & redarguuntur'; Erasmus Bartholin's 1665 citation-form of the printed edition: 'Apologetica responsio ad cujusdam Peripatetici in Scotia dubia, sibi de parallaxi cometarum opposita')
Form
Treatise (this catalogue)
Date
1589 secure

the edition's year 1589; a reply to Craig's critique of De mundi (printed 1588, Nielsen).

Composition is fixed within 1589 by the correspondence at both ends. John Craig's three letters of objection are of May, 18 June and 9 July 1589 (TBOO VII, pp. 175–182, 191-193, 193; Dreyer's note ad p. 474,5, TBOO IV, p. 521); Tycho 'immediately composed a copious Apologetica Responsio' ('At Tycho continuo Apologeticam Responsionem copiosam composuit', TBOO IV, p. 517) and sent it to Craig with his letter of 25 October 1589 (TBOO VII, pp. 195–196). Dreyer's own head-title dates the piece '(1589)'. Note that 1589 is the year of WRITING; the (lost) Uraniborg printing is of 1591, and a further Hamburg/Wandsbek printing is reported for 1598 — see 'printed'. Tycho himself says he dictated it to an amanuensis between other business, 'prout in buccam venerunt' (as the words came into his mouth), which explains its unevenness (Tycho to Hagecius, 25 January 1590, quoted TBOO IV, p. 518).

Addressee
John Craig (addressee)
Language
Latin
Summary
A long polemical treatise-in-address (some sixty printed pages in TBOO; Mosley calls it 'a forty-page document'), cast as a continuous reply to a named opponent and answering, point by point, the objections John Craig had raised in three letters against Tycho's De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588). It opens with elaborate courtesy — 'Pergratus mihi fuit tuus ille eruditus labor... Doctissime CRAIGE' — thanking Craig for having examined the book so closely, since truth 'shines out more clearly only when what can be adduced against it has been weighed in a just balance', and then registers Tycho's astonishment that a man so skilled in mathematics should be so enslaved to Aristotle's authority. The substance is a defence of the two claims Craig had attacked: that the comet of 1577 showed no sensible parallax and therefore stood far beyond the Moon in the ether (Craig held that the comet's own proper motion vitiated Tycho's parallax determinations), and that there are no solid celestial orbs — the planets move freely through a fluid heaven, the Earth resting immobile at the centre. It closes by defending the Tychonic hypotheses (Mars at acronychal rising nearer the Earth than the Sun), by referring to the circelli Tycho had explained to Duncan Liddel ('Dunchanus'), and by inviting Craig to weigh the whole 'per otium justa ingenii et judicii trutina'.
Occasion
Fully recoverable. In 1588 a Scottish soldier-diplomat of James VI, William Stewart of Houston, visited Uraniborg; when he sailed home he carried a presentation copy of Tycho's De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588) inscribed by Tycho to John Craig, physician in Edinburgh, 'Vraniburgi anno 1588 Nouemb. 2.' — the copy still in Edinburgh University Library (Dreyer, TBOO IV, pp. 515–516). Craig thanked Tycho and, in three letters of May-July 1589, raised Aristotelian objections: comets are sublunary phenomena of the air, and Tycho's parallax argument is invalid because it fails to allow for the comet's own motion; the abolition of the solid spheres is also rejected. Tycho answered at once with this Apologia and despatched it with a (deliberately genial) covering letter of 25 October 1589. Dreyer's judgement of the whole affair: 'this gift gave occasion to the contest between Tycho and Craig on the nature of comets; had it not existed, Craig's name would scarcely have been handed down to posterity' (TBOO IV, p. 516). Almost immediately Tycho conceived a further, editorial occasion for the piece: he decided to print it, together with Craig's letters, as an appendix to De mundi liber secundus, and told Hagecius (25 Jan and 23 Feb 1590), Peucer (1590 or 1591) and Craig himself (14 Nov 1591) so (TBOO IV, p. 517).
On the addressee
John Craig (Joannes Craigius, d. 1620), Scottish physician and mathematician, at the time of the dispute practising medicine in Edinburgh; later physician to James VI and, after 1603, a member of the London Royal College of Physicians (1604) and incorporated M.D. at Oxford (1605). He had taught mathematics and logic at the University of Frankfurt an der Oder — Duncan Liddel was his pupil there before going to Wrocław to learn mathematics from Paul Wittich — and returned to Scotland in 1584; he never visited Denmark. He was the younger brother of the jurist Thomas Craig, who in 1594 wrote to Tycho to apologise for him. (Dreyer, TBOO IV, pp. 516–517; Mosley, 'Tycho Brahe and John Craig', 2002, p. 75 and n. 22; Familia, s.v. John Craig, where he is one of Westman's four Tycho disputants — Ursus, Wittich, Rothmann, Craig — and the man whose transcription of a Wittich note supplied the key to the Wittich hand.) A secondary addressee is the learned public: the Praefatio Tycho later drafted for the projected printed edition speaks past Craig to the 'optime et benevole Lector' (TBOO IX, p. 156).
Transmission
The words survive in manuscript, not in the print. Dreyer's source-lemma (TBOO IV, p. 416) states the position exactly: the Apologetica Responsio, 'written in 1589 and printed at Uraniborg in 1591, since not even one printed exemplar appears to survive, we edit from the Copenhagen codex Nov. Coll. Reg. 93b in folio; we have also collated a manuscript fragment appended to the Berlin exemplar of the first book of the Progymnasmata and of De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis.' The Copenhagen manuscript (Kongelige Bibliotek, Ny kgl. Samling 93b fol.) is a fair copy 'written apparently not long after Tycho's time', reasonably accurate; the Berlin witness — the Tycho convolute in the Staatsbibliothek — carries, after the printed De mundi, Craig's three letters entire (nowhere else transmitted) and the FIRST PAGES ONLY of the Apologia (to TBOO IV, p. 421,10). Nielsen argues that this Berlin fragment was copied from the lost printed edition and therefore shows how that edition was made up: Craig's three letters first, then the Apologia (Nielsen 1921, pp. 194–195). Tycho also circulated the piece in manuscript to friends (Hagecius, Peucer, and William Fuller, who read it at Uraniborg). Its first appearance in public print is therefore Dreyer's — 'quae nunc primum in publicum emittitur' (TBOO IV, p. 517) — in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, tom. IV (Copenhagen, 1922), pp. 415–476, with the editor's notes at pp. 515–521. Directly attached to it are three further texts, all edited by Dreyer: Craig's three letters and Tycho's covering letter of 25 Oct 1589 (TBOO VII); Craig's counter-attack, the Capnuraniae restinctionis fragmentum (TBOO IV, pp. 477–488), never published by Craig; and the paratexts Tycho drafted for the projected printed edition — the 'Praefatio in Apologiam sequentem', an epilogue on the Capnurania and even a German instruction to the compositor — first printed by Dreyer & Raeder from cod. Vindobonensis lat. 9737f as 'Additamenta ad Apologeticam responsionem ad Craigum Scotum de cometis', TBOO IX (1927), pp. 151–157 (a separate record here: brahe-t_apologetica-responsio-additamenta).
Channel
Separately printed by Tycho (the Uraniborg print of 1591, no copy known (Nielsen 1921, pp. 193–195))
Printing
printed in his lifetime — Uraniborg, Hven, 1591 (Tycho's own press (printer not named; no copy survives to bear a colophon)); Nielsen none — Nielsen assigns no Dansk Bibliografi number, because no copy survives; the printing is established in his 'Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen' (1921), pp. 193–195

printed IN TYCHO'S LIFETIME, BUT NOT ONE COPY SURVIVES, AND THE PRINTING WAS LONG DENIED. Dreyer states it flatly: after communicating his plan to Hagecius, Peucer and Craig, 'ac re vera a. 1591 Uraniburgi typis descripta est. Sed ne unum quidem exemplum Apologiae typis descriptum ad nostram aetatem pervenisse videtur' (TBOO IV, p. 517). The evidence is Erasmus (Rasmus) Bartholin, De cometis anni MDCLXIV & MDCLXV (Copenhagen, 1665), p. 49, who quotes the work and says he owns the print: '... in Apologetica Responsione ad cujusdam Peripatetici in Scotia dubia, quam impressam habeo Uraniburgi Anno 1591 (neque ut putat eximius Gassendus in Vita Tychonis, Manuscripta tantum reservata est a Longomontano & Frommio)' — an explicit correction of Gassendi, who had said the work survived only in manuscript, kept by Longomontanus and then by Jørgen From. All four passages Bartholin quotes are found in the Copenhagen codex (Dreyer, TBOO IV, p. 517). Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668), p. 391, also lists the Apologetica Responsio, with Craig's letter and the Capnurania restinctio, as appended to De mundi liber II — though without saying in so many words that they were printed. The lost print is entered in the older astronomical bibliographies with a title-form matching Bartholin's: Lalande, Bibliographie astronomique (1803), p. 123, and Houzeau & Lancaster, Bibliographie générale de l'astronomie (1887), which calls it 'très rare'. AGAINST this: Gassendi (Vita Tychonis, 1654/55, p. 240 of the Paris ed.), and — before Nielsen's 1921 article — BOTH modern biographers, F. R. Friis (Tyge Brahe, 1871, p. 265) and Dreyer himself (Tycho Brahe, 1890, p. 209 n.; German ed. p. 219), concluded that the Apologia was never printed. Nielsen 1921 overturned that with the Bartholin passage; Dreyer, editing TBOO IV in 1922, cites Nielsen's article and now asserts the 1591 printing as fact. A second, LATER printing is reported but unconfirmed: Houzeau & Lancaster list, after the 1591 Uraniborg edition, a further '[Wandesburgi] 1598', which agrees with Tycho's letter to Bartholomäus Scultetus of 7 January 1600 (from Prague) mentioning 'defensive writings' he had had printed in Hamburg. Nielsen accepts this only tentatively — the 1592 arrival of Craig's Capnuraniae restinctio may have made a revision necessary — and adds 'Forholdet er dog ikke helt klart' (the matter is not entirely clear): Nielsen 1921, p. 195. No copy of any printing is known.

Open questions
  • Was it in fact printed? The whole printing claim rests on one witness — Rasmus Bartholin's 1665 statement that he owned a printed copy — plus the bibliographies (Lalande 1803, Houzeau & Lancaster 1887) that may simply depend on him, plus Resen 1668 (who does not say in so many words that the pieces were printed). Gassendi (1654/55), Friis (1871) and Dreyer (1890) all denied the printing; Dreyer reversed himself in TBOO IV (1922) after Nielsen's 1921 article. No copy of any printing is known, and no copy has been reported since. The reversal is recorded here rather than smoothed over; that Nielsen's article is what changed Dreyer's mind is a plausible inference (Dreyer cites it in TBOO IV, p. 491 n. 3) but is not stated by Dreyer.
  • The reported second printing, '[Wandesburgi] 1598' (Houzeau & Lancaster), is unverified. Its only corroboration is Tycho's own reference, in his letter to Scultetus of 7 January 1600, to 'defensive writings' printed at Hamburg — which he says he intends to print AGAIN, since a further refutation of 'a learned Scot' has still to be added. Nielsen accepts it only tentatively and says outright that the matter is not clear. Whether the 1598 item was a reprint of the 1591 Apologia, an enlarged version answering the Capnurania, or something else entirely is unknown.
  • Who commended Craig to Tycho? Dreyer (TBOO IV, p. 515) says William Stewart of Houston 'seems to have' done so; Mosley (2002, p. 75 n. 21) says Craig's own first letter makes clear that Stewart merely carried the book, and that it was Duncan Liddel who named Craig to Tycho. Mosley's reading rests on the primary letter and should be preferred, but the disagreement stands in the literature.
  • The relation of the Berlin manuscript fragment to the lost print. Nielsen infers that the Berlin fragment (Craig's three letters + the opening pages of the Apologia, bound after the printed De mundi) was transcribed FROM the printed edition, and uses this to reconstruct that edition's make-up. Dreyer merely uses the fragment as a textual witness and does not endorse the inference. The Berlin shelfmark is not recorded in the sources consulted here.
  • The exact extent and title of the printed edition are unrecoverable. Dreyer's title 'Apologetica Responsio' is a reconstruction ('illa esse videtur, si Bartholino et Resenio credimus, quam exhibuit editio typis descripta'); the two surviving manuscripts give different headings, and Tycho in his letters sometimes says simply 'Apologia'.
  • Nothing establishes how far the printed 1591 text differed from the Copenhagen codex Dreyer printed. Bartholin's four quotations are all found in the codex, which is reassuring but not decisive; and the Additamenta (TBOO IX) show Tycho drafting paratexts for the print that the manuscript tradition does not carry.

Additamenta ad apologeticam responsionem ad Craigum Scotum — Additions to the apologetic reply to the Scot Craig

SupplementuncertainHvenBRead the text →brahe-t_apologetica-responsio-additamenta

Preface and supplementary documents assembled for a printed edition of the reply to John Craig, recounting the course of the controversy over the celestial location of the comet of 1577 and its sequel — Craig's counter-tract Capnurania and the letters exchanged with the chancellor of Scotland (Joh. Metellanus), who had visited Tycho on Hven in his king's retinue.

Full heading
Additamenta ad Apologeticam responsionem ad Craigum Scotum de cometis
Form
Supplement (this catalogue)
Date
1592–1601 uncertain — the edition: 1589

the edition's year 1589 (grouped with the Apologia); internal references show composition continuing into the early 1590s.

Correction. The edition's 1589 is the year of the Apologia the dossier was to accompany; the connective matter was assembled for a printed edition projected in the 1590s and never made.

Dreyer prints the piece without a year (the half-title, TBOO IX p. 151, carries none, unlike the Apologia's '(1589)' at TBOO IV p. 415). The 1589 of the edition is the date of the Apologia itself; the Additamenta cannot all be that early. The second section refers to Craig's 'Capnuraniae restinctio' as already received 'tertio demum anno' after the Apology was sent (sent 25 Oct. 1589; the Capnurania came with Craig's letter of 27 March 1592, TBOO IV pp. 521–522), and to Tycho's letter of August 'the same year' to the Chancellor of Scotland (19 Aug. 1592, TBOO VII pp. 338–341) and to Craig's mockery of that letter. So the piece post-dates 1592 in its present state; it was drafted while the enlarged Craig dossier was being made ready for the press, a project still alive on 31 Dec. 1598 (letter to Longomontanus) and in early 1601 (Kepler set to write the refutation), and it ends with Tycho's death, 24 Oct. 1601. The opening Praefatio alone could in principle go back to the 1591 Uraniborg printing of the Apologia.

Addressee
John Craig (the adversary answered)
Language
Latin
Summary
Not a work but a small dossier of connective and editorial matter that Tycho drafted for a projected enlarged edition of his second cometary volume (De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis, 1588 = Progymnasmata tom. II), in which his Apologetic Reply to John Craig, Craig's three letters, and Craig's counter-attack 'Capnuraniae restinctio' were to be printed together. It contains (i) a 'Praefatio in Apologiam sequentem' narrating how Tycho had the cometary volume printed on his own press, sent copies to mathematicians for their censure and some to the Frankfurt fair, and had one carried to a mathematician in Scotland (an opportunity offered by the sailing route and the then-pending royal marriage-alliance between the two kingdoms), only for Craig alone to oppose him; (ii) a passage, prefaced by a German instruction to the compositor ('So bald wan die Capnurania auss ist, sollen dissen nachfolgende wordt mitt kleine antiquis gesetz werden' — as soon as the Capnurania ends, set the following words in small roman), dismissing the Capnurania as arrogant and futile, recalling that it reached him amid unwelcome legal business and was read aloud to him by a student on the boat to the Diet at Copenhagen, and declaring that he would not answer it; and (iii) a short linking note announcing the letter of the Scottish Chancellor to Tycho and Tycho's reply. The set is the visible seam of a book that was never finished.
Occasion
The dispute with John Craig. Tycho sent Craig a copy of De mundi (inscribed at Uraniborg 2 Nov. 1588, now Edinburgh University Library); Craig answered in 1589 with three letters defending the Aristotelian sublunary comet against Tycho's parallax argument; Tycho wrote the Apologetica responsio and sent it to him on 25 Oct. 1589. Having decided to make the whole exchange public by appending it to his second book — and, after Craig's mocking 'Capnuraniae restinctio' arrived in March 1592, to append that too — Tycho wrote these supplementary pieces as the front matter, the transitional note and the closing link of the enlarged volume. The German note to the typesetter shows they were written as printer's copy; the surviving manuscripts of Craig's letters and of the Capnurania carry gathering-numbers showing they had actually been handed to a compositor (TBOO IV p. 522). The book never appeared: Longomontanus was ordered to write the refutation and had not done so by 31 Dec. 1598; Kepler began one about the start of 1601 and abandoned it when Tycho died.
On the addressee
No dedicatee. The Praefatio addresses the reader of the projected volume ('optime et benevole Lector'); the adversary throughout is John Craig (d. 1620), the Edinburgh physician-mathematician, Wittich's sometime associate, later physician to James VI. The third section introduces the Chancellor of Scotland, 'Ioannes Metellanus' — John Maitland of Thirlestane — who had visited Tycho at Uraniborg in the retinue of James VI and to whom Tycho wrote on 19 Aug. 1592 (TBOO VII pp. 338–341); the Chancellor's letter to Tycho of 16 May 1592 (TBOO VII pp. 336–337) was to follow at this point in the book.
Transmission
The words survive in a single manuscript witness: Vienna, Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. Vindobonensis lat. 9737f (the volume that also preserves part of Tycho's dealings with and about Craig, and the Craig correspondence Dreyer printed in TBOO VII). Dreyer's source-note at TBOO IX p. 152 reads 'edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 9737 f', and his Annotationes (TBOO IX p. 320) say 'Addimus nunc pauca eodem pertinentia e codice Vindobonensi lat. 9737 f' — i.e. first publication. The related texts are edited elsewhere in the same edition: the Apologia from Copenhagen KB Ny kgl. Saml. 93b fol., collated with the Berlin copy (TBOO IV pp. 415–476), the Capnuraniae restinctio fragment from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686 (TBOO IV pp. 477–488), and the Craig and Maitland letters in TBOO VII.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (first printed in TBOO IX (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1927

Nielsen has no entry for these Additamenta, and no authority states that they were ever set in type. What Nielsen's material does record is (a) the Apologia itself, printed at Uraniborg in 1591 — not in his numbered series, contested by Friis and Dreyer on Gassendi's authority, but attested by Rasmus (Erasmus) Bartholin, De cometis (Copenhagen 1665) p. 49, who owned a printed copy; no copy survives; and (b) a contested lost enlarged Apologia said to be '[Wandesburgi] 1598' (Houzeau & Lancaster 1887), for which the evidence is Tycho's letter to Scultetus of 7 Jan. 1600 about 'apologetica' printed in Hamburg — a claim Norlind 1970 corrects Nielsen on. If such an enlarged reissue existed, matter of this kind could conceivably have been set for it; but no copy is known, and nothing in Dreyer connects these particular pages to any press. Treat as unprinted in Tycho's lifetime and first published by Dreyer and Raeder in TBOO IX (Copenhagen 1927), pp. 151–157.

Supports the printed status and its note.

Open questions
  • Exact date. Dreyer prints the piece undated; DSL/tekstnet dates it 1589 (the Apologia's year). The internal evidence (the Capnurania received in the third year after Oct. 1589; the August 1592 letter to the Scottish Chancellor; Craig's mockery of that letter) puts the second and third sections in or after late 1592, but nothing fixes them more closely within 1592–1601.
  • Which press was the German compositor's note written for? A German-speaking typesetter served Tycho both on Hven and later; if the instruction belongs to the Wandsbek/Hamburg phase (Philip de Ohr, 1597-98) it would connect these pages to the contested lost enlarged Apologia of 1598. Undetermined — Dreyer says nothing about it.
  • Whether any of this matter was ever set in type. The manuscripts of Craig's letters and of the Capnurania carry compositor's gathering-numbers (TBOO IV p. 522); it is not stated whether cod. Vindob. lat. 9737f shows the same, and no printed copy of any enlarged Apologia survives.
  • Whether the opening Praefatio was drafted for the 1591 Uraniborg printing of the Apologia rather than for the later enlarged compilation; it does not itself mention the Capnurania.
  • Whether Resenius (Inscriptiones Haffnienses, 1668, p. 391) was describing a real printed compilation — Apologia + Craig's letter + Capnuraniae restinctio appended to the second book of the Progymnasmata — or conflating Tycho's plan with the book. Dreyer reports him without endorsement.

IX 192IUDICIS est æqui verum rectumque tueri, Non obstare bonis nilque iuvare malos. The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
Iudicis est aequi (untitled epigram, cited by its incipit: 'Iudicis est aequi verum rectumque tueri')
Form
Epigram (this catalogue)
Date
1592 probable

The poem's own dated subscription: 'Anno 1592, die 15 Febr. in itinere a Ringstadio domum'; preferred over the DSL metadata year 1588 (the edition's metadata), which conflicts with the text.

Correction. The edition's 1588 is a metadata error; the lawsuit the epigram concerns ran in 1592.

The piece dates itself. Both surviving print traditions carry the same subscription: 'T. B. | Anno 1592, die 15 Febr. in itinere a Ringstadio domum' (TBOO IX, p. 192; Danske Magazin II, 1746, p. 279, where the editors print from Tycho's own autograph draft). Dreyer repeats the date in his 1890 biography ('In February 1592 Tycho had to attend the provincial court at Ringsted', p. 220). The year 1588 given by the edition's index, which files the piece under 1588, immediately after the four epigrams on the death of Frederik II (printed on the same TBOO page, from the same Langebek excerpt-volume) — is therefore wrong or at best unexplained; see open_questions. Composed 15 February 1592, on the ride home from Ringsted.

Addressee
Lauge Beck, judge (addressee)
Language
Latin
Summary
A short, angry epigram: four elegiac couplets, eight lines, untitled in the sources and cited by its incipit. It tells a judge what a judge is for — 'Iudicis est aequi verum rectumque tueri, / Non obstare bonis nilque iuvare malos' (it is the part of a fair judge to uphold what is true and right, not to obstruct the good and give no help against the wicked) — then accuses him of doing the opposite: 'Tu tamen impulsum (testis Deus) aequa movere / Negligis et nequam fersque fovesque malum' (you, God is my witness, neglect to move the just cause when pressed, and you bear with and foster the worthless wrongdoer). It closes on a threat and a barb: the avenger of right and wrong will soon exact the penalty for an insolent cause, so 'if you are wise, look to your own safety, Lago; and if you will not spare me, spare yourself' ('Si sapis ergo, tuae bene consule, Lago, saluti, / Et mihi si non vis parcere, parce tibi'). It is signed 'T. B.' and subscribed with the date and place of composition — on the road home from Ringsted, 15 February 1592.
Occasion
A lawsuit lost. Tycho had been at the Sjællandsfar landsting (the provincial court of Zealand, which sat at Ringsted), the judgment went against him, and he wrote the epigram on the ride home the same day — the subscription 'in itinere a Ringstadio domum' says as much, and the 1746 Danske Magazin biographer draws exactly that inference: Tycho 'evidently' had a suit before the Sjællandsfar landsting early in 1592 in which the verdict must have gone against him, 'for he gives all too plain expression to his dissatisfaction with the landsdommer Lage Bek, and holds that the greatest injustice has been done him by him' (DM II, p. 279). Dreyer, editing the Carmina in 1927, identifies the litigation as Tycho's long, ugly suit with his tenant Rasmus Pedersen (Erasmus Petri) of Gundsømagle, a peasant on Tycho's Roskilde prebend whom he had put in irons, carried to Hven and held six weeks in prison, and whose case Tycho had lost before four commissioners (April 1591) and again on appeal before the king's Retterting (10 July 1591) — cross-referring to the documents at TBOO XIV pp. 57 ff. and 63 ff. Parts of that matter had been remitted to the herredsting and the landsting, which is why it came before the landsdommer at all. Both eighteenth- and twentieth-century editors hedge on WHICH of the outstanding cases was tried that day (see open_questions), but the general occasion — a judgment against Tycho at Ringsted on 15 February 1592, in the litigation with Rasmus Pedersen — is as well grounded as anything in this register.
On the addressee
Lave (Lauge, Lage) Beck, landsdommer of Zealand — addressed only by the vocative 'Lago' in line 7, and identified by both editorial traditions: 'Landsdommeren Lage Bek' (Danske Magazin II, 1746, p. 279) and 'scriptum est ad Lagonem (Lauge) Beck judicem' (Dreyer, TBOO IX, p. 323). He is the Lauge Beck who appears constantly in the chancery registers as lensmand of Roskildegaard and, in the royal letters of 17 November and 1 December 1592, as 'landtzdommer wdj Sieland', ordered by Christian IV's regency government to take the whole Tycho–Rasmus Pedersen quarrel before him and judge it without further delay (TBOO XIV, nos. 96 and 98). Per Toftgaard 2023 he is Lave Beck til Førslev (1530–1607), who held Ringsted abbey as a fief from 1592 and lived there 1592–1605. He is not a member of Tycho's familia and has no entry in Christianson's Biographical Directory.
Transmission
Manuscript, in two eighteenth-century Copenhagen antiquarian channels, converging on the Royal Library. (1) Tycho's OWN DRAFT. The Danske Magazin editors state that they print from 'Tyge Brahes egenhændige Udkast' — Tycho's autograph draft — 'iblandt de rare Papirer, som Hr. Etats Raad Gram har haft den Godhed i denne Materie at meddele os', i.e. among the rare papers communicated to them by Hans Gram (1685–1748), royal historiographer and librarian (DM II, 1746, p. 279). That is the source of the first printing. (2) LANGEBEK'S EXCERPTS. Dreyer's copy-text in TBOO IX (1927), p. 192, is a different witness: his lemma reads '[Ex excerptis Langebekianis Hauniensibus nr. 179]' — the excerpt-volumes of Jacob Langebek (1710–75) in the Royal Library, Copenhagen. The same excerpt-volume supplied the four chronogram epigrams on Frederik II's death printed immediately above it on the same page; the neighbouring volume nr. 178 supplied the Vedel epigram at TBOO IX, p. 174, of which Dreyer expressly says it is there 'ipsius Tychonis manu scriptum' (TBOO IX, p. 322). He says nothing of the kind for nr. 179, and whether Gram's autograph draft is the very leaf Langebek's collection preserved is not stated by any authority consulted (open question). Dreyer's editorial note identifying the addressee and the lawsuit is at TBOO IX, p. 323. The words therefore survive because two eighteenth-century Danish antiquaries thought a nobleman's private insult to a judge worth copying, not because Tycho ever published it.
Channel
Printed after his death (Danske Magazin II, 1746)
Printing
printed posthumously — Copenhagen, 1746

not printed in Tycho's lifetime, and NOT first printed in TBOO — both would be easy errors here. Nielsen (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen) has no entry for it, and can have none: it is a private lampoon on a sitting judge, written in the saddle, and there is no trace of a sixteenth-century printing at Uraniborg or anywhere else. Its first appearance in print is posthumous, 154 years after composition: Danske Magazin, Bind II (Copenhagen, 1746), 21. Hefte, p. 279, inside the anonymous 'Efterretninger om Tyge Brahes Levnet', where it is printed in full from Tycho's autograph draft. A German version of that life carried it further: Dreyer cites 'Weistritz, ii. p. 226' alongside the Danske Magazin page (Tycho Brahe, 1890, p. 220 n. 1) — i.e. Philander von der Weistritz's translation of the Danish Magazine life. Dreyer reprinted the text in TBOO IX (1927), p. 192, from a different witness; that is the standard citation today, but it is not the first printing. The publisher/printer of the 1746 Danske Magazin volume has not been verified here and is left blank.

The case tried on that occasion was probably one of those referred to the provincial court by the Commissioners.'), with n. 1 ('Also printed in Danske Magazin, ii. p. 279 (Weistritz, ii. p. 226)'); and p. 88 n. 1 (the same poem cited on the Zealand jurisdiction of Hven) — That Ringsted was the seat of the provincial court (landsting) of Zealand and that Tycho attended it in February 1592; the poem's survival; the further printing in Weistritz's German version; Dreyer's hedge on which case was tried
  • TBOO XIV, no. 88 (10 July 1591, the Retterting judgment confirming the commissioners' verdict — Rasmus Pedersen had been chained, carried to Hven and held six weeks in prison), pp. 57–60; no. 96 (17 Nov 1592, the king warning Tycho and announcing an open command to 'Lauge Beck … landtzdomer her vdj Wortt landt Sielandt'), pp. 63–64; no. 98 (1 Dec 1592, 'LAUGE BECK, LANDTZDOMMER WDJ SIELAND, FICK K: M: BREFF, ATT HAND SCHULLE DOMME EMELLOM TYGE BRAHE OCH EN WED NAFFN RASSMUS PEDERSSON'), p. 65 — The litigation behind the epigram and its chronology; Lauge Beck's office as landsdommer of Zealand and his role as the judge in the Rasmus Pedersen matter — the documents Dreyer cross-refers to in his note at TBOO IX, p. 323
  • Zeeberg 1994, p. 46 with n. 71 ('Et enkelt er – siger overleveringen – skrevet i vrede på vej hjem fra et retsmøde der var gået Tycho imod. … 71. Epigrammet Iudicis est aequi … IX.192') — The modern scholarly reading of the piece: an epigram written in anger on the way home from a court session that went against Tycho; its place in Tycho's genre of short polemical epigrams on friends and enemies
  • Toftgaard 2023, 'In 1592, the building was given by Lave Beck to Førslev (1530–1607) as a fief, and Lave Beck lived there from 1592 to 1605' (Ringsted Abbey) — Identification and dates of Lave Beck; his tenure of Ringsted from 1592 — the same year and place as the epigram
  • Kancelliets Brevbøger, the regest of the royal letter of 17 Nov 1592 ('Kongen er til Sinds at lade udgaa aaben Befaling til Landsdommer Lauge Beck om i Forening med nogle andre dertil forordnede gode Mænd at tage Sagen for sig …') — Independent Danish-chancery confirmation of Lauge Beck as landsdommer and as the judge charged with the Tycho–Rasmus Pedersen suit
  • Nielsen 1921, no entry (negative check: the epigram appears neither among the Uraniborg prints nor among the lost/disputed prints) — That the piece was never printed in Tycho's lifetime — printed status
  • Norlind 1970, pp. 249–250 (the Rasmus Pedersen process; 'Varken hur processen började eller hur den slutade, är helt klarlagt i handlingarna') — That the course and outcome of the litigation are not fully documented — the ground for the open question about which case was tried at Ringsted on 15 February 1592
  • Familia (Rasmus Pedersen; Christen Jude; Dr Anders Christensen) and Loca (Hven), familia records for Rasmus Pedersen ('later a tenant on Tycho's Gundsømagle fief … his most litigious adversary') and the loci note correcting the 1592 judge 'from Jacob Langebek (the 18th-c archivist) to Lauge Beck, the Sjælland landsdommer the document names' — Corroboration of the parties and of Beck's identity; the confusion of Langebek the excerptor with Lauge Beck the judge is an easy one
Open questions
  • WHICH lawsuit was decided at Ringsted on 15 February 1592? No authority states it outright. The Danske Magazin biographer (1746) says only 'perhaps one of the cases mentioned in the Herredags-Dom printed above' (i.e. the Retterting judgment of 10 July 1591 in the Rasmus Pedersen matter, which had remitted some points to the herredsting and some to the landsting); Dreyer 1890, p. 220, says the case was 'probably one of those referred to the provincial court by the Commissioners'; Dreyer 1927 (TBOO IX, p. 323) states it as the Rasmus Pedersen suit but hedges with 'videtur'. Norlind adds that neither the beginning nor the end of that process is fully clear in the documents. No landsting record has been consulted here. The occasion is therefore secure in kind (a judgment against Tycho, before Lave Beck, at Ringsted) but not in the precise cause of action.
  • The year 1588. The edition's index files this epigram under 1588, while the poem's own subscription — in both print traditions, one of them taken from Tycho's autograph draft — reads 'Anno 1592, die 15 Febr.'. The likeliest explanation is a grouping artefact: in TBOO IX the epigram sits immediately below the four chronogram epigrams on Frederik II's death (1588), from the same Langebek excerpt-volume, on the same page (p. 192). Whether the edition argues for 1588 or merely files the piece there is not stated in its metadata. If the edition does argue for 1588, that is a live disagreement with Dreyer and with the eighteenth-century editors; if it is a slip, the year is 1592.
  • Does Tycho's autograph draft survive, and is it the witness Dreyer used? Danske Magazin (1746) printed from 'Tyge Brahes egenhændige Udkast' among Hans Gram's papers; Dreyer (1927) printed from 'excerpta Langebekiana nr. 179' in the Royal Library. Both collections ended in the Royal Library, and for the neighbouring volume nr. 178 Dreyer explicitly notes a Tycho autograph — but he does not say that of nr. 179, and no source consulted here identifies the two witnesses with each other. The Langebek excerpt-volume 179 should be inspected.
  • 'Lago' is the only name in the poem. The identification with Lave/Lauge Beck rests entirely on the eighteenth-century editors and on Dreyer, not on the text; it is strongly corroborated by Beck's office (landsdommer of Zealand), by the Ringsted venue, and by the chancery letters of Nov–Dec 1592, but the epigram itself names no surname.
  • Whether the epigram was ever actually sent or shown to Beck, or remained a private discharge of temper, is unknown. It is subscribed like a letter ('T. B.') but no address, no recipient copy, and no reaction from Beck is recorded in any source consulted.

CUR antiqua adeo, cur tempore dissita et orbe Nunc Lacedæmoniων, Cragie, facta novas? Et cur non potius patriæ mage cognita gesta, Vel quam nunc habitas, urbis aperta facis? 5Tutius est forsan Veterum monumenta referre; Nostra ut scire juvat, sic memorare nocet.
