Urania Titani — Urania to Titan

Verse epistlethe edition'sHvennot yet researchedRead the text →brahe-t_urania-titani

Verse epistle of exactly 600 lines in the manner of Ovid's Heroides, written by Tycho in the voice of his sister Sophie Brahe ('Urania') to her absent fiancé Erik Lange ('Titan'), fictively dated from Eriksholm castle as the Sun re-enters Pisces.

IX 193A 1r Urania Titani

En tibi sexcentos tribuit quos Pagina versus, Accipe, mi Titan, et lege quando vacat. Sunt ideo multi ne sit responsio promta, 5Ipse sed hanc nobis ore referre velis.

Venit ab Urania quam cernis Epistola Titan, Nil sibi rescribi, te sed adesse cupit. Littera multa quidem perarata est, multa supersit, Ast cùm te caream, quid tua charta juvat? Te retinet nimium nostris ars invida votis, Nec tanti Hermes nec tota Chimia foret. Ars vana et linquens vacuatas ære crumenas, Quam propter vacuo linquor et ipsa thoro. Quam propter sine sole dies, sine sidere noctes Orba traho, quòd abes Solque, Jubarque meum. Ars utinam tenebris, unde orta, perîsset Averni, Quæ mihi tot nitidos abstulit atra dies. Jure vocanda atra est, quia fit carbonibus atris, Non decuit niveas res ita nigra manus. Ast ego quòd linquar modicum est, tu læderis inde, Ægra fit hinc tua mens, hinc malè corpus habet. Quando etenim curis nimiis noctesque diesque Carperis, ut votis Ars sit amica tuis. Et tandem inventum NIHIL est, quod, et usque requiris, Nonne animus tantâ spe cecidisse dolet? Dum per anhela trahis fœdos spiracula fumos, Quos simul et carbo, materiesque parit; IX 194Nonne tenella tibi languescere pectora sentis, Pectora pectoribus quæ magis apta meis? Quæ comperta loquor, quia et ipsa sat omnia novi Quot vestræ species, quot mala carbo, ferant. Ah quoties faciem spurcas, quotiesque labella, Quæ servanda mihi bella labella forent. A 1vSæpe cutis toto maculis tibi corpore liuet, Mollior antè novâ candidiorque nive. Nuper enim Stygias satagenti impellere Lymphas, Cum tonitru Nitrum vincula rupit atrox. Fœtor et hinc fusus vitalem polluit auram, Semianimes socios quo cecidisse liquet. Tu licet elapsus (precibusque hoc accipe nostris) Crebra tuo tamen hinc corpore sparsa nota est. Talia namque meo, de te modò quærere jusso, Rettulerat nato Bangus, at ille mihi. Hinc ego concepi majora pericula veris, Ô Fons solliciti plene timoris Amor! Sulphura mox timui, timui Arsenicalia monstra, Et Salia et Stibium, Mercuriosque vafros. Denique quicquid erat, quod Carbonaria fallax Suppetit, id totum causa timoris erat. At nostro affulsit Veneris benè Sidus amori, In cineres abiit sospite carbo viro. Rettulit ille etiam, propè quòd Schonburgica rura, Effrænes per equos versa quadriga tua est: Teque genu lapsum læsisse atrociter inde, Sub medicaque diu decubuisse manu. Quæ licet huc misso haud prorsus cælata ministro, Ne mihi fortè aliàs cresceret inde dolor. Tu tamen astutè damnum molemque pericli Texisti, in propriis Ingeniose malis. At mea, quæ eventum perrarò insomnia fallunt, Obvenisse istud præmonuêre satis. Cor mihi namque, velut currenti, è corpore lapsum, Parte sui visum est inferiore premi. A 2rMox ego sic, Genio (nondum experrecta) monente, Vociferor; Titan cor mihi sicne cadis? Sed benè tunc Phœbus, Medicæ qui præsidet arti, Subveniens, nostri fautor amoris erat. Attulit is pedibusque tuis genibusque, redires Quò citiùs, nec te plus remorentur, opem. IX 195Hunc nondum ob casum mea Sollicitudo remisit, Cùm penetrat gravior corda priore dolor. Diceris isse etenim, famulo comitatus ab uno, Per juga præruptis Alpibus alta nimis. Et Venetûm aurivoras cupidè sectarier offas, Quas fallax istic Ars et ubique coquit. Tene viæ placuit temerè committere tantæ? Quàm benè cautus abis, quàm memor antè mei? Nonne brevi id decuit priùs admonuisse litura, Saltem ut votivis te sequerer lachrymis? Fallar: et hæc potiùs vanescat fama sub auras, Lætabor, modò te Teutonis ora tenet. Hinc quia spes aliqua est de te resciscere quicquam, Et capere, atque animi mittere sensa, notas. At cur te cupiam Germano limite claudi? Heu nimiùm limes latus et iste patet. Cùm non scire licet, quâ tandem parte moraris Teutoniæ, vel quâ conditus urbe lates. Lentus abes, neque nota mihi sat caussa morandi, Aut quæ te nimiùm terra vel unda tenet. Quisquis ab Austrino veniens vada Baltica tangit Littore, non de te pauca rogatus, abit. Traditur et nostris charta huic signata labellis, Si fortè audierit, quo tibi danda loco. Heu mihi Cœlestis quòd cernitur undique Titan, Terrestrem, huncque meum, non reperire datur! A 2vSæpè Ducem Ulricum te detinuisse putavi, Caussa tuæ forsan nec fuit ille moræ. Sæpè etiam timui, te, dum freta Baltica tranas, More tuo, infesto vela dedisse mari: Ut ratis in scopulos, quos Mœnia suggerit, acta, Membra aliquo cogat læsa fovere loco. Quid multis? cùm scire nequit cur lentior absis Mens mea, per caussas irrequieta volat. Tempora si memores, benè quæ memoramus amantes, Nostra querela suam non venit ante diem. Nam mihi discedens tremulo es sic ore locutus, Pallentes lachrymis cùm maduêre genæ: Sol priùs auriferi non tanget Velleris astrum, Quàm tibi Me reducem Scania vestra ferat. Cœlicus is Titan Vellus bis terve revisit Phryxæum, at Titan Terree noster abes. IX 196Non puto quòd ratibus secteris Iasonis aurum, Aut furtum lanæ versicoloris ames. Nec Medæa fui, nec ero, nil fraudibus utor, Colchida si cupias, híc quoque Colchis erit. Pergula læta mihi est, pulcher quam circuit hortus, Vix cui par dabitur, Colchida utrumque vocem. Læta vocata quidem; sed nondum cernere lætam Me potuit, quamvis híc tua imago patet. Quam quoties specto, suspiria cordibus imis, Alta traho, et lachrymis ora genasque rigo. Mox caput inclinans, unique innixa lacerto, Sic mecum tacito murmure verba premo: Ô si is, quem pulchro referens bellè exprimis ore Afforet, ô coràm hunc cernere quando datur! Hancque diu aspiciens, oculis ac sensibus ipsis Linquor, et ancillis excipienda, cado. A 3rQuin mihi vix rediens, iterum hanc, iterumque videre Mens avet; in damnum tam studiosa suum est. Imò hæc dum memoro, sanguis præcordia stringit, Vix teneor, quin mox exanimata ruam. Ater sanguis abi, mens et præcordia firma Este mihi, et saltem his addere pauca date: Hæc ubi scripta sient, si tunc mihi parcere iniquum est, Auditu et visu me spoliate; feram. Et sat sueta feram, (quàm consolatio dura est, Quòd nequeam expertis succubuisse malis.) Nil sed ago precibus, quò plùs tego, sæviùs instat, Susceptumque dolor linquere cogit opus. Ferte citæ lymphas, sal, vinum, aromata, acetum, Ancillæque omnes, Virgoque, ferte citæ. Ah satis ah; redeam ô liceat calamumque resumam, Quàm mirè cunctis sensibus orbus habet! Ista abeant; adsis Titan, citò meque revise, Colchiacas artes, si cupis, ipsa dabo. Non opus ut subeas, veluti Pagasæus Iason, Phasiacas Argo nave repostus aquas. Et superes tot monstra tuis Hecatæa venenis, Ignivomos Tauros, terrigenasque viros: Et colubrum, herbarum, vigilem, Virtute, sopitum, Hinc tandem aurato ut vellere dives eas. Fortè sub his technis, (si vera est fabula) tecta Ars etiam technis Chrysiopœa latet. IX 197Sint ea vera tamen; quid enim non credimus ambo, Quos animis uno corpore nectit Amor? Pergula (quam dixi) quæcunque petuntur ad artem Auriferam (si qua est) exhibitura satis. Fornaces varias, carbones, lampada, flammas, (Ô Flammæ flammis cedite quæso meis.) A 3vMateria híc deerit, quæ sat reperitur ubique? Vilis et hæc fertur, nec preciosa nimis. Hîc lapidem arcano simul ambo fovebimus igne. Nempè columbæ ovis, femina masque cubant. Hunc si multiplici nimiùm sub cortice tectum, Credibile est ullos antè habuisse Sophos: Non dubito, quin tu, vel ego inveniemus eundem, Sol pater (ut referunt) Lunaque mater erit. Sis igitur Titan pater et sim, Femina, Lunæ Persimilis Mater, sexus et ordo juvant. Scandit is in cœlos, iterum terrena revisit; Sic terrena etiam dicor ego Urania. Primitùs et Sophia ipsa vocor, Lapis ille Sophorum est, Forsitan hinc nostrum nomen, et omen habet. Ventus et hunc utero fertur portasse, vel isto Fortè etiam possit qui meliora mihi est. Ingeniumque (ajunt) subtile et suave requirit, Haud ego grossitiem fallar ob ingenii. Sic orbem hunc constare putant, sumus Orbis uterque, Per me alius mundus parvulus esse potest. Colchide at ex veteri nova cur exempla petuntur Antiqui Hermetis cur ita dicta placent? Quærimus heu variè, frustraque aliundè vocamus, Hoc satis in nobis quod latet artis opus. Conjugio assimilant, cùm mas et femina ponunt Mollia fœcundo corpora juncta thoro. Contigeritque illis prolem si quando creari, Arcani Lapidis protinùs instar habet. Inque utero veluti nutritur sanguine fœtus, Sic humore suo fotus et ille viget. Ingenitusque velut calor et moderatus et udus, Maturat partum dum fovet igne levi. A 3brSic etiam lapidem liquido lenique calore Naturæ ad normam, quá datur arte, fovent. Alterat augendo ut formam, mutatque colorem Infans claustra tener dum genetricis habet. IX 198Haud aliter Lapis hic crescit variatque colores, Fomenta Athânor debita quando regit. Ut Lucina suos dat adhuc à matre rubentes, Et teneros fœtus crescere lacte facit; Sic rutilans fulget jam natus Chimicus Infans, Fermentoque suo crescit, et auctus abit. Utque alios iterum natus progignit adultus, Sic Lapis hic sobolem multiplicare potest. A 4rQuàm benè conveniunt nostris ista omnia Votis, Quique operi arcano competat Hortus adest. Non qui pestiferos foveat, vigilesque Dracones, Et terræ in proprias monstra parata neces: Naribus aut Tauros spirantes undique flammas, Vel Medæa tuâ mixta Aconita manu. Brachia sint angues mutuis circumdata collis, Terrigenas acies terrea vasa putem. Si collisa cadant, minima est jactura; Bovesque Ipsi erimus juncti conveniente jugo. Æstus et ira absint, proque herbis grata nocivis Hortus, qui tribuat Pharmaca, noster erit. Sensus at (ut perhibent) si fortè his mysticus insit, Pandere et hunc nobis difficile esse nequit: Tu modò, mi Titan, patrias te confer in oras, Aspirent Votis Ventus et Aura meis. Tunc benè nota Redux intrans Pomaria, cernes Quàm locus híc aptus sit tibi, quamque mihi. Hîc simul occultum, junctis modò viribus optes, Artis ut auriferæ conficiatur opus. Intereà votis, quæ nunc mihi sola supersunt, Orabo Superos, ut tibi adesse velint. Utque brevi incolumis (modo ferre negotia possint Quæ versas manibus) restituâre mihi. Non etenim cupio festinus quòd tibi damno sit reditus, quia me nil tua damna levant. Quin tibi cum fidam satis ipsa, ubicunque moreris, Nostra aliis tamen est suspiciosa fides. Credula quòd fuerim nimiùm, quod stultius urar, Te quoque me leviter deseruisse, putant. A 4vPlura feram modò sis tu saltem corpore salvus, Id Dii si renuant, te sine nulla feram. Objiciunt, blandis quòd sim delusa loquelis, (sic deludi abs te fæmina crebra volet) IX 199At non mellifluis, quorum tibi copia, verbis, Quòd decepta queror, si qua ea culpa, mea est: Sponte tuis cessi votis, te sponte probavi, Ut Chalybem magnes attrahit, ipsa sequor. Inter tot genere illustres, quos Dania nutrit, Solus es ex imo qui mihi corde places. Teipsum, non tua verba moror, nil indiga verbis Forma tua est, Virtus me Probitasque movent. Sit fœcunda aliis, velut est facundia prægnans, Me tamen in partes non trahet illa suas. Suave quidem mel est, at Fel sub cortice dulci Quòd tegat, exemplis res mihi nota satis. Nec tua fictitia est, hac te Natura beavit, Quâ superas reliquos, grata loquela, viros. Hanc tibi Mercurius Veneri sociatus in ortu, Ædibus è propriis largus habere dedit. Nec mirùm Superûm Præconi quòd Venus adstans, Blanda tibi et pariter verba diserta parit. Quin simul his Phœbus Geminorum jungitur astro, Noster et hinc Geminus fortè oriundus amor, Sed levis est Stilbon, levis est Cytheræa, Gemelli Sunt duplices, constans quid queat inde sequi? Sol etiam radiis, qui pandit et omnia condit, Gradivi et Veneris prodidit antè dolos. At quid ea huc refero? Spurci valeatis amores, Concessos thalamos, vincla probata loquor. Si qua tamen levitas hinc aut aliundè subintret, Mox abeat, nostro sitque ab amore procul. A 5rMe priùs, hanc habeant, quotquot petulanter amasti, Aut obiter si quam nunc quoque forsan amas. Ista licet de te malè non ego suspicer unquam, Ast aliis dubium vestra libido movet. Te procul ex oculis, quæ distas, scilicet, unam Absens, tamque diu, tamque remotus amet? Quid faciat quæso longinquis deses in oris, Qui Paris alter ut est, nil nisi amare potest? Crede peregrino captivus amore tenetur, Quænam illa Urania est forsan, et unde rogat, Sic ajunt; surdæ at frustrà mihi talia narrant, Et surdam et cæcam me facit Arctus Amor. Quicquid at his poterit (me non credente) subesse, Ipsa etiam leviùs sit levitate precor. IX 200In vacuas Stilbon pennis diventilet auras, Inque maris bullas efflet id omne Venus. Vos duplices Gemini vanum hunc dissolvite amorem, Sub duplici et ficto corde sit iste velim. Lumine quique suo citò detegit omnia Phœbus, Te prodat, casto si quâ in Amore noces. Me sed fixus amor, (si quid tibi sidera fixi, Si quid perpetui contribuêre) juvet. Hunc Jovis intuitus quinta de cuspide firmet, Jupiter es constans, Quinta es amica domus. Displicet invisæ constringi Virginis astro, Vosque premi opposito tardigradoque Sene. At mihi Virgo favet, nostro quia fulsit in ortu, Heu nimiùm nobis forsitan illa favet. Perpetuò est sterilis, sterilem quoque transigo vitam, Virgo nec ulla parit, nec vidua ulla parit. Artibus at facit oblecter, velut altera Pallas, Mercuriique sacris Ingeniosa litem. Ipse etiam in propriâ feliciter æde locatus, Et Lunam aspiciens, promovet Artis opus. A 5vScilicet hoc unum longi est Solamen Amoris, Ut tua Penelope tela retexta diu. Nec placet in signo tibi quòd saltem unicus Erro, Hospitium fixo, Marsque malignus, habet. Culmine tecta cadens malè quique inimica subintrat, Quin mihi sic etiam Mars inimice cadis? Hoc habeas solido quicunque inimicus amori es, Spero quòd hinc nostris hostibus omen erit. Et licet est fixum Martem quo Corniger abdis Hospitium, tamen id vix placuisse potest. Aversum à proprio est, simul hîc nocet ille Dianæ, Pronuba quæ Tauri scandere tergus avet. Et licet alternâ juvet hanc quòd sede recepit; Attamen his obstat plùs Duodena domus. Mars igitur valeas, alibi infortunia figas, Nunc, quæ agitas, non vult Cornua noster amor. Falcitenens potiùs validos benè firmet amores, Is quamvis etiam dicitur esse malus: Non tamen esse malum Mystes Ægyptius olim Credidit, hunc habuit sed potiore loco. Esse bonus nobis poterit, sublimior extat, Inque Jovis Solio, vix mala blandus agit. IX 201Cuius ad aspectum (licet haud bona quadra putetur Est mage Sextilis) applicat alma Venus. Est mihi, sitque bonus precor, et te figere possit, Ut tuus in nobis perpetuetur Amor. Non tamen ut fixus maneas ubicunque moreris, Te revocet potiùs quæ cita Luna pede est. Ad cuius radios pergit Venus alma, quadrati Sint licet, evadunt ex brevitate boni. Tunc simul ipsa Jovis, qui Conjugialia curat, Sextilem intuitum (Lux benè fausta) petit. Hinc ego concipio spem firmam, nocte quòd ista Monstrabit thalamis tæda cupita viam. Cypria nam maribus, Juno et quoque pronuba fertur, Conjugiumque illis signat Amoris opus. A 6rAdde, quòd et Phœbum radii Jovis inde benigni Excipient, qui nos prole beare volent. Quid dicam? Genesis nostra et sub tempore eodem Ad Veneris radios te quoque Luna movet. Mox Venus ipsa Jovis sidus quod præsidet almo Hîc benè conjugio gestit adire Patris. Quàm benè utrinque cadit sub idem directio tempus, Aspirant thalamis sidera ubique piis. Quin mihi Saturnus Venerem sat fixit in ipso Quo satagunt ambo sceptra tenere loco. At timeo ne sede cadens (sed Sole receptus) Hanc nimiùm radio figat ab opposito. Hinc mihi tot forsan, quot castum propter amorem, Perfero languores, tristitiæque fluunt. Jupiter ast moderans loca, quæ tribuêre periti Conjugio, in proprio limine faustus agit. Sol, quem Fæmellis perhibent signare maritos, Adjuvat hunc flammis irradiatque bonis. Ille etiam signo, quod habet tibi Septima, gaudet, Septima Conjugiis ritè dicata domus. Auguror et placidos et lætos hinc Hymenæos, Acceleres sacras ô Hymenæe faces. Sepone invidiam, utque tuo mox nomine gaudens, Ô Erycina Venus, des Ericina vocer. Adde, Planeta quòd elatus vel sedibus altis, Vel residens propriis bis mihi binus adest. Nec me perpetuis patietur fluctibus abdi, Tandem etiam nobis tempora Veris erunt. IX 202Nil mirêre tamen, quòd cœlum et Sidera pando, Utpote Fæmineo quæ minus apta colo. Sum quoque, si nescis, præter muliebria dona, Astrologa, id propter dicor et Urania. Sidera suspicio, Genesesque recludo, nec istud Contribuit frustrà nomen Apollo mihi. Tuque velut quæ prona videns, hanc expetis artem, Quæ terrâ effossis rebus anhelat opes: A 6vSic ego, sic sursum, quæ sunt cœlestia specto, Ars mea (condones) celsior arte tuâ est. Ut Cœlum terras, sic nostra Ars Chimica vincit, Adde quòd hæc vera est, Chimia falsa nimis. Ast tibi quæ placeant, quæcunque vel unde petantur, Non poterunt unquam displicuisse mihi. Tu modò fac redeas, revocantiaque Astra sequaris, Quæ citò Conjugii tempora læta notant. Quicquid erit, quod te reficit, delecter eodem, Chimica sive voles, Carmina sive voles. Nam cùm te multùm recreet quoque blanda Poësis, Altera sim Sappho, metra sonora canam. Sola nec ipsa tibi sim caussa, ut promptior adsis, Quin tenerum natum respice quæso meum. Ætas (dante Deo) veniet mage firma Tagoni, Consiliis foret hæc nunc moderanda tuis. Ut virtute acri referens utrumque, Parentem Teque sequi studiis gestiat usque bonis. Hei mihi quot morbis fuit ille obnoxius, et quot Dum tu tardus abes, sæva pericla tulit. Ast spero Numen mihi quod dedit huncce supernum, Servet, et haud seros auferat ante dies: Lætitiæ ut nobis decorique existat adultus, Longævus nostris insideatque bonis. Si quid habent, ut habent, cœlestia corpora veri, Nascenti huic puero fata benigna dabant. Pone ortum Venus alma fuit sub Sidere Cancri, Quare in amore illi Blande Cupido faves. Sol Geminos tenuit, capit hunc consuetus Achates Hospitio Stilbon, undecimoque loco. Clarus is hinc fiet, simul ingeniosus, ut artes Percipiat doctas; multus amicus erit. Culmine Mars supero mox se sublimior effert, Huic Aries solio dat residere suo, IX 203Ascendens videt is Trino (licet ille quadratus Esse queat) radio; te quoque Phœbe videt. A 7rHunc etiam recreat Lunæque Jovisque benignus Intuitus, nec lux Falcitenentis obest. Prævideo hinc, rebus felicem aptumque futurum, Quas nimiùm toto Mars ferus orbe gerit. Hincque canes et equos, bombardas, arma, sagittas, Si qua foret, doctâ gnarior arte reget. Ast utinam Gradive Pater (seu Vitrice prorsus) Filiolo hæc non des munera, des aliis. Nulla Salus opere in Martis, Pax aurea præstat, Inque malâ poterit re nihil esse boni. Quin mage Saturnum, quem Septimus ordo domorum Continet, extimeo; lentus atroxque nocet. Is tamen in propria requiescens sede triumphat, Pocla suus præbens huic Ganymedes adest. Conjugio haud obstat, sed firmum et gratius adfert, Fortè tamen remoras stans repedansque facit. Id saltem metuo, radiis ne quando sub ortum †Venerit† oppositis, damna proterva ferat. Est etenim octavæ Præses, quæ mansio dira est, Annus et is novies bis numerandus erit. Hunc pravum intuitum, simul et mox cauda Draconis Fascinat excipiens, ingeminatque malum. At quia tamfaustas Quinta sub sede tabernas Jupiter, atque illi juncta Diana, tenent: Isque suo gaudens venientem lumine et auctam Accipit hospitio; dissipat omne malum. Lætitiam importat, vitam prolongat, honores Dans et opes; natis Conjugioque favet. Res quoque rara patet; quatuor sunt nempe Planetæ Ædibus in propriis præcipuisque locis. Omnibus in gestis, hæc, toto tempore vitæ Eximia natum prosperitate beant. Singula quid referam? Genesis vix faustior ulla est, Si pariam, similem sæpè redire velim. At supera ex voto quamvis sint sidera fausta, Cuncta simul faveant inferiora precor. A 7vIpsum homines et ament, seu mas, seu femina, et ipsum Quicquid terrestris continet orbis, amet. Nulla salus tamen ex astris, tellureque nulla est, Te, Tago, perpetuum sospitet, oro, Deus. IX 204Dum loquor; heutristis nimiùm mihi fama refertur, Quòd modò præcipuus noster amicus obit. Charior haud illo mihi, vixque fidelior alter Suppetit, Ô nimiùm Mors inimica bonis! Spero tamen quòd inanis erit tam concita fama, Hoc meus in somnis nec monuit Genius. Quàm lugubre foret charo hoc privarier astro, Talia nam nobis Sidera rara micant. Eurialo et Niso similis quamplurimus olim, Tam tibi, quamque mihi, fidus amicus erat. Quàm benè jam reliquos digitis numerabimus omnes, Ambobus vix nunc unus et alter adest. Tempora læta ferunt multos, sed nubila tollunt, Fortunæ arbitrio stantque, caduntque simul. Penè mihi solus superest sine felle, vel astu, Qui perstet firmâ Frater Apollo fide. Nec frustrà huic placidus roravit Aquarius ortum Fixus, et humanus, Tardigradique domus. Cum Jove, qui Venerem facit undique cingere Eöas, Scandentesque fores; lux ea fausta micat. Jupiter alternum paritèr cum Falcitenente Hospitium mutans, plus gravitate juvat. Mars etiam proprias aurati Velleris ædes, Alterna è cathedra Sole receptus, habet. Unde Animo est acri et rebus citus instat agendis, Fortiter Herculei fertque laboris onus; Quinetiam Stilbon Saturni limina grata, Hujus et amplexu Soleque cinctus, adit. Cumque sua Lunam gradientem Virgine, Trino, Qui menti aspirat, respicit intuitu. A 8rInde magis constans habet, ingeniumque profundum, Utque operæ precium nil, nisi grande, putet. Hinc quoque judicio consultus prævalet alto, Vulgus ut hunc nugis nil remoretur iners. Ergò minùs mirum est, quòd nostro plaudat amori, Hunc temerè ex Atomis nec putet esse satum. Scilicet hic restat de tot mihi fratribus unus, Qui capiat, quòd te non temulenter amem. A 8vHoc facit Ingenium, Gravitas, Prudentia, Virtus, Hoc et amor Recti, Judiciumque facit. Sufficiat nobis primævus, candida, frater Quòd nostro facilis, corda, in amore gerat. IX 205Quid si etiam ex astris tandem ventura revolvens, Hinc tacitus nostros prævideat thalamos? Sidereisque ideò frustrà haud obsistere fatis Audeat; Ô quantum fata in amore valent! Fato junguntur, Fato solvuntur amores, Non habet híc semper Gaza, Genusve locum. Quàm pulchrum est hominem simul et præscire futura, Et simul, affuerint si bona fata, sequi. Incauti hîc titubant, quos Ignorantia turbat, Frater at hic noster callet utrumque satis. Hic mihi frater erit semper, quem fautor Apollo, Ex quo etiam meritò nomina gestat, amet. Sive igitur faveant alii, seu lumina vibrent, Ut soliti, torvo torva supercilio. Nil tamen impedient, quin nos constanter amemus, Etpro mille aliis frater is unus erit. Imò haud obstabit, decuit quos ferre levamen, Quòd noceant reliqui verbaque sæva crepent. Si non Titanem (dicunt) tam perditè amares, Ditior et major Vir tibi (crede) foret. Ipso in Amore tamen si qua est Sapientia, certè Haud credam, quòd te desipienter amem. Non ego divitias, non mundi sector honores, Officioque gravi complacuisse viro. Omnibus Officiis, fundis, aurique talentis, Nam Persona mihi charior una tua est. Plura etiam agglomerant, mea quæ nunc cuncta referre, Vel meminisse semel, mens sibi recta, piget. Hi dicant, quæcunque volent, tua dicar oportet, Titanis maneam semper ego Urania. Absis sive diu, celer hîc me sive revisas, Corde meo fixus tu tamen usque sedes. Nec tu sponte tua, sed valdè invitus abesse Cogeris, ac malles semper adesse mihi. Hucque subinde etiam, perque intervalla redires Sed metuis, crescat suc quod utrinque dolor. Ne me iterùm ut linquas, tibi dum sit forte necessùm, Tristitiæ nimiùm multiplicetur onus. Ergò voles potiùs peregrinis degere in oris, Hospitia hîc donec Sors tibi firma dabit. Intereàque mihi non scribere negligis ultrò, Res ea sit quamvis te remorata diu. IX 206Sive quòd ex votis nemo internuncius adsit, Sæpè viam ingressæ seu periêre notæ. Quicquid id est, facit hoc non ulla aversa voluntas, Scribere satque cupis, satque redire cupis. Perque tuum quoties venit huc portata ministrum, Littera, sic illum diceris ore sequi. Hanc ego, Serve, tibi, qua me felicior ibis, Fortunam invideo; Servus ego ô fierem. Et chartam iratè alloqueris, quam rumpere velles, Altera nî calamo mox peraranda foret. Tune meis digitis, quibus es conscripta, bearis Charta magis? digitis te citò Nostrateret. A 9rTeque oculi inspicient, quos his ego cernere mallem, Oscula fortè dabit, quæ mea sola forent. Hoc simul ut faciam fas est, priùs oscula libo, Nomen ubi augustum scribitur Uraniæ. Spero quòd illa brevi pariter tibi Basia figat, Qua suus hîc Titan nomina parte tenet. Vade igitur visas toto hanc quâ pulchrior orbe Nulla meis oculis Femina, vade citò. Heu mihi quòd sine me tam grata palatia vises, Heu quòd scriptori non licet ire tuo! Sic loqueris, (dicunt) sic crebrò nos adeuntes, Insequeris famulos; grata loquela mihi est. Singula scire juvat, missi cunctosque ministri Ut nutus referant, cunctaque verba, volo. Ergò sive adsis, seu non, seu scribere, seu non Sæpè voles, modò ames, semper amandus eris. Nec tamen addubito, quin tu Charissime Titan, Perpetuò Uraniam, quæ Tua semper, ames. Si te etiam nunquam, (quod Dî prohibete) viderem, Ex oculis tamen his non abolendus eris. Mente meâ impressus Titan sine fine manebis, Fixus eris cordi tempus in omne meo. Te præter nemo nostro potietur Amore, Mille Proci fuerint, commoda mille ferant. Attamen haud credam, quòd sint tam Numina sæva Nuper ut inceptâ spe spoliare velint. Id saltem vereor, ne dum lentissimus absis, Quòd mea sit reduci forma probata minùs. Nam quæ pulchra satis, te discedente, videbar, Altera, quando redis, forsitan esse puter. A 9vIX 207Non quòd adhuc annis onerer, rugasve timescam, Sæpè etiam Senium Sollicitudo parit. Anxietas me multa premit, nec deserit unquam, Hæc quoque dum scribo durior ecce redit. Nam modò qui fuerat de morte incertus amici Rumor, en hunc nimiùm littera missa probat. Heu mala quòd semper sibi constet fama, nec unquam Eventus habeat prospera quæque bonos. Nil licet in somnis hoc admonuisse recorder, Signa tamen Genius, me vigilante, dedit. Quàm mihi mira fui, simul et quàm tristis eodem Abstulit hunc terris quo Libitina die. Omen erat tanti (modò quid sint omina) luctus, Dixi aliis, certè res metuenda subest. Attamen haud potui citò persentiscere, rumor Quòd nimiùm verus (proh dolor) iste foret. Nempè ægrè, quæ grata minùs sunt, credimus at quæ Sunt accepta satis, mox meruêre fidem. Non tamen exponam quis sit, mens ipsa tremiscit Dicere, nec nomen sustinet ore dolor. Sit signasse satis, quòd erat Tuus Optimus ille Et meus, et nostri fratris Amicus: habes. Forsan habes nimiùm, nec enim te scire volebam, Sponte sua pernix sat mala fama venit. Nunc igitur dolor hinc auctus, me sistere pennam Cogit, et, ut vellem, scribere plura vetat. Ast ubi sis præsens, simul et jungamur in uno, Quæ modò subticeo, plurima aperta dabo. A 10rTunc quæ passus eris, mihi denarrabis acerba, Ipsaque nostra tibi; fortè levamen erit. Quod superest benè vive diu; ut salvusque revisas Uraniam; ô Titan semper Amate Vale.

10Hæc in Erichsholmi perarata est litera Castro, Cùm geminos Pisces Sol redeundo capit. Dî citò dent gemini híc pisces capiamus Amantes, Tuque redux Titan, et Tua ego Urania.

Epistolae astronomicae — Astronomical letters

Printed correspondenceprobableHvennot yet researchedRead the text →brahe-t_epistolae-astronomicae

Tycho's printed volume of astronomical correspondence with Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel and his court astronomer Christoph Rothmann, printed at Uraniborg in 1596, dedicated to the young Landgrave Moritz, and including a description with woodcuts of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg. Six honorific poems by learned contributors accompany the volume, and Tycho's own memorial poem on Wilhelm IV grants the dead Landgrave an apotheosis through astronomy.

Forord til Epistolae Astronomicae vol. II — Preface to Epistolae astronomicae, volume II

Prefacethe edition'sHvennot yet researchedRead the text →brahe-t_epistolae-astr-2-praefatio

Preface to the reader written for the planned second volume of the Epistolae astronomicae, which was never published, introducing Tycho's correspondence on the new star of 1572 and the comets with Thaddaeus Hagecius, whose friendship dated from the election and coronation of Rudolf II at Regensburg in 1575.

Ad Daniam elegia — Elegy to Denmark

Revised text of the 1597 farewell elegy to Denmark, followed by Tycho's own prose note recounting how a copy reached the Danish king through the carelessness of Heinrich Rantzau's servants.

Full heading
Ad Daniam elegia
Form
Elegy (this catalogue)
Date
1597 secure

Correction. The revised text of the elegy of 20 October 1597; its exact revision date is not documented. The edition's 1573 is a metadata error on the source site.

Composed at Wandsbek (Wandesburg, near Hamburg) on 20 October 1597. The autograph colophon in Tycho's observation log reads: 'T. B. feci Anno Domini 1597 20 die Octobris cum Wandesburgi Obseruationes Astronomicas antea circa AEquinoctium vernum Vraniburgi inuite omissas continuare coepi' (TBOO XIII, p. 104). Thoren dates it to the same day. The year 1573 sometimes attached to the piece is an artefact of the edition's metadata and is wrong.

Addressee
Denmark, personified (addressee); Henrik Rantzau (saluted in the closing lines)
Language
Latin
Summary
A long poem in elegiac couplets addressed to Denmark personified, opening 'Dania, quid merui, quo te, mea Patria, laesi, / Usque adeo ut rebus sis minus aequa meis?' Tycho asks what he did to deserve his fatherland's ingratitude, rehearses what he built and gave (Uraniborg; the restoration of astronomy, propping up a heaven whose 'orbits' Ptolemy, Alfonso and Copernicus had got wrong; free medicine dispensed to the sick, for which Norway and Sweden will speak if Denmark will not), scorns the ignorant emissary sent to inspect the instruments on Hven, and turns his expulsion into freedom: he is no exile, for the whole world is now his fatherland ('Nunc mihi pro Patria maximus orbis adest'). He expressly exonerates King Christian IV ('Inscius hic culpa, Rex generose, vacas') and lays the blame on a few envious enemies, and he closes by saluting his host Henrik Rantzau at Wandsbek. Resen's 1668 heading calls it an 'elegia hecatonsticha' — an elegy of a hundred lines.
Occasion
His self-imposed exile. Tycho left Hven with his household on 29 April 1597, moved to Copenhagen, then to Rostock, and in October 1597 to Henrik Rantzau's castle of Wandsbek. On 20 October, the day he resumed at Wandsbek the observations broken off at Hven at the spring equinox, he entered into his observation log first a prose account of his departure ('De occasione interruptarum observationum & discessus mei', TBOO XIII, pp. 101–102) and then, immediately after it, this elegy. It is his apologia and indictment: the poem alludes to the inspection of Hven by the professors Thomas Fincke and Iver Stub (Dreyer 1890, p. 240), exonerates the young king, and thanks Rantzau. Copies went out at once to his correspondents; Rantzau kept one so prominently that Christian IV came upon it and read it through in silence (Dreyer 1890, pp. 254–55; Thoren 1990, p. 385).
On the addressee
Denmark itself ('Dania'), his fatherland, apostrophised throughout. Two living persons are addressed within the poem: King Christian IV (1577–1648), 'magnanimi Friderici Heroica proles', explicitly cleared of blame; and, in the closing salute, Henrik Rantzau (1526–1598), the Holstein royal governor, humanist and 'multos per annos fautor... Tychonis' (Dreyer, TBOO IX, p. 323), who housed Tycho at Wandsbek.
Transmission
Two recensions, both edited by Dreyer. (1) The log recension: Tycho wrote the elegy into his own observation journal for 1596-97 — Dreyer's Codex G, 'Ant. Coll. Reg. 316' = Copenhagen, Kongelige Bibliotek, GKS 2 fol. 316 — immediately after the prose 'De occasione interruptarum obseruationum & discessus mej' (Dreyer, TBOO X, Prolegomena, p. XVIII); the passage is in Tycho's own hand, with the colophon of 20 October 1597. Dreyer printed it there at TBOO XIII (1926), pp. 102–104. (2) The collected recension: Tycho later gathered his own poems, and the fair copy in Vienna, Cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10686, carries a lightly revised text; Dreyer printed that among the Carmina at TBOO IX (1927), pp. 208–211, noting 'quamquam inter observationes inseruit Tycho, et nos inter has edidimus (tom. XIII p. 102 sqq.), tamen hic quoque non deesse voluimus... hic correctiones paucas intulimus, quae Tychoni carmina sua colligenti magis placuerant, ut e Vindobonensi codice patet' (TBOO IX, p. 327). Manuscript copies were circulated: Rantzau's, stitched into his printed Calendarium Ranzovianum (Hamburg 1590), was the copy King Christian IV found and read; the copy Tycho sent to Joseph Scaliger in 1598 (23 pp. folio), carrying Tycho's own note on that episode, is in the University Library at Leiden (Dreyer 1890, p. 255 and n. 3; the same story is in Danske Magazin II, p. 340 sq., and was told again to Herwart von Hohenburg). So the words survive first in Tycho's autograph observation journal, and TBOO is the critical, not the first, printing.
Channel
Printed after his death (Gassendi's Vita, 1654 (this catalogue))
Printing
printed posthumously; Nielsen none — no printing of the elegy is recorded among Tycho's printed works

not printed in Tycho's lifetime. Nielsen (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921) records no printing of it, and Tycho's press had left Hven with him in April 1597; Dreyer states plainly that 'copies of the poem were sent to various correspondents' in manuscript (1890, p. 255), and Christian IV had in any case forbidden Tycho to print his letter to the king (Thoren 1990, p. 385). The poem first reached print posthumously. Dreyer (1890, p. 254 n. 2) lists the early printed texts: Historia Coelestis (ed. 'Lucius Barrettus' [Albert Curtz], Augsburg 1666), p. 802; Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen 1668), p. 347 — verified on the page image, headed 'Wandesburgi An: 1597 die Octobris Elegiam Hecatonsticham condidit Tycho Brahaeus quae haec est'; Casseburg, Tychonis Brahe relatio de statu suo (Jena 1730); and 'less correctly given by Gassendi, p. 143' (Tychonis Brahei... Vita, 1st ed. Paris 1654; 2nd ed. The Hague 1655) — which, if Dreyer's page reference is right, is the earliest printing by date, though it was not inspected here. Extracts also in Danske Magazin II (Copenhagen 1746), p. 340 sqq.

Correction. Tycho's own colophon in the observation log: 20 October 1597, Wandsbek. The edition's 1573 is a metadata error on the source site.

Subscribed in the autograph: 'T. B. feci / Anno Domini 1597 20 die Octobris cum Wandesburgi Observationes Astronomicas antea circa Aequinoctium vernum Uraniburgi inuite omissas continuare coepi' (TBOO XIII, p. 104). Dreyer 1890, p. 253, dates the entry to 20 October 1597 at Wandsbek. The year 1573 carried by the edition's metadata is contradicted by the autograph colophon and by the poem's whole subject-matter (the 1597 departure from Denmark, the six children in exile, Rantzau's hospitality at Wandsbek); the year is 1597.

Addressee
Denmark, personified (addressee)
Language
Latin, with a Danish translation in the edition — the edition's translation, translator not named, complete
Summary
An elegy of some fifty-one elegiac couplets (c. 102 lines), opening 'Dania quid merui, quo te mea Patria laesi', in which Tycho arraigns his native country for repaying his services with ingratitude. It recites what he did for Denmark's fame, mocks the ignorant emissary sent to inspect Hven who sneered at instruments he could not name, sets his own labours beside those of Hercules and against the errors of Ptolemy, the Alfonsine tables and Copernicus, recalls the medicines he gave the sick without charge, and turns from complaint to release: he is no exile, for the whole world is now his country. It exculpates King Christian IV by name ('magnanimi Friderici Heroica proles') and closes with a salute to Heinrich Rantzau, who first gave Urania lodging, at his castle of Wandsbek near Hamburg. In the observation journal it stands immediately after Tycho's prose account of why the observations stopped, 'De occasione interruptarum observationum et discessus mei' (TBOO XIII, pp. 101–102).
Occasion
The resumption of observing in exile. Tycho had left Hven on 29 April 1597 and Denmark before midsummer; after a quarter-year at Rostock he accepted Heinrich Rantzau's invitation and moved to Wandsbek in mid-October 1597. On 20 October, at the point in the observation journal where the Wandsbek observations begin, he wrote in first the prose statement of the causes of the interruption and of his departure, and then this elegy as its verse counterpart (TBOO XIII, pp. 101–104; Dreyer 1890, pp. 253–254). The occasion is thus documented, not inferred: the poem is the emotional settlement of accounts entered into the working record at the moment observing began again.
On the addressee
Denmark itself, apostrophised throughout ('Dania quid merui...'); there is no dedicatee in the formal sense. Within the poem King Christian IV is expressly exculpated, and the closing paragraph salutes the host, Heinrich Rantzau (1526–1598), royal Statthalter of the royal portions of Schleswig-Holstein, builder of Wandsbek, and Tycho's protector there from October 1597 to autumn 1598. Manuscript copies were sent to correspondents: Tycho sent one to Joseph Scaliger (Dreyer 1890, p. 255 n. 3, reporting it then in the University Library at Leiden), and he related the same story to Herwart von Hohenburg.
Transmission
Autograph. Tycho entered the elegy in his own hand into the observation journal now Copenhagen, Kongelige Bibliotek, GKS 316 fol. — Dreyer's siglum G, 'Codex Hauniensis Ant. Coll. Reg. 316' (TBOO IX, Varia scripturae, p. 316, s.v. 'Ad elegiam in Daniam'), the volume of the 1596-97 observations — immediately after the prose 'De occasione interruptarum observationum et discessus mei' and immediately before the Wandsbek observations, subscribed 20 October 1597. Dreyer printed this text in situ among the 1597 observations at TBOO XIII (1926), pp. 102–104. A second recension survives in Vienna, cod. Vindob. lat. 10686 (fasc. 49) — Dreyer's siglum V — representing the few corrections Tycho preferred later, when he was collecting his poems, and carrying the appended prose anecdote of Christian IV reading the poem at Haderslev; Dreyer printed that recension among the Carmina at TBOO IX (1927), pp. 208–211, stating expressly that the poem was one Tycho 'inserted among the observations, and we have edited it among them (tom. XIII p. 102 sqq.)', giving in vol. XIII the text as Tycho first had it written and in vol. IX the poet's later corrections (TBOO IX, Annotationes editorum, p. 327). The two recensions differ in a handful of readings (e.g. XIII 'Nostra licet iamnunc gratia muta silet' against IX 'Gratia sit nostro tempore muta licet'; XIII 'ut fertur' against IX 'ut referunt'). Additional witnesses: the copy Tycho sent Scaliger (Leiden), and the copy Rantzau bound into his Calendarium Ranzovianum. TBOO is thus not the first printing (see the printed block).
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (the observation log GKS 316; TBOO XIII)
Printing
printed posthumously — Paris, 1654

not printed in Tycho's lifetime, and not printed by Tycho at all: it has no entry in Nielsen's bibliography of the printed Tycho corpus (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600 / Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen), which records nothing of the kind for the Wandsbek year beyond the Mechanica and its companions. The poem circulated in manuscript (Rantzau had a copy stitched into his Calendarium Ranzovianum, where King Christian IV came upon it at Haderslev). The printings are all posthumous, the earliest cited by Dreyer being Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei... Vita (Paris, 1654), p. 143, 'less correctly' given; the observation-journal text then reached print in the Historia Coelestis, p. 802 (the folio edition of Tycho's observations, i.e. the very manuscript this recension stands in), and again in P. J. Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen, 1668), p. 347, and in Casseburg, Tychonis Brahe relatio de statu suo (Jena, 1730). See Dreyer 1890, p. 254 nn. 1-2.

Ad Martinum Braschium — To Martin Brasch

EpigramprobableExileBRead the text →brahe-t_ad-martinum-braschium

Epigram for the Rostock poet Martin Brasch, written in Tycho's own hand on a wrapper of gold coins sent in thanks for a poem Brasch had addressed to him, and alluding to the philosopher's stone Brasch had promised. Behind it lies a larger correspondence in which Tycho acted as editor of his own praise: he rejected a philosophical poem Brasch offered as unsuited to the imperial court, steered him instead to a didactic poem on the famous astronomers, and supplied the bibliography, directions for its composition, and the first seven verses in his own draft.

IX 208AD MARTINUM BRASCHIUM.

Post carmen Martini Braschii ad Tychonem datum.

Cum hoc carmen per Studiosum quendam mihi notum Poëta ille misisset, et ego per eundem rescribi jussissem, chartulæ. cui aureos nummos gratitudinis ergo involvebam, eisdem literis impositæ, sequens Epigramma mea manu subscripsi.

5HÆC Aganippeâ pro venâ munera venæ Auriferæ, Braschi, consule missa boni. Quando talenta potens Auri lapis ille Sophorum, Quem spondes, dederit plurima, plura feres.

The text entire; the citable locus is the text page.

Full heading
Ad Martinum Braschium
Form
Epigram (this catalogue)
Date
1597 probable

Undated in the text; Tycho's documented contact with Martin Brasch runs from his Rostock stay of 1597 to April 1601 (Norlind 1970, pp. 168, 199, 339; TBOO VIII letters), and TBOO IX prints the epigram at IX 208 immediately before the October 1597 farewell elegy in its chronological sequence.

Correction. The range 1597–1601 spans Tycho's documented contact with Brasch; the epigram belongs to the Rostock stay of 1597 (Dreyer prints it before the October 1597 elegy). The edition's 1573 is a metadata error.

The epigram itself is undated in the manuscript. It is dated by its occasion, which Dreyer states: Brasch wrote the poem it answers when Tycho, having left his native country, came to Rostock in the year 1597 ('cum a. 1597 Rostochium Tycho venisset patria relicta, carmen scripserat »Ad Tychonem Brahe in Germaniam transeuntem«, quod inter chartas Tychonis reperitur; post hoc reperitur epigramma, quod attulimus', TBOO IX, p. 327). Tycho was at Rostock from about midsummer to mid-October 1597, then at Wandsbek; the reply could have been sent from either place, so 1597 (or very early 1598) is the honest bracket. Its position in Dreyer's Carmina, immediately before the Ad Daniam elegia of 20 October 1597 (IX 208-211), agrees with a 1597 date. The edition's year 1573 is impossible: Martin Brasch was born in 1565 (TBOO VIII, Index virorum doctorum, p. 453); it is the same metadata artefact as on the two Ad Daniam elegia records. Nor is the piece a letter: it is a four-line epigram, printed by Dreyer among the Carmina, not among the Epistolae.

Addressee
Martin Brasch (addressee)
Language
Latin
Summary
A four-line Latin epigram in two elegiac couplets (incipit 'Haec Aganippeae pro vena munera venae / Auriferae, Braschi, consule missa boni'), which Tycho wrote in his own hand on the slip of paper in which he wrapped a few gold coins as a thank-offering to the Rostock poet Martin Brasch. The prose rubric that carries it in the manuscript sets out the whole transaction: the poet had sent his poem to Tycho by a student known to him; Tycho ordered a reply to be carried back by the same man, and 'subscribed the following epigram in my own hand' on the little sheet, 'in which I was wrapping some gold coins by way of gratitude', enclosed with the letter. The verses turn on a pun on vena: the gold-bearing vein (the coins) repays the Aganippean vein (Brasch's poetic inspiration, Aganippe being the Muses' spring). They close on an alchemical joke — when that potent Stone of the Sages which you promise ('lapis ille Sophorum, quem spondes') has yielded its many talents of gold, you shall have more.
Occasion
Recoverable, and stated by Dreyer. It is a payment-and-thanks piece. Brasch had written a laudatory poem, 'Ad Tychonem Brahe in Germaniam transeuntem' ('To Tycho Brahe crossing over into Germany'), on Tycho's arrival at Rostock in 1597 after he had left Denmark; that poem survives among Tycho's papers, and the epigram stands immediately after it in the same manuscript (TBOO IX, p. 327). Tycho's answer was a fee: gold coins wrapped in a paper, with these four lines written on the wrapper in his own hand and sent back by the student who had brought the poem. What exactly Brasch had 'promised' (quem spondes) — whether his poem predicted that Tycho's chymistry would achieve the philosophers' stone, or whether Brasch had pledged something of his own — is not explained by Dreyer and is not recoverable from the four lines alone.
On the addressee
Martin Brasch (Martinus Braschius), born 1565, professor of logic at Rostock, died 1601; 'auctor est carminum atque orationum multarum' (TBOO VIII, Index virorum doctorum, p. 453). Tycho calls him 'Poeta Rostochiensis' and, with Taubmann, one of the 'Poetae laureati' who supplied him with verse. He is not a member of the Hven familia and does not appear in Christianson's Biographical Directory; he belongs to the exile years. From 1598 he sent Tycho a series of laudatory poems — heroic, lyric and elegiac — which Tycho collected, criticised and corrected with a view to printing them with his own works (Tycho to Oliger Rosenkrantz, 28 June 1598 and 9 Sept. 1598, TBOO VIII 75 and 110; to Paulus Melissus, 7/17 Feb. 1600, VIII 249). Seven letters between them survive: Tycho to Brasch 19/29 March 1600, 5/15 Sept. 1600, 6/16 Nov. 1600, 4/14 April 1601 (TBOO VIII 290-291, 357-360, 391, 410-413); Brasch to Tycho 8/18 Aug. 1600, 20/30 Sept. 1600, 8/18 March 1601 (VIII 337-339, 379-380, 402).
Transmission
Manuscript, in the Vienna Tycho papers. Dreyer's source lemma is '[E codice Vindobonensi lat. 10686...]' (the printed siglum carries a superscript sub-number), and his marginal folio mark in the text is 9v — i.e. Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. Vind. lat. 10686, fol. 9r-v. That codex is one of the fair copies made for the printers of the never-finished Epistolarum astronomicarum liber secundus and is the manuscript from which Dreyer and Raeder drew most of the letters in TBOO VII (TBOO VII 393-394). The epigram stands there immediately after Brasch's own poem 'Ad Tychonem Brahe in Germaniam transeuntem', which Dreyer saw among the same papers but did not print (it is not Tycho's). First published by J. L. E. Dreyer and J. Raeder, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (Hauniae, 1927), Carmina, p. 208, with the editors' note at p. 327; indexed in TBOO XV, s.v. 'Brasch, Martinus, poeta': 'epigramma Tychonis ad eum IX 208'.
Channel
Manuscript until the Opera omnia (first printed in TBOO IX (this catalogue))
Printing
first printed in the Opera omnia — 1927

Not printed in Tycho's lifetime. It was a private note written on the wrapper of a coin-gift, and Lauritz Nielsen's enumerative bibliography of Tycho's whole printed output (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, the 12 publications and 4 lost prints) contains no such item. Tycho did nevertheless mean it for print: the text was copied into one of the fair-copy manuscripts written out 'nitide in typographorum usum' for the projected Epistolarum astronomicarum liber secundus, in which, as he announced in the 1596 preface to Book I, 'Carmina nonnulla... a nobis interdum animi caussa conscripta' were to be interwoven with the letters (TBOO VI 22; TBOO VII 393-394). That volume was broken off after half an alphabet when Tycho left Hven in 1597, was abandoned by his heirs, and no printed quire of it is known to survive — so the epigram never reached print in his lifetime. Dreyer prints it from the Vienna manuscript and, unlike his practice elsewhere in the Carmina (where he names Resen 1668 for the Urania Titani, Gassendi for the Mechanica epigram, Vingaard's 1572 broadsheet for the Fratri gemello), records no earlier printing. On present evidence the first printing is TBOO IX (Copenhagen 1927), p. 208; that it was never printed earlier is an argument from Dreyer's and Nielsen's silence, not a positive statement by either.

Open questions
  • The exact date and place. Dreyer fixes Brasch's poem to Tycho's arrival at Rostock in 1597 but does not date the epigram itself, which is undated in the codex. Tycho was at Rostock c. midsummer to mid-October 1597 and at Wandsbek from October; the reply could have been written at either. 1597 is probable, not secure.
  • The unnamed 'Studiosus quendam mihi notum' who carried Brasch's poem to Tycho and the coins back to Brasch is not identified by Dreyer.
  • What Brasch 'promised' (lapis ille Sophorum, quem spondes). Whether his poem predicted that Tycho would achieve the philosophers' stone, or whether Brasch was himself making an alchemical promise, is not explained anywhere in TBOO; the joke's target is therefore only half legible.
  • Whether the epigram was printed anywhere before TBOO IX (1927). Dreyer names prior printings for other Carmina but none here, and Nielsen does not record it; neither, however, positively states that TBOO is the first printing. F. R. Friis's 19th-century publications of Tycho material have not been checked for it.
  • The precise manuscript siglum. Dreyer prints 'E codice Vindobonensi lat. 10686' with a superscript sub-number; the marginal folio mark on the text is 9v. The sub-part and the present-day OeNB foliation have not been verified against the codex.
Notes
  • Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 47–48): the Brasch correspondence (TBOO VIII, 290-413) shows Tycho rejecting a philosophical poem of Brasch's as unsuitable for the imperial court, commissioning instead a didactic poem on famous astronomers, and supplying bibliography, directives, and the first seven verses in his own draft — Zeeberg's summary: 'Tycho Brahe er astronomien i egen person' (p. 48).

Elegythe edition'sExilenot yet researchedRead the text →brahe-t_ad-daniam-excusatio

Poem absolving Denmark, King Christian IV, and the Danish people of blame for Tycho's exile, which it lays instead on 'three or four' hostile men driven by envy and greed.

IX 213A 11vAD DANIAM ET DANOS INTEGROS EXCUSATIO.

DANIA sis facilis, non te, mea patria, tango Nilque vices nostræ minus aequas imputo sortis, Nec quod ego immerito peregrinis verser in oris; Chara mihi, velut ante, manes, quia noxia non es, 5Rexque tuus magni Friderici splendida proles, Christianus numero quartus, nihil intulit ultro Damnosi nobis, sed enim clemente favore Usus erat, quem forte dies auxsset in omnes, Ni malesuada suis vetuisset lingua cavistis. 10Vosque alij, Virtutis amor cognataque recti Integritas quibus est cordi, de stemmate claro Innumeri populusque omnis, nihil inde moveri Convenit, exponant quod nostros carmina casus. Vestra etenim non ulla subest hîc culpa; doletis 15A 12rQuin potius, gratum quod sic avellere membrum Tres quatuorve viri invisi potuere, quid atrox Non agit invidia et nummorum insana cupido? Quid non inscitia et vacui censura cerebri? T. B. F.

Dania ad Tychonem Braheum suum alumnum — Denmark to Tycho Brahe, her foster-son

Elegythe edition'sExilenot yet researchedRead the text →brahe-t_dania-ad-tychonem

Poem in which a personified Denmark addresses Tycho, her foster-son, in Bohemia, urging him to bear his lot with courage and predicting that his cause will triumph and his countrymen will be ashamed.

IX 213A 12rDANIA AD TYCHONEM BRAHEUM SUUM ALUMNUM.

SI labor et virtus, meriti si gratia Celsi Pondus habere queant, non te Braheia proles Ora Bohemorum nostro cum lare teneret. Quo recti favor et constantia cessit avita? 5At quia sic non æqua mihique tibique tulêre Fata, vel illorum potius qui fata gubernant Publica, nullus amor doctrinæ, quosque fatigat Livor iners et opes glomerandi sacra cupido, Esto animo forti, velut es: fert omnia Virtus 10Intrepide, nec dura timet, quia nescia frangi. Tandem tempus erit, quo cæcutijsse pudebit Nostrates, quos culpa manet, vel nunc pudet ultro, Dissimulent quamvis taciti cælentque dolorem. Nam magnis errare viris non competit, imo 15Errori facilem nôrunt inducere fucum. IX 214Jura illis, qui jura regunt, sunt ludicra jura, Unde Polos repetens terras Astræa reliquit. Quin tua (crede mihi) tandem bona causa patescens Clara triumphabit nullis obnoxia technis.

Pyronomæ secreta Artis, quæ Terrea versat, Ætheris astriferi viribus æquipara, Huc quoque RUDOLPHI traduxit cura SECUNDI, Hæc alijs pariter dum reprobata forent. 5IX 215Ergo illi ut superus modo se manifestat Olympus, Sic reseret gazas infima Terra suas. Quæ renuere alij, RUDOLPHUS sacra SECUNDUS Huc Clemente manu transtulit VRANIÆ. Gratiaque Astrorum Authori fit summa, quod astra Exilium in terris non tolerare sinit. T. B. fecit.

Epigram in which the poet declares that though mortal and pressed by the mortal condition, in mind he traverses the courses of the stars and the mystic fates of the aetherial pole, lifting his head above the clouds to feast on ambrosia with Jove.

6Transmission and printed witnesses

Tycho never collected his poems, and the texts here reached us by different roads: printed inside his own books, printed separately at his order, printed by others in his lifetime, first printed after his death, or in manuscript until Dreyer and Ræder printed them. The five channels are Zeeberg's account of the transmission as this catalogue partitions it; each record is placed under one channel on the evidence stated beside it, and the records whose channel is not yet established are listed last. Where the printed witness survives as a book, the Typographica entry and the census of its copies are linked; where a print is lost, the Typographica entry that records the loss.

8Threads

Three literary threads that the research record has documented across several texts, each with its member texts in the order of the argument. A thread is a reading, stated once and sourced; the texts themselves are in the register.

The Urania allegory, 1573–1601

The muse Urania runs through Tycho's poetry. In the elegy printed at the close of De nova stella (1573) she appears to Tycho by the stream at Herrevad and gives him the new star as his calling. The foundation stone of 1576 dedicates the house on Hven to her, and the epigram Typographiae commits the work "brought forth by Urania's lofty enterprise" to the press. In the poems printed at Uraniborg in 1584–85 she is an exile who has wandered through lands that failed astronomy and found refuge on Hven: the theme of the epistles to Jacob Ulfeldt and Niels Kaas and of the fragment Si quid agat. In Urania Titani (1594) Tycho lends her name to his sister Sophie; over the observatory door at Benátky her rites, refused elsewhere, pass to Bohemia; and in the late exchange with the Rostock poet Martin Brasch, for whose didactic poem on the famous astronomers Tycho supplied the bibliography, the directions and the opening verses, the identification of Tycho with Urania's art is complete. The reading is Zeeberg's (1993, 2006).

The Denmark quarrel, in verse

Tycho's break with Denmark runs through the exile poems as one thread. The farewell elegy was entered in his observation log at Wandsbek on 20 October 1597, and revised; a copy reached the young king through the carelessness of Heinrich Rantzau's servants, as Tycho's own note records. The epigram written on arriving at Benátky in August 1599 reproaches his homeland and thanks Rudolf II; the Excusatio absolves Denmark and Christian IV and lays the blame on "three or four" hostile men; and Dania ad Tychonem gives Denmark's reply, urging her foster-son to bear his lot with courage. The witness for the quarrel's reception is Kepler's letter of December 1599 in the Epistolarium.

Sophie Brahe and the unfinished second volume

The Epistolae astronomicae of 1596 was the first volume of a planned series. The second was never published: Tycho left Hven in 1597 and the exile press gave its time to the Mechanica. Its contents were largely assembled — the correspondence with Thaddaeus Hagecius on the new star and the comets, and Sophie Brahe's long Danish letter on alchemy and astrology with Tycho's reply. What survives of that plan in this chapter is the prose preface Occasio et argumentum, which was to introduce her letter, the preface for the volume itself with the Muñoz letters appended, and the poem in which Tycho, writing in his sister's name to her betrothed Erik Lange, had already made her Urania: Urania Titani (1594). Dreyer settles the authorship on Tycho's own testimony in a letter to Thomas Craig; Sophie's letters of 1599 and 1600 to her brother are printed in the Opera omnia, tom. XIV.

159950Ad Daniam et Danos integros excusatio1599 the edition'sthe edition's year 1599; transmitted in exemplar A (fols. 11v-12r) within the Dania poem group alongside the Ad Daniam epigramma that Tycho subscribed at Benátky, August 1599.Exile
159951Dania ad Tychonem Braheum suum alumnum1599 the edition'sthe edition's year 1599; the poem presupposes Tycho resident in Bohemia ('Ora Bohemorum') and is transmitted in exemplar A (fol. 12r) with the Dania group beside the epigram subscribed at Benátky, August 1599.Exile
159952Disce puer virtutem1599 probableDated in the text itself: 'Anno 1599 Feb. 28 Vitebergæ'; matches Tycho's documented Wittenberg winter 1598-99 (Dreyer reference map).Exile
159953Medicamentum in usum Imperatoris Rudolfi II1599 probablethe edition's year 1599, consistent with the Bohemian setting (request via the captain of Brandeis; Tycho at Benátky from 1599, Thoren App. 5).Exile
159954Supra januam novi laboratorii in eadem arce Benaticac. 1599 probableThe DSL's own descriptive label uses circa — '(c. 1599)'; a variant of the verses was sent to Kepler in a letter of 9 December 1599 (apparatus note in the file)Exilebenatky
159955Supra januam observatorii in arce Cæsareana Bennaticac. 1599 probableThe DSL's own descriptive label uses circa — '(c. 1599)'; a variant of the verses was sent to Kepler in a letter of 9 December 1599 (apparatus note in the file)Exilebenatky
160056Calculi de obliquitate eclipticæ1600 probableThe text's own heading carries the date '(1600)'; the edition's year 1600; Prague-period contentExile

Dates: the evidence and the corrections

No.TextThe edition's yearDisplayedReason
1Diarium anni 15731572–1573 secureWritten in the autumn of 1572 for the year 1573 (this catalogue).
4Astrologiæ meteorologicæ fragmentumundated (the edition: 1574) unknownDreyer, who prints it after the Oration: 'Quando hoc confectum sit, non constat' (TBOO I 313). The edition's 1574 follows that placement.
8Additiones ad commentationem de eclipsi lunæ anni 15731573after April 1588 probableThe edition files the Additiones under 1573, the year of the eclipse they annotate; the notes themselves were written after April 1588, for insertion into the book (Dreyer, TBOO I, Annotationes).
9Epitaphium Johanni Pratensi1576; printed 1584 secureComposed after Pratensis's death in June 1576, on Tycho's own testimony; printed at Uraniborg in 1584. The edition dates the print.
13Indskrifter fra Uraniborg1576c. 1580–1585 uncertainThe edition's 1576 is the year of the foundation stone; no source dates the nine inscriptions, which survive only in Resen's transcription of 1668.
16Jacobo Ulfeldio1584 secureThe edition's 1585 corrected to 1584: the print carries the date 25 November 1584 (Nielsen 426).
17Typographiæ1584 or later uncertainThe edition's 'c. 1580' predates the press it celebrates: Tycho's printing house was set up in 1584. Transmitted only by Resen (1668), the epigram is undated.
20Si quid agatundated (the edition: c. 1585) unknownDreyer prints the fragment undated ('non apparet, quo pertineat', TBOO IX 328); the Hven years are the only bound.
30Additamenta ad apologeticam responsionem ad Craigum Scotum15891592–1601 uncertainThe edition's 1589 is the year of the Apologia the dossier was to accompany; the connective matter was assembled for a printed edition projected in the 1590s and never made.
32Iudicis est æqui1592 probableThe edition's 1588 is a metadata error; the lawsuit the epigram concerns ran in 1592.
38Observationes geographicae15981598 (the edition) the edition'sThe edition dates the text 1598; the survey it records was made on Hven, not later than 1597.
39Ad Daniam elegia1597 secureThe revised text of the elegy of 20 October 1597; its exact revision date is not documented. The edition's 1573 is a metadata error on the source site.
40Ad Daniam elegia (fra observationsprotokollen)1597 secureTycho's own colophon in the observation log: 20 October 1597, Wandsbek. The edition's 1573 is a metadata error on the source site.
41Ad Martinum Braschium1597 probableThe range 1597–1601 spans Tycho's documented contact with Brasch; the epigram belongs to the Rostock stay of 1597 (Dreyer prints it before the October 1597 elegy). The edition's 1573 is a metadata error.
48Sub pyramide tegumento quodam cooperta1598 probableThe edition's 1597 corrected to 1598 on the text's own evidence.

10Desiderata

What this catalogue does not hold, by class. First, Tycho's writings outside the edition's selection: the three pieces of Dreyer's Carmina the edition omits, the verse Dreyer prints inside the other volumes of the Opera omnia, the printed books and the star catalogue — each with its locus and its home in this portal where it has one. Then the work that remains on the records themselves.

The work that remains on the records

rights Written permission from Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab for the republication of the edition's Danish translations, textual notes and commentary. Until it is given, the pages carry the edition's Latin and link to the translations and the notes at the source.
attribution The translator of the Mechanica's Danish instrument chapters (sections 4–27, 32–33), reproduced by the edition in a pre-1948 orthography; the local copy names no one. The Danish Mechanica of Ræder, Strömgren and Strömgren (Nordisk Astronomisk Tidsskrift, 1948–1955) is the likely source and should be confirmed.
research Full records — summary, occasion, addressee, printing, transmission, references, open questions, grade — for the 28 texts that carry only their identifying fields. The 29 researched records set the standard.
text The Latin of Occasio et argumentum, which the edition prints only in Danish; Dreyer prints it at TBOO IX 324–326 from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686. A transcription from the page images would make the record a Latin–Danish pair.
text Dreyer's text of every work here, from the page imagess of the Opera omnia, as a second witness beside the edition's text — the public-domain fallback should the edition's permission be refused.
apparatus The edition's key to its witness sigla, which the harvest did not capture; sigla are listed per text as they occur, with a meaning only where the note itself gives one.
concordance The entries of the Epistolae astronomicae that could not be joined to an Epistolarium letter on their date alone (listed in §5); each wants a hand join.
concordance The letters of Jerónimo Muñoz appended to the preface for the second volume have no Epistolarium record; the authorship of the letter dated 6 December is to be settled against TBOO VII 395–403.
bridge The Kronborg inscriptions have no site record in Loca; the bridge waits on one.
bridge Horoscopi has no per-item anchors; the three nativities, the almanac preface and the fragment link to the pillar page only.
bridge Persons named on these pages who have no Familia record: Niels Kaas, Jacob Ulfeldt, Hans Frandsen, Lauge Beck, Rudolphus Caukerchius, Jerónimo Muñoz, James VI, the six poets of the Epistolae astronomicae, Tycho's children.
text The verse Dreyer prints inside the other volumes (§10 a) is outside the edition; the pieces inside the letters are read in the Epistolarium, the rest only in the Opera omnia.
text The edition transmits the figures of the 1573 almanac, the nativity charts and the Mechanica's woodcuts as placeholders; the woodcuts are seen in Instrumenta, the rest only in the scans.
